metadata.title: How To Buy Mineral Rights (Get Into This $800B Industry)
metadata.author: Steven Hatcher | Minerals Guy
metadata.shortDescription:
Want to get into mineral rights? Start with Your First Mineral Prospect, my 30-minute, $27 workshop: https://learnminerals.com/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=organic&utm_campaign=how-to-buy-mineral-rights-get&utm_content=description_top

In this video, I explain what mineral rights are and how mineral owners receive royalties when oil and gas is produced. I also discuss where buyers look, how they identify mineral owners, and the main methods used to value mineral rights.

What you'll learn:
- What mineral rights and royalty interests are
- Why mineral ownership can be separated from surface ownership
- How to research mineral ownership and chain of title
- Where mineral development is taking place
- Three mineral valuation methods: cash flow multiples, price per acre, and discounted cash flow

________________________________________________________________________

Own mineral rights? Get a private, no-obligation offer: https://deal.mineralsguy.com/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=organic&utm_campaign=how-to-buy-mineral-rights-get&utm_content=description_footer
Learn the mineral rights business ($27 workshop): https://learnminerals.com/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=organic&utm_campaign=how-to-buy-mineral-rights-get&utm_content=description_footer
Email Steven directly: steven@mineralsguy.com

________________________________________________________________________

About Minerals Guy:

Minerals Guy provides tailored content and resources to oil and gas mineral and royalty owners across the country with the goal of educating and empowering owners to better understand mineral rights as an asset class and the potential value of their minerals and royalties.

Steven Hatcher is the creator of Minerals Guy. He is a professional mineral buyer, an oil and gas attorney and has spent the last decade buying and selling oil and gas properties across the country. He is an expert in oil and gas mineral rights, having worked in the private practice of law, for oil and gas operators, and for mineral and royalty acquisition companies.

________________________________________________________________________

metadata.title: 5 Fundamentals of Buying Mineral Rights
metadata.author: Eckard Enterprises | Oil & Gas Investing
metadata.shortDescription:
Buying mineral rights starts with understanding the fundamentals that drive real economic value.

Troy W. Eckard, Chairman and Founder of Eckard Enterprises, explains the five key fundamentals he considers when evaluating mineral rights. He outlines how proven assets, capable operators, and disciplined capital deployment contribute to consistent cash flow and long-term value.

---

Unlock the power of direct energy investing. Whether you're an accredited investor seeking portfolio diversification, long-term passive income, or smarter tax-advantaged strategies, this channel provides the education and insights you need to invest confidently in U.S. oil and gas assets.


What You’ll Learn on This Channel: Our videos are designed to help investors understand and evaluate opportunities in the energy sector, including:

   - Clear explanations of mineral rights, royalties, and working interest
   - Education on oil and gas investing and the U.S. energy industry
   - Market insights, trends, and economic outlooks
   - Tax-advantaged investment strategies
   - Expert discussions from industry veterans, including Troy W. Eckard



Contact Us: https://lp.eckardenterprises.com/contact-our-team?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=youtube_videos_2026&utm_content=youtube_2026_mineral_rights


    - Book a Call with a Wealth Manager: https://eckardenterprises.com/contact/
    - Download the Mineral Rights Investing E-Book: https://eckardenterprises.com/contact/
    - Learn About Working Interest and Tax Benefits: https://eckardenterprises.com/investi...
    - How Real Estate Investors Use a 1031 Exchange for Mineral Rights: https://eckardenterprises.com/1031-ex...



Download the Eckard Insight App:
- Apple: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/eckard-...
- Google: https://play.google.com/store/apps/de...


About Eckard Enterprises: Eckard Enterprises is a family-owned oil and gas company built on 40 years of experience in the U.S. energy industry. Founded by Troy W. Eckard, the firm focuses exclusively on identifying, acquiring, and developing tangible energy assets for accredited investors seeking long-term, strategic wealth building.


Disclaimer: The material included in this video is intended only for informational purposes and convenient references and is not intended to be complete. This information should not be relied upon for accounting, legal or tax advice or investment recommendations.

The third thing I need to know who's

know who is the who that will actually
deploy the capital to drill the wells on
the mineral rights that I own. Why? If I
get Johnny come lately oil company who
has just enough money to drill a well

normally looking at the analog or
comparison to other like kind of mineral
rights should have four to eight to 12

will Johnny come lately be able to drill

mineral rights might look like if I have
a under capitalized oil and gas operator
as the lei. The fourth thing I want, I
want to be very careful in the mineral
rights what the commodity looks like. I
don't want to be in a dry gas reservoir.
I don't want to be in the Marcelus. I
don't want to be in the Hannesville.
Would I buy mineral rights there?

Probably not. Why would I probably buy
mineral rights? Well, if I can get a
great price underneath a solid operator
and I know it's proven and derisked and
all I'm buying the minite for is

So what I need is I need the the the

being deployed is the situation of the

conducive for an oil and gas company to
put the mineral rights that I'm bought
or I'm buying or I own today at the top
of their list as priority mineral rights
to be harvested because everything I
just described is in place. So what's a
perfect scenario? Simple. I want
producing cash flowing mineral rights
from day one. I want large well-
capitalized oil and gas companies. I do
not want to be in single geological
formations where there's only one zone
to produce. I want to be in oil and gas
revenue uh reservoirs where there's a
balance between the oil and the gas and
the liquids within the geological
formation to make sure I'm not pinned

last but not least, I want to be in
areas that have lots of infrastructure,

roadways, water wells, and other things
that don't really help extract the
amount of oil and gas for my minerals
that will make me a healthy financial
return. I'm Troy Ecker. Thanks for
listening.

metadata.author: Steven Hatcher | Minerals Guy
metadata.shortDescription:
Want to get into mineral rights? Start with Your First Mineral Prospect, my 30-minute, $27 workshop: https://learnminerals.com/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=organic&utm_campaign=can-mineral-rights-make-you-rich&utm_content=description_top

In this video, I explain how mineral rights work and how oil and gas leases can provide mineral owners with royalties when wells produce. I also discuss why some owners choose to sell their minerals for a lump sum, while others hold them and pass them down.

What you'll learn:
- What mineral rights allow an owner to do
- How oil and gas companies lease mineral rights and pay royalties
- What can affect royalty payments and how long they may continue
- Why some mineral owners choose a lump sum instead of ongoing payments

About Minerals Guy:

Minerals Guy provides tailored content and resources to oil and gas mineral and royalty owners across the country with the goal of educating and empowering owners to better understand mineral rights as an asset class and the potential value of their minerals and royalties.

Steven Hatcher is the creator of Minerals Guy. He is a professional mineral buyer, an oil and gas attorney and has spent the last decade buying and selling oil and gas properties across the country. He is an expert in oil and gas mineral rights, having worked in the private practice of law, for oil and gas operators, and for mineral and royalty acquisition companies.

metadata.title: Oil, Gas, Mineral Rights & Royalties: A Guide to Protecting & Transferring Family Wealth | Tim Pawul
metadata.author: The Wealth Transfer Podcast
metadata.shortDescription:
Most people have heard of oil and gas royalties, but very few understand how mineral rights actually work.

In this episode of The Wealth Transfer Podcast, Matt Templeton sits down with Tim Pawul, President of Minerals & Royalties Authority LLC and Partner at Tokenized Energy, to unpack the world of oil and gas minerals, royalties, non-operating interests, and energy investing.

Tim explains why mineral rights are often described as “underground real estate,” how they can produce passive income, and why they have become increasingly institutionalized over the last decade. He also breaks down how investors may be able to use 1031 exchanges, DSTs, royalty trusts, and IDC funds to diversify into oil and gas-related assets.

Whether you inherited mineral rights, are considering selling royalty interests, or are looking for tax-efficient ways to diversify beyond traditional real estate, this conversation offers a practical look inside one of the most specialized asset classes in wealth transfer.


📅 Book a Free Strategy Session with Real Estate Wealth Advisor, Matt Templeton: https://calendly.com/templeton/strate...


Connect with Tim Pawul & Minerals & Royalties Authority:
📧 tim@mineralsauthority.com
📞 (631) 891-8414
https://www.mineralsauthority.com/

Tune in to the Minerals and Royalties Podcast for deeper conversations on mineral rights, royalties, non-op interests, deal trends, and energy investing.

[00:28] Mineral Interests vs. Non-Operated Working Interests

[00:42] How Mineral Interests Can Hedge Against Energy Costs
[00:43] Common Mistakes Families Make When Inheriting Mineral Rights
[00:45] Suspense Funds, Lease Negotiations, and Hidden Value
[00:47] When Selling Mineral Rights May Make Sense

Like, that can be a barrier sometimes. I went through this process with my father. He's liquidating, a business real estate asset. He's retired now, and this is one of his final liquidation events. We looked at tax wrappers, we looked at IDCs, we looked at 1031s, and the way him and my uncle own that asset 50/50 inside an entity With the leverage on it and that structure, it was really difficult to get it into oil and gas. The, the non-op IDC fund actually was the most attractive option that he ultimately went with. But, every situation's gonna be a bit unique, right? And so that's just one thing to point out. Now, whether you're transferring, you know, proceeds from real estate into minerals outside of 1031 or inside 1031, one of the attractive things could be interest rate arbitrages in market cycles. Because you're not using any debt in minerals, when interest rates spike and deal flow locks up, in the real estate space, and you might find yourself struggling to find something that is interesting to 1031 into, you can 1031 into minerals, and you kind of get that, that hedge on, on interest rate, environments. And maybe interest rates go back down and, and real estate properties start to become really interesting, you can 1031 back into real estate or some iterations of that. There's a lot of oil and gas fund managers that specialize in minerals but also specialize in real estate, maybe got into real estate first, went into minerals or vice versa, that just do this daisy chain back and forth, right? Playing the tax arbitrage, playing the market cycle arbitrages. And if you can understand that, it, it's really interesting, right? And I think when you specialize in something… You know, I, I always-- I'm not a real estate guy, but whenever I meet with investors and family offices that really make a lot of their wealth in real estate, it's the niches that they specialize in, right? And it's the same thing in minerals. And if you can get smart enough on both of these and kind of rifle shoot the opportunities in both and play them together in a portfolio, I think, I think you're cooking with gasoline, right? Totally. Yeah, and so this brought me, I mean, and then we do have a number of clients that own their real estate in cash, right? Some people, like to use leverage, some like to, to have it all paid off. And sometimes you have certain assets that are paid off and others that don't, and so you can be more… We can come up with a strategy around that. Sometimes we're, we're trying to th- to get the stuff that's paid off and get it leveraged so that we can get cash out before we do a 1031, but there's always a different strategy. That's why we do planning so Alan, I'm, I'm forgetting what that's called. I wanna call it like a post te- 1031 financing or something, where essentially you're recapping the asset afterwards to get some cash out, right? There you go. So, so there is an option potentially for that even on the… Correct But that brought me to, and the question that I thought of was, so how do you value, especially when you're talking about specific interests, how does the industry value those assets? How would somebody know, like, here's kind of the going rate for an interest, and what causes things to be both more valuable or less valuable? Yeah. So that, that's the million-dollar question. It-- unlike real estate where you have pretty clear comps and you have Zillow and things of that nature, and if you're in a certain zip code and you have certain square footage, certain amount of bed and baths, you know, a pool, what-whatever, you can kind of figure out the dollar per square foot, right? And there might be, you know, my wife just falls in love with this certain house, and we're willing to pay a little bit more. There, there's always that dynamic, but minerals are very different. You know, I think this is one of the things that scares people about getting into oil and gas is just the complexity of understanding it. That's why, you know, I always say as long as you're alongside professionals that know what they're doing, it's a great asset class to get into. Don't, don't close that door just because, oh, it's too complex, you can't understand it. But don't kid yourself, there isn't gonna be a Zillow where you go online and you go, "Oh, th-this is what it's worth." There's the neurology, just like real estate to a certain extent, but there's an understanding of what's going on below the ground, right? This is subsurface oil and gas real estate, as I mentioned. And, you know, there's all sorts of-- th-there's all sorts of variables that go into how much value, your minerals will be worth. You know, you could be in two units side by side, one unit could be worth way more. And why is that? Well, mineral rights are actually Oil and gas molecules trapped in rock below the surface. And in each formation, those, you know, some formations are more porous than others. You know, there's a variety of geologic descriptions, and factors that go into whether it's more economic or less economic to drill and extract that for an oil and gas company, right? And so all those different factors go into it, into determining how much oil and gas you can actually extract out of that, how much it's gonna cost you to do that. And then, you know, if there's faults, if there's certain types of water, you know, un-underground, like there's a variety of things that can make it less attractive. You might have H2S. You know, these are things that you ha- that can be very dangerous if they're, you know, emitted into the air, and so you have to have extra infrastructure cost to like contain that stuff. You know, is there infrastructure in the area to take away the, the gas and the oil? Does that need to be built? That's a, that's a risk that you're waiting on that stuff to be built. Is there water takeaway? So on and so forth. There are so many variables, Matt. Like what, what makes my seat really fun is, you know, I get to see the way everyone skins a cat in this game. And what minerals buying is and minerals underwriting, it's taking imperfect signals and combining them into a thesis to then buy and predict development as it's gonna happen. You know, when you're buying existing production, that's engineering, right? For the most part, you can guess, okay, this is producing 10 barrels a day. It was producing 30 barrels a day two years ago. You can kind of fit the decline curve, and you can statistically kind of figure that out. It's what's gonna happen in the undeveloped location. One, if it's an area that… If it's Class A real estate in Manhattan, you can kinda understand like the underground piece, but then when is it gonna get drilled? You know, time value money That is some-- You don't control when that development happens. You can't call Chevron and be like, "Hey, Chevron, I own a lot of minerals in this unit. Can you tell me when you're gonna drill or can you go drill?" They're gonna be like, "Yeah, get lost," right? You have no influence on that as a mineral owner. And so these mineral funds go and they say, "Well, we tracked the s- the sat- the cellphone signals of frac crews from Schlumberger, and we saw that there was a drilling pad, drilled from satellite imagery three months ago. And there's some, you know, a gravel company that we have intel from that gives gravel for roads that are, you know, going to a drill pad. They just got a contract from Chevron in this area, and they're, you know, blah, blah, blah, blah." And they can put it all together and go, "We think it's gonna get drilled in 24 months." And then they, they underwrite that based on 24-month timing. Sometimes it gets drilled in three months, sometimes it gets drilled in 48 months. They build a portfolio that statistically hones in on their underwriting parameters. And, you know, sometimes, you know, the tailwinds align. You know, prices go up, drilling happens earlier, and you get these phenomenal returns, and you don't, you don't pay for any the development upside, right? It's just timing risk. That's, that's the beautiful thing about the asset class. So Th- t- a long-winded answer of saying it's complicated. You wanna get with the right professionals. You know, if you wanna go down that road of doing a 1031 directly, I can get you with those professionals. If you wanna invest into funds and, and pick a jockey that is gonna build the right portfolio for you, I can help you, you know, get into those funds with the right managers with track record and skin in the game for alignment and all those things. And then, and then from there, it's like for that level of uncertainty or that risk, if you may, there is risk for sure, but risk adjusted to a lot of other things you can do in the market for the returns you're getting it, you know, a lot of us in the space think it's one of the greatest investment products in the world because, you know, as, Carl Brincicki at, at, Haymaker Minerals, he, he just launched a minerals fund to funds concept. I just had him on my podcast. His episode's gonna go live shortly. He's one of the OG guys in the space, and he just said, you know, what other asset class does… do you pay for once, you never pay any costs ever again, and then some of the largest, w- most well-capitalized businesses in the world spend all their time and money and resources making your asset more valuable because it makes their asset more valuable, and you don't pay them anything additional. It… And then you get the benefit of technology innovation and all these things, for free, essentially. So that's what's so cool about it. Time, time is your friend. The longer you own these things, typically good things happen because Who could have thought the shale revolution would come? Who would have thought AI data centers would incr- infinitely increase electricity demand for natural gas? Like, who would have thought these things? And there's gonna be more versions of this. And mineral owners ultimately benefit. They're at the top of the cap stack, and they're gonna benefit from that. So it's, it's a really interesting time for the space, Matt, and it's a lot of fun to be in it. And you know, I always… A, a lot of us that are in it, and we, we might be biased because this is what we do. We know about it, every, every angle of it. We eat it for breakfast, for lunch, for dinner. You know, it's all we think about. But it's just a tremendous asset class, and we feel like everyone should have access to it and have some level of exposure to it. Again, I'll quote Carl in this episode I just did. He said, you know, "At a minimum, you should own some sort of mineral exposure as a hedge on your energy consumption." So the average individual might spend 4,200 bucks a year on gas, right? And, and if you have gas heating, in your home, something like that, you know, do something that… You know, do a 40, $50,000 investment in a public entity or a fund or something to, to where you're offsetting that energy exposure and, and you're getting yield. And, and if you like the asset class, you can do more for the returns 'cause it's great returns. But at a minimum, that hedge on inflation, for, for energy costs is, is just an attractive thing to have in the portfolio, right? You know, that's, it's so funny. My grandmother has some, some mineral interests and, that's every time the payout, the payment, the, you know, the monthly payment goes up, she says that like, "You know, I know gas went up, but don't worry, we've got, we've got it covered." The, you know, the you can just think about, yeah, all, that's a great point. All of your energy consumption could be, like, as that goes up or as you're paying more there, you could easily have offset that by, by owning an interest, And if, and if gas and oil prices go down, you save on the energy cost proportionally. And yeah, your monthly check might go down a little bit, but you're benefiting somewhere else, so it-- you're, you're covered in that, that capacity for sure Now, as people are thinking about ma- you know, from a wealth transfer perspective, you know, there's families that are saying, "I need to organize my stuff," or, "I need to figure out how I'm gonna transfer these things," or often sometimes it's not well planned and all you've got is just fractionalization kind of situations. What are either some mistakes people regularly make when transferring these assets? Or what are the, the warnings that you have for people when it comes to, pres- a- and I-- we think about this from a building, protecting, transferring wealth. What are the warnings and the, mistakes people make? Well, one thing I think a lot of people don't know what they own. So actually, where we were introduced, shout out to Chase Daly, who heads oil and gas at Farmers National. They are the largest private mineral manager in the country. I have a great relationship with Chase, been working with his team for a long time. Like, you just don't know what you own, especially if you, you own a lot of stuff, right? If you're getting checks in the mail, and this is what happens, minerals start to produce and people get checks in the mail. It's like, "Okay, you know, I'm gonna cash the check and this is good." Are the decimal interests correct with the oil and gas company? There's mistakes. I don't think there's malice out there where oil and gas companies like intentionally committing fraud, but you have to understand, there's tens of millions of mineral owners, and your decimal interest in a well could be 0.00000786%. And what if it's supposed to be 0.00000797%? On a well that's producing tens of millions of dollars a year, that, that could be material to you on years and years and years. So if you kind of like have inherited something and it's a, it's a just a hot mess, it's something's been in the family drawer forever and no one's looked at it, I think engaging someone like a Farmers National makes all the sense, 'cause they're gonna go out and figure out what you own n- not only producing, but non-producing. You know, if you own what's called open minerals or unleased minerals, th- there's gonna be companies that approach you, oil and gas companies, that say, "Hey, we wanna lease your minerals and have the right to drill them." Negotiating those lease terms, you need to know what you're doing, you know, so you don't kinda get screwed out of potential upside economics. You wanna make sure that, that you're getting paid correctly. If there's any discrepancies a- and a company doesn't know what to pay you, where to pay it, et cetera, it'll… There'll be, money put in suspense. And you could have… Th- there's so many stories, Matt, of very sophisticated mineral owners that start just digging through and cleaning stuff up and they go, "Hey, we found 10 million in suspense." And then as soon as they, they clean up all the paperwork, boom, it gets released, boom, 10 million bucks. Like it's wild. And that's the job of a mineral manager is to find all that stuff. And so there's a lot of inefficiencies and just not knowing what you, you own and just kinda getting visibility on that, and I think that's money well paid if you're not from the industry to get that full visibility. And then from there, once you understand what you own, you know, I'm, I'm not a- an attorney, but I think if you're trying to do estate planning and figure out how to pass it on, I think you need to speak with someone with that kind of expertise. There's, you know, a lot of different attorneys, w- within Texas, I'm sure you know a lot of them, with oil and gas experience that can, you know, help you out with that. And then separately, if you're looking to monetize them There are a lot of groups who have raised capital, who buy mineral interests, who pride themselves in kind of rolling up their sleeves and buying the hairy deals. So they'll, they'll be able to go and kinda clean stuff up and buy it from you and get everything and pay stat. Like, that's their job. And as long as there's a fair trade to be had and you feel like you're getting the monetary value you think is fair, you know, that, that's kind of-- You can pass on a lot of the heavy lifting to an industry fund that knows what they're doing, has access to all the right attorneys, can do the title, can do all those things to acquire them and, and take those off your plate. And that's-- I, I think as we have more and more generational wealth transfer, you're gonna have more and more people, especially if interest gets smaller, that say, "Nah, I don't wanna really wanna deal with this," right? It, it's either too small or it's too complex or whatever. I'd rather have the cash, and that's fine. It's a great asset class, but if some people just don't wanna deal with it, or one sibling does and one sibling doesn't, like hitting the eject button and getting the cash is just-- it's an option. So I think there's never been more liquidity in the market. There's a lot of buyers, and, you know, that's another thing I'll say. If, if anyone's kinda thinking about exiting, I'd happy, happy to be kind of the gatekeeper at the beginning of those conversations, either point you in the right direction or formally advise for you, because I know, who the right buyers are for certain re- areas, and I can help maximize the, the value of your exit. That's one of the things I do as an advisor, so. That's awesome. As we wrap up, what, obviously I'd love for people to be able to connect with you, listen to your podcast. Tell us where can they find you? W- tell us more about the podcast Sure. Email is tim@mineralsauthority.com. You can go to mineralsauthority.com, is my website, just kind of an overview of what we do and the ability to schedule calls. There's all, all sorts of buttons on there. If you wanna just kinda stay in tune with what's going on in the industry, just look up, Tim Pawul on LinkedIn. I post anywhere from one to four pieces of content a day. Very sp- everything is specific outside of some philanthropic personal stuff that I do, everything is minerals and non-op. It'll be news, it'll be repurposed content, you know, anything you can think about, from different angles I'm posting about, and so I've kind of become the de facto newsletter of the industry, if you may. There's a lot of things, Matt, that aren't innovative. You would think a newsletter and stuff is not innovative in the world of twenty-four/seven news, but in my space, it's, it's quite unique. So a lot of people follow me on LinkedIn for that. And then as you get in my ecosystem, I have a monthly newsletter that kinda consolidates all that. And then for the deeper dive stuff, the Minerals and Royalties podcast. I've been doing it since February of 2020. I'm getting close to 300 episodes. It's a weekly episode with a CEO, a fund manager, just usually someone running a company that has some sort of fingerprint on minerals and non-op. And, we don't really spend the time to spell out the basics. We kinda just jump right in. It, it's really meant for someone who's kind of interested in, in diving deep, and it's deal trends and deal activity and financings and, everything in between. So I, I have a blast doing that. And, you know, I, I guess I always… I spend 90% of my time in private meetings and calls, so I would love to… Don't, don't be bashful. Reach out to the email, tim@mineralsauthority.com. Love to get to know you. What is your personal situation around minerals and non-op, what you're looking to do, and whether I can help you directly or I can introduce you to the right people, I'd love to do that. And so, I, I welcome anyone to reach out directly, and I, I look forward to building a relationship That's awesome. Well, this has been highly valuable. I've thoroughly enjoyed it. I'm ready to go put some money in minerals. I'm pumped about this. But also I can see how this would be super valuable for, for various families and, and people kind of trying to get their fingers and arms around what they've got or what they want, might wanna use their money for. So thank you again, Tim. I really appreciate it. No, Matt, thanks for having me on. I've really enjoyed, getting to know you, and I, I know we're gonna do a lot of reciprocal business and intros over the years, so I look forward to that Thanks, Tim.

metadata.shortDescription:
Own mineral rights? Get a private, no-obligation offer on your minerals: https://deal.mineralsguy.com/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=organic&utm_campaign=thinking-about-selling-mineral-rights-reasons&utm_content=description_top

In this video, I discuss common reasons people choose to sell oil and gas mineral and royalty interests, including real estate, business investments, and life events. I explain how selling shifts price and production-volume risk to the buyer, and why an owner may choose to sell only part of their minerals.

What you'll learn:
- Reasons owners sell minerals to buy or improve real estate
- How mineral sales can fund a core business or a small business
- Life events that may lead owners to sell, including college costs, weddings, retirement, and estate planning
- The opportunity costs of holding or selling minerals
- How selling a portion of your minerals may be an option

________________________________________________________________________

Want to get into the mineral rights business? Start with my 30-minute, $27 workshop: https://learnminerals.com/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=organic&utm_campaign=thinking-about-selling-mineral-rights-reasons&utm_content=description_footer
Get a private, no-obligation offer on your minerals: https://deal.mineralsguy.com/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=organic&utm_campaign=thinking-about-selling-mineral-rights-reasons&utm_content=description_footer
Email Steven directly: steven@mineralsguy.com

________________________________________________________________________

About Minerals Guy:

Minerals Guy provides tailored content and resources to oil and gas mineral and royalty owners across the country with the goal of educating and empowering owners to better understand mineral rights as an asset class and the potential value of their minerals and royalties.

Steven Hatcher is the creator of Minerals Guy. He is a professional mineral buyer, an oil and gas attorney and has spent the last decade buying and selling oil and gas properties across the country. He is an expert in oil and gas mineral rights, having worked in the private practice of law, for oil and gas operators, and for mineral and royalty acquisition companies.

metadata.shortDescription:
Oil prices grab the headlines, but the stories that shape what your minerals are worth over the next decade usually sit a layer deeper. metadata.title: MRP 335:  Mineral Rights News June 2026
metadata.author: Matt Sands
metadata.shortDescription:
If you've filled up your gas tank lately, you already know something big is happening in energy markets — and it doesn't look like it's going away anytime soon. The ongoing conflict in the Middle East has shut down roughly 14% of the world's oil supply through the Strait of Hormuz, sending oil and gas prices on a roller coaster ride that has the Federal Reserve worried about inflation, analysts predicting $3+ gas prices through the end of the decade, and even major OPEC members quietly making moves to protect their own interests. For mineral and royalty owners, higher oil prices are a double edged sword. While it can mean stronger royalty checks in the short term, higher gas prices and the trickle down effect into higher prices for just about everything can offset those gains. In this month's news episode, Justin and I break down what's actually happening, cut through the noise, and talk through what it all means for you as a mineral owner.
 

As always, links to the articles discussed can be found in the show notes at mineralrightspodcast.com (https://mineralrightspodcast.com/mrp-335-mineral-rights-news-june-2026/) .

metadata.shortDescription:
In this month's news episode, we break down the energy market fallout from the U.S.-Iran conflict and what it actually means for oil prices (and your royalty checks) for the forseeable future. As compared to the start of the conflict, recent infrastructure damage has fundamentally changed the price recovery timeline. We also review how global strategic petroleum reserves are being tapped as a stopgap measure, which specific facilities were hit and why it matters, and why U.S. natural gas prices have so far been shielded from the chaos overseas. On the home front, we also cover a brewing political battle in Colorado that could directly affect mineral and royalty owners in the state, and close with a look at the rig count and what to expect from drilling activity in the months ahead.
 

As always, links to the articles discussed in this episode can be found in the show notes at mineralrightspodcast.com (https://mineralrightspodcast.com/mrp-327-mineral-rights-news-april-2026/) .

metadata.title: MRP 314: Organize Your Mineral Legacy Before It's Too Late
metadata.author: Matt Sands
metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode, we tackle one of the most overlooked aspects of mineral ownership: organization and communication with your heirs. Whether you have a small mineral interest or manage a complex portfolio across multiple states, proper organization isn't just about neat filing—it's about preserving your family's financial future and preventing costly mistakes after you're gone. We explore practical systems for documenting your mineral assets, strategies for having productive conversations with family members about your holdings, and critical warning signs that indicate your estate plan needs attention. From simple spreadsheet templates to comprehensive documentation strategies, this episode provides a roadmap for ensuring your mineral legacy doesn't become a burden of confusion and lost value for the next generation.
 

As always, links to the resources mentioned in this episode can be found in the show notes at mineralrightspodcast.com (https://mineralrightspodcast.com/mrp-314-organize-your-mineral-legacy-before-its-too-late/) .

In this month's news episode, we break down four major developments shaking up global energy markets in May 2026. From the UAE's sudden departure from OPEC to a widening gap between paper and physical oil prices, the episode covers what these fast-moving events mean for royalty owners who are trying to make sense of their income outlook. We also discuss the Trump administration's meeting with major oil executives, a temporary waiver of the century-old Jones Act, and what the latest rig count data tells us about where the industry is actually headed.
 

As always, links to the articles coverd in this episode can be found in the show notes at mineralrightspodcast.com (https://mineralrightspodcast.com/mrp-331-mineral-rights-news-may-2026/) .

metadata.shortDescription:
https://mineralrightspodcast.com/A ballot fight in Erie, Colorado could unwind a $35 million mineral deal, an Arkansas court just handed royalty owners a win on post-production deductions, and oil prices are once again bouncing around based on whatever the headlines say about Iran that day. In this month's news episode, we break down what's really happening in Erie and why the outcome may matter less than residents think, then we unpack a ruling that reinforces one of the most important lessons in mineral ownership — your lease language rules everything. We'll also look at what a small but steady rise in the rig count tells us about where operators think prices are headed, and why you shouldn't put too much stock in President Trump's saber rattling about oil company price gouging. If you own minerals or royalties, this is your monthly download on what's changing and what it means for your bottom line.
 

As always, links to the articles discussed can be found at mineralrightspodcast.com (https://mineralrightspodcast.com/mrp-345-mineral-rights-news-august-2026/) .

In this month's news episode, we examine the latest developments affecting mineral rights owners as 2025 draws to a close. The discussion centers on how major geopolitical events and infrastructure developments are shaping energy markets heading into 2026. Natural gas continues its strong performance driven by surging demand from data centers and LNG exports, while oil prices face downward pressure from increased global supply and potential peace agreements that could bring Russian crude back to international markets. The episode provides you with context for understanding how these macro trends translate into production decisions and royalty payments in the months ahead. As always, we wrap up with an analysis of the latest rig count numbers.
 

Links to the articles and resources mentioned in this episode can be found in the show notes at mineralrightspodcast.com (https://mineralrightspodcast.com/mrp-312-mineral-rights-news-december-2025/) .

metadata.title: MRP 334:  Finally Know What You Own: Use AI to Turn Your Old Deeds Into a Complete Mineral Rights...
metadata.author: Matt Sands
metadata.shortDescription:
Most mineral owners are sitting on tools that could save them hours of time, catch payment errors they'd never find on their own, and make them far more informed at every step of owning minerals and royalties — and they don't even know it. In this episode, we cover easy, free things you can do right now using tools like ChatGPT and Claude to streamline your mineral management. We also pull back the curtain on the more advanced ways the industry is already using AI to streamline title work, track drilling activity, and audit royalty payments. The key theme running through all of it: AI is an amplifier, not a replacement. The more you understand about your minerals, the more you can get out of these tools.
 

Get my free AI Prompt Guide for Mineral Owners to turn a pile of old deeds into a clean, organized mineral rights inventory (https://unique-motivator-6128.kit.com/ai-prompt)  — even if you have no technical background and no idea where to start.
 

As always, the links to the resources mentioned in this episode can be found in the show notes at mineralrightspodcast.com (https://mineralrightspodcast.com/mrp-334-finally-know-what-you-own-use-ai-to-turn-your-old-deeds-into-a-complete-mineral-rights-inventory/) .

metadata.author: Matt Sands
metadata.shortDescription:
Thanks to Helen, Linda, Cheryll, Melissa, Greg, and James for emailing us with your questions this month! In this episode, we cover a wide range of situations. From how many continuing education hours the Mineral Management Basics (https://mineralrights.teachable.com/p/mineral-rights-basics)  online course earns toward NARO certification, what a newly drilled gas well means for a lease nearing the end of its primary term, what to consider when an oil & gas company wants to buy part of you land (this one led to Episode 337 (https://mineralrightspodcast.com/mrp-337-what-to-do-when-an-oil-company-wants-to-buy-your-land/) ). We also hear from a listener who is both a landman and a mineral owner and is trying to recover royalties from a former mentor, to how to calculate interest in a Texas allocation well when the operator won't share title, how to know whether your attorney is acting appropriately and how to size up a landman's ethics. Finally, we discuss where the money goes when you never signed a lease and you own minerals in Louisiana. 
 

As always, links to the resources mentioned in this episode can be found in the show notes at mineralrightspodcast.com (https://mineralrightspodcast.com/mrp-358-listener-questions-november-2026/) .

metadata.title: MRP 357: Helium Shortage and the Opportunity for Mineral Owners with CEO, Tim Rynott
metadata.author: Matt Sands
metadata.shortDescription:
Most of us think of helium as the gas that makes balloons float and voices squeak. But it's also essential for making computer chips, running MRI machines, and launching rockets, and the supply behind all of that is far more fragile than most people realize. A few outages can cut off a big share of the world's helium, and prices have jumped several times over in just a few years. For mineral and royalty owners, that raises a practical question: could helium be sitting under your property, and what should you do if a company comes knocking?
 

As always, links to the resources mentioned in this episode can be found in the show notes at mineralrightspodcast.com (https://mineralrightspodcast.com/helium-shortage-opportunity-tim-rynott/) .

metadata.title: MRP 288:  Our Favorite Tools for Managing Your Minerals in 2025
metadata.author: Matt Sands
metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode, we share our favorite tools and resources for managing mineral rights and royalties effectively. As we have discussed in the past, there are four key phases to getting a handle on your minerals: knowing what you own, understanding different types of oil and gas interests, locating your property and researching activity, and determining value. Mineral and royalty management is a step-by-step journey where different tools become relevant at different times so we talk about the essential tools that we recommend for each step in your mineral management journey.
 

Be sure to bookmark the show notes for this episode which you can find at mineralrightspodcast.com (https://mineralrightspodcast.com/mrp-288-our-favorite-tools-for-managing-your-minerals-in-2025/) .

In this episode of the Mineral Rights Podcast, we provide a comprehensive checklist for mineral owners on handling division orders. From what division orders are, how to verify your decimal interest is correct, when to get professional help, and best practices for documentation. This essential guide helps ensure you get paid correctly from the start so you can protect your interests when a new well begins producing.
 

As always, the resources mentioned in this episode can be found in the show notes at mineralrightspodcast.com (https://mineralrightspodcast.com/mrp-285-the-mineral-owners-guide-to-division-orders) .

metadata.title: Working Interest vs Royalty Interest in Oil & Gas - Which is Better for You?
metadata.author: Tracy Lenz
metadata.shortDescription:
If you've heard of an oil and gas "working interest" you might be wondering what it is. Is it a good thing or bad? What's the difference from a royalty interest? Do I recommend investing in working interest? 

https://www.PecanEstimate.com 

~~~~~~~~~~~~
CONTACT ME:

tracy@pecantreeog.com 
512-578-9160

~~~~~~~~~~~~ 
The Mineral Rights Forum (I answer questions here often) 
https://www.mineralrightsforum.com/ 

~~~~~~~~~~~~ 
PECAN TREE OIL & GAS: Pecan Tree was founded by Tracy Lenz as Limited Liability Company in January 2020 (registered Texas Engineering Firm F-21124) to bridge the gap between mineral owners and the confusing, high-dollar world that is oil and gas. After being on the operator side for over a decade, Tracy witnessed firsthand how mineral owners rarely can afford the same data, experts, or software to be on a level playing field with the operators and buyers, yet have MORE at stake when deciding what to do with their minerals. Pecan Tree’s focus and efficiency make these resources available without a hidden agenda. We don’t buy minerals, we don’t work with billion dollar companies, and we run our shop 100% debt free. This flexibility lets us be innovative with technology, maintain the highest of standards (work quality, customer service, and ethics), and tailor pricing and scope to each client’s specific needs. 

~~~~~~~~~~~~~ 
ABOUT TRACY: 
- Licensed Professional Engineer in the State of Texas, PE# 132654 
- Certified Mineral Appraiser by the International Institute of Mineral Appraisers (IIMA), #2020-06 
- Master of Science in Petroleum Engineering from the University of Southern California 
- Bachelor of Science in Petroleum Engineering from the University of Texas at Austin 
- Experience with oil & gas minerals in Texas, Oklahoma, New Mexico, Louisiana, North Dakota, Utah, Colorado, and Kansas. 

http://www.pecantreeog.com 
tracy@pecantreeog.com

metadata.title: MRP 2: What’s the Difference Between Minerals and Royalties?
metadata.author: Matt Sands
metadata.shortDescription:
In this Episode, we talk about the different forms of ownership as it relates to mineral rights and the difference between minerals and royalties.  We also talk about ways that ownership is conveyed and the sometimes ignored Non-Participating Royalty Interest and an example of how you could use it.

metadata.title: Fixed & Floating Non-Participating Royalty Interests Issues in Texas & Ohio
metadata.author: Oliva Gibbs
metadata.shortDescription:
Join Oliva Gibbs’ team members Margaret Chavez, Ally McCluskey, and Josh Peterson as they compare Texas and Ohio case law surrounding a heavily litigated topic in oil and gas: the fixed v. floating non-participating royalty interest (NPRI).

The program expands on the difference between mineral and royalty interests, as well as fixed versus floating NPRIs. Also covered is the notable Texas case Van Dyke v. Navigator Group and its subsequent cases. Additionally, the program examines Ohio cases like Moore Family Trust and Crum vs. Mooney.

00:40 Overview
02:03 Fixed vs. Floating NPRIs
03:18 Pre-Van Dyke Rules in Texas: Estate Misconception Theory
09:29 Van Dyke v. Navigator Group
16:14 Texas Cases Following Van Dyke v. Navigator Group
26:25 Ohio Case Law: 
41:04 Conclusion

metadata.title: MRP 263:  What You Should Know About Fixed vs Floating NPRIs
metadata.author: Matt Sands
metadata.shortDescription:
When you grant a portion of your royalty right to someone without granting any of the other rights, you are granting what is called a Non-Participating Royalty Interest (NPRI). It does not "participate" in the ability to receive bonus payment or delay rentals, or the executive rights. A Non-Participating Royalty Interest or NPRI allows the owner to receive a portion of the royalty payments from any oil and gas that is sold but does not give them the right to lease the associated mineral rights. In this episode, we dive into the world of NPRI's and the difference between "floating" and "fixed" NPRI's and what you need to know if you own an NPRI or if you own mineral rights that are burdened by an NPRI.
 

As always, links to the resources mentioned in this episode can be found in the show notes at mineralrightspodcast.com (https://mineralrightspodcast.com/mrp-263-what-you-should-know-about-fixed-vs-floating-npris/) .

metadata.title: MRP 3: How to Calculate your Net Revenue Interest in 3 Simple Steps
metadata.author: Matt Sands
metadata.shortDescription:
In this Episode, we show you how to calculate your Net Revenue Interest (NRI) in a well in 3 simple steps.  We also cover how to estimate your royalty check amount based on this and other readily available information.

3 Steps to Calculate Net Revenue Interest (in any order):

What you will need to get started is an understanding of how many Net Mineral Acres (NMA) you own,
The size of the Drilling Spacing Unit (DSU) where the well is located, and
The agreed royalty rate from your oil and gas lease.
Usually, these 3 items are fairly easy to find and we cover how to find them if you don’t already know.

Side Note:  In this example, we assume that the royalty is not burdened by a Non-Participating Royalty Interest (NPRI).  Identifying if there is a NPRI usually requires performing a title search to understand the history and if anything was carved out.  For the purposes of this article, we will assume that the royalty is not burdened by a NPRI.  If your family has owned the minerals back through time then this situation likely would not apply to you anyway.

If you aren’t familiar with NPRI’s, then listen to Episode 2 where we cover briefly the definition of an NPRI and how they are created.

metadata.title: What's the difference? Gross vs. Net Mineral Acres
metadata.author: Tracy Lenz
metadata.shortDescription:
How many "net" mineral acres someone owns is a common point of confusion. What's the difference between gross and net acreage? How does the legal description of the acreage correspond to what I own, and why wouldn't it be the same? 

https://www.PecanEstimate.com 

~~~~~~~~~~~~
CONTACT ME:
tracy@pecantreeog.com 

~~~~~~~~~~~~ 
The Mineral Rights Forum (I answer questions here often) 
https://www.mineralrightsforum.com/ 

~~~~~~~~~~~~ 
PECAN TREE OIL & GAS: Pecan Tree was founded by Tracy Lenz as Limited Liability Company in January 2020 (registered Texas Engineering Firm F-21124) to bridge the gap between mineral owners and the confusing, high-dollar world that is oil and gas. After being on the operator side for over a decade, Tracy witnessed firsthand how mineral owners rarely can afford the same data, experts, or software to be on a level playing field with the operators and buyers, yet have MORE at stake when deciding what to do with their minerals. Pecan Tree’s focus and efficiency make these resources available without a hidden agenda. We don’t buy minerals, we don’t work with billion dollar companies, and we run our shop 100% debt free. This flexibility lets us be innovative with technology, maintain the highest of standards (work quality, customer service, and ethics), and tailor pricing and scope to each client’s specific needs. 

~~~~~~~~~~~~~ 
ABOUT TRACY: 
- Licensed Professional Engineer in the State of Texas, PE# 132654 
- Certified Mineral Appraiser by the International Institute of Mineral Appraisers (IIMA), #2020-06 
- Master of Science in Petroleum Engineering from the University of Southern California 
- Bachelor of Science in Petroleum Engineering from the University of Texas at Austin 
- Experience with oil & gas minerals in Texas, Oklahoma, New Mexico, Louisiana, Gulf of Mexico, North Dakota, Utah, Colorado, and Kansas. 

http://www.pecantreeog.com 
tracy@pecantreeog.com

The Enverus Subsurface Studio's Well spacing calculator is a utility to compute distances between and among wellbores. Users can input parent and child well candidates plus date information to use in this investigation. This workflow will walk users through the data set up, results & charts, plus theory behind the tool, examples and tips.

segments.text: the well spacing calculator is launched
by selecting the calculate well spacing
option under the engineering item on
transform's main menu bar along the top
of the application
the wall spacing calculator is a utility
to compute distances between and among
wellbores
these distances are three-dimensional in
that full x y z coordinates along
wellbores are used first a few critical
definitions
we define a child wellbore
as the source well to which distances
are referenced and assigned
a parent wellbore to a child wellbore is
one which is closest to a particular
location along the child wellbore
a child well may have more than one
parent well especially if the child well
is deviated or horizontal
for example the trajectory of a
horizontal well which may well be over
ten thousand feet long may pass close to
several vertical parent wells
user controls on these distance
calculations as a as will be discussed
in the well spacing setup video
permit the following
the distance calculations to be made
over the entire world bore or confined
to a wellbore zone for example we only
want those distances over the horizontal
lateral length
in either of these options a specified
number of sample points are defined over
the portion of the wellbore of interest
when looking for the nearest parent well
at any sample point the search may be
either spherical or it may be
cylindrical where we limit the vertical
search distance maximum distances are
used to filter candidate parent wells
candidate parent wells may be based on
either current spacing or filtered to
spacings that occurred at specific time
intervals relative to some reference
date in the child wellbore
typically reference dates include spud
date completion date first production
date and so forth
distances may also be filtered to the
projection angle from the sample point
in the cha wellbore to the sample points
in the parent well
examples of the utility of this option
are given in the usage tips and examples
video
results from the distance calculations
may be saved as either well logs or as
well bore scalars
there are four tabs within the
calculator user interface the first is
the well spacing setup which provides
wellbore selection for child wells
selection for candidate parent wells
and distance date and angle filtering
the second tab is the spacing results
tab which provides a table with the
spacing solutions namely the spacing
distance scalers other useful scalers
and the ability to view the distances
along sample points in log view
the third is the results map which
provides a pseudo base map with options
to display distance lines from child
apparent wellbores and to display
distance scalars as bubble maps
slider bars provide the means to filter
distance and scalar values and to filter
along date lines
the fourth provides charts such as
histograms and cross plot options for
investigating the distributions and
relationships of the distance scalers
the well spacing setup tab is where you
specify the weld bores for which you
want distances calculated
the left table which is titled select
child wells is where this is done
the right table is for specifying the
candidate parent wellbores
all candidate parents are investigated
as to which may be closest to the child
wellbores the term closest
is dependent on distance maxima date
dependencies and projection angles
the right side panel is where this
parameterization is defined
the tables in this panel are well bore
tables with the standard toolbar and
right mouse click options
well and wellbore lists may be selected
using the combo box widget
this is particularly useful if well and
wellbore lists have been constructed
using other utilities such as well
targeting and decline curve analysis
all columns are sortable including
multiple sorting
columns may also be hidden or made
visible to customize what you view
the radio buttons along the base of the
tables permit you to compute distances
over the entire wellbore or to limit the
calculations to defined wellbore zones
this is particularly useful for deviated
and horizontal wellbores
child and candidate parent wellbores may
be selected or deselected using the
toolbar icons the plus to select all and
the minus to deselect all or the right
mouse options for selecting or
deselecting highlighted rows
wellbores in the currently specified
well or well-born list that do not have
the specified wellbore zone are
annotated in the select column with a
blue dot these are not selectable
now let's look at the parameters
available for controlling distance
calculations and candidate wellbore
pairings for child apparent

metadata.title: Horizontal Drilling Method
metadata.author: Expand Energy
metadata.shortDescription: After a well-site has been carefully prepared to meet environmental health and safety standards, drilling can begin. In this video, we walk you through Expand Energy's process for horizontal drilling in natural gas operations.

segments.text: After the well site has been carefully
prepared to meet environmental health
and safety standards, drilling can
begin.
This is an intricate operation requiring
a well-planned infrastructure.
A variety of processes and expert
well-trained specialists are used to
bring natural gas to the surface.
Expand works with these experts during
every aspect of the project while
strictly adhering to all individual
state regulations.
During the drilling process, the rig
typically is in constant operation 24
hours a day, 7 days a week for
approximately 21 to 28 days.
As an added precaution, in some areas,
a protective mat covers 2/3 of the pad
site.
Utilizing heavy-duty industrial strength
drill bits, a typical well is drilled in
several stages.
Starting with a large diameter drill bit
and then successively smaller drill bits
as the drilling is advanced.
After drilling each portion of the well,
nested steel protective casing is
cemented into place. This will protect
ground water and maintain the integrity
of the well.
Initially and prior to moving in the
drilling rig, a large diameter hole is
drilled for the first 90 to 110 ft.
Conductor casing is then cemented into
place, stabilizing the ground around the
drilling rig and wellhead, and isolating
the well from most private water wells.
Freshwater zones extend several hundred
feet underground.
The freshwater zone consists of porous
sandstone and rock strata containing
water within the pore space of the rock.
Expand typically utilizes air or
freshwater drilling fluids until the
hole is advanced below the base of the
freshwater zone.
This provides added protection to the
freshwater zone.
Air or freshwater is used to lift the
rock cuttings out of the hole into steel
bins.
The rock cuttings are then disposed of
within state guidelines and permits.
After reaching the base of freshwater,
the drilling equipment is retracted to
the surface
and stored for the second stage of
drilling.
To protect the integrity of the hole and
to protect the surrounding deep
freshwater zone, typically a second
layer of steel casing called surface
casing is installed and cemented inside
the newly drilled hole and conductor
casing.
Cement is pumped down through the
surface casing and up along the sides of
the well to provide a proper seal.
This isolates the well from the deepest
of private or municipal water wells.
A blowout preventer BOP system is then
installed on the wellhead and consists
of multiple pressure control components
designed to safely contain wellbore
pressure.
BOPs are function tested and pressure
tested at regular intervals in
accordance with regulatory standards and
company well control policies.
After each layer of casing is installed,
the well is pressure tested to ensure
its integrity for continued drilling.
Next, a smaller drilling assembly is
passed down through the surface casing.
At the bottom of the casing, the bit
drills through the float equipment and
cement, continuing its journey to the
natural gas target area approximately 6
to 15,000 ft below the surface.
The drilling method employed below the
surface casing uses drilling mud, which
is a non-hazardous mixture based on
bentonite clay or synthetic thickeners.
In addition to lifting the rock cuttings
out of the hole, drilling mud also helps
to stabilize the hole, cool the drill
bit, and control downhole pressure.
A few hundred feet above the target
shale, the drilling assembly comes to a
stop.
The drill string is retracted to the
surface to adjust the drilling assembly,
allowing the bit to be steered from a
vertical orientation to horizontal.
This change in trajectory can be
accomplished using either a rotary
steerable system, RSS,
or a downhole motor assembly with an
adjustable bend.
The remainder of the well is drilled in
this horizontal plane while in contact
with the gas-producing shale.
Drilling continues horizontally through
the shale at lengths up to 28,000 ft
from the point where it entered the
formation.
Once drilling is completed, the drill
string is retracted to the surface. Then
a smaller diameter casing called
production casing is installed
throughout the total length of the well.
The production casing is cemented and
secured in place by pumping cement down
through the end of the casing.
The cement creates a seal to ensure
zonal isolation and long-term well
integrity.
A cross-section of the well below
surface reveals several protective
layers.
Cement, conductor casing, cement,
surface casing, cement, production
casing, and then production tubing,
through which the produced gas and water
will flow.
Seven layers of protection.
Horizontal drilling offers many
advantages when compared to vertical
drilling.
Since horizontal wells contact more of
the gas-producing shale, fewer wells are
needed to optimally develop a gas field.
Multiple wells can be drilled from the
same pad sites. For example,
development of a 1,280
acre tract of land using conventional
vertical drilling techniques could
require as many as 32 vertical wells,
with each having its own pad site.
However, one multi-well pad site with
horizontal wells can effectively recover
the same natural gas reserves from the
acre tract of land while reducing the
overall surface disturbance by 90%.

metadata.title: What Landmen Actually Do (No One Explains This)
metadata.author: Steven Hatcher | Minerals Guy
metadata.shortDescription:
Most people hear “landman” and think it’s just knocking on doors and signing leases.

That’s surface level.

What landmen actually do is build the legal foundation for every oil & gas well that ever gets drilled.

Before a company can put a rig on location, someone has to:
• Figure out exactly who owns the mineral rights
• Trace the chain of title through decades (sometimes 100+ years) of deeds
• Identify title defects
• Cure those defects so no one gets skipped or underpaid

If they get it wrong?
The operator could be committing trespass.
Or paying the wrong party millions in royalties.

When I started my career working with upstream operators, the landmen would send us banker boxes full of title documents. Our job as attorneys was to confirm ownership and issue drilling and division order title opinions so the company knew two things:
They had the right to drill.
They knew exactly who to pay.

This isn’t glamorous work.
It’s detailed. It’s technical. It’s high-stakes.

But without it, nothing in oil & gas moves forward.

If you’re curious, resourceful, and willing to dig through courthouse records while everyone else scrolls TikTok… this might be the business for you.

#LandmanLife #MineralRights #OilAndGasIndustry #EnergyBusiness #SubsurfaceRealEstate #OilAndGasLaw #TitleResearch #RoyaltyIncome #EnergyInvesting #LearnMinerals

metadata.title: Who Owns the Minerals Under Your Louisiana Land? A Landman Explains | RE: Real Estate Podcast
metadata.author: RE: REAL ESTATE PODCAST
metadata.shortDescription:
Who Owns the Minerals Under Your Louisiana Land? A Landman Explains | RE: Real Estate Podcast

Episode Number
102
Content Type
Interview
Primary Goal
Know whether you likely own the minerals under a Louisiana property and when mineral rights should factor into a purchase, sale or inheritance.
Keywords
louisiana mineral rights, mineral servitude, 10-year prescription, landman, surface rights vs mineral rights, oil and gas lease, royalty interest, working interest, overriding royalty, usufruct, inherited land louisiana, undivided interest, smackover lithium, south louisiana real estate, houma thibodaux
Summary
Lafayette landman Chris McGuirt joins Ben and Clint to untangle Louisiana mineral rights for buyers, sellers and heirs. He explains how landmen trace title back to the original patent, how the 10-year prescription rule works, and how royalty, working and override interests split the money. The conversation also covers inherited land, usufruct, subdivisions, unleased owners and the open questions around lithium in the Smackover.
Key Topics
•  What a landman does and how mineral title is traced back to patent
•  Louisiana's 10-year prescription rule and how production pauses the clock
•  Royalty vs working interest vs overriding royalty, using the 25/75 split
•  Inherited land: wills, intestate succession, usufruct and the sell or keep decision
•  Trusts, LLCs, partitions and reserving minerals undivided
•  Undivided interests with dozens of heirs and how escrow keeps a sale moving
•  Why minerals rarely matter when buying a house in a subdivision
•  Unleased mineral owners, lithium in the Smackover and the win-win negotiation

Title Options
•  Louisiana Mineral Rights: What Buyers, Sellers & Heirs Need to Know | RE: Real Estate Podcast
•  Surface vs Mineral Rights in South Louisiana: A Landman's View | RE: Real Estate Podcast
•  Do You Own Your Minerals? Louisiana's 10-Year Rule Explained | RE: Real Estate Podcast
Sound Bites
“It's just a stopwatch that pauses the ownership of the minerals for a period of time.”
“There is absolutely no downside to reserving the minerals.”
“Nobody's gonna ask somebody to tear down their house so we can drill an oil and gas well.”
“There's no form of energy that doesn't inconvenience somebody at some level.”
“Their job is to make sure that it's a win-win for everybody.”

So, southern Arkansas, North Louisiana, this lithium uh is is just going to it's it's a game changer because it hasn't been lit litigated to my knowledge at this point exactly how how you handle lithium. So, lithium is a is is a product that comes out of the ground, yes, but it's not by definition an oil or gas. Um and so, does at least cover it? Well, is it a hydrocarbon? Yes. Okay. Is that going to be covered? And um you know there could be a whole different process for extracting lithium um than oil and gas and and and and we know that the highest concentrate of that is in a formation called smackover which is north Louisiana and south Arkansas. metadata.shortDescription:
Own mineral rights? Get a private, no-obligation offer on your minerals: https://deal.mineralsguy.com/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=organic&utm_campaign=minerals-management-series-everything-you-need&utm_content=description_top

In this video, I explain what a division order is, how operators use it, and what it records about an owner’s interest in a well. I walk through how to calculate a decimal interest and discuss what signing a division order means, including how requirements differ by state.

What you'll learn:
- What information a division order includes and when operators use one
- How net mineral acres, lease royalty rate, and unit size determine decimal interest
- How to adjust the calculation for cross-unit or allocation wells
- What signing a division order means and how requirements vary by state

Email Steven directly: steven@mineralsguy.com

About Minerals Guy:

Minerals Guy provides tailored content and resources to oil and gas mineral and royalty owners across the country with the goal of educating and empowering owners to better understand mineral rights as an asset class and the potential value of their minerals and royalties.

Steven Hatcher is the creator of Minerals Guy. He is a professional mineral buyer, an oil and gas attorney and has spent the last decade buying and selling oil and gas properties across the country. He is an expert in oil and gas mineral rights, having worked in the private practice of law, for oil and gas operators, and for mineral and royalty acquisition companies.

would multiply that times 640 acres the size of the unit divide that by .20 or the royalty rate and you would arrive at 40 acres now in modern horizontal development in States like Louisiana and Texas it's not uncommon for operators to drill across unit boundaries essentially stacking existing units on top of one another now here's an example of two 640 acre production units that are being pulled together with multiple 2m lateral horizontal Wells now if you're dealing with a cross-unit well or allocation Wells as they're known in Texas you need to take an extra step to calculate your decimal interest correctly this is because each of those units is going to share in production from that cross unit well based on the length of the lateral in each unit so if 50% of that well board is in your unit you would take your unit decimal as we calculated above and multiply it by 50% part three should you sign division orders so when we think about whether to sign division orders there's the legal application which is going to be different for every state and then there's the practical application and we're going to talk about both now from a legal perspective in Most states division orders will not modify the terms of your oil and gas lease meaning that if the decimal interest provided to you by the operator on your division order is wrong signing that division order is not going to change the amount that you're owed basically you're not agreeing that you're going to own less or more acreage or that some other provision of your oil and gas lease doesn't doesn't exist what you are agreeing to is that if the operator pays you incorrectly so think overpayment you are going to be responsible for paying those funds back or indemnifying the operator now this could be done through recruitment where the operator will place you in suspense until they recoup the overpayment but I've also seen where operators have actually filed suit against less ORS to recoup those funds so when we think about proper management of mineral rights it is important to review your division orders review your decimal interest and to ensure that that decimal interest is correct so are you required to sign division orders well it depends on where you live in some states like Louisiana execution of a division order is not required to receive payment from an operator and it's actually illegal for the operator to withhold funds for failure to sign a division order however in other states like Texas operators can legally require execution of the division order before rendering payment as a practical matter if you see something wrong with your division order for example you do the calculation above and it appears that you're being credited with 20 acres rather than 40 reach out to the land department at the operator and see if you can work it out my experience both running the land department for an operator and receiving division orders as a mineral owner the division order analyst and landman at the operator want to pay everyone correctly but mistakes do happen if everything looks correct sign the division order and send it in this is the easiest way to ensure that you start receiving your royalty checks so now that we've covered division orders what's next well I'm going to show you how to read check stubs and to make sure that you're being paid correctly stay tuned for just a few more seconds and you'll see that episode coming up if you're getting value from our content don't forget to hit the like And subscribe buttons If you have any questions for us you can reach us on the website minerals guide.com you can also reach me by email stepen minerals guide.com thanks and we'll see you the next next episode

metadata.title: Texas Division Orders: What You Can Sign and Refuse
metadata.author: Royalty Clerk
metadata.shortDescription:
An operator sent you a division order to sign. Texas law lists exactly what that paper may contain.

Texas law lists exactly what a division order may contain (Natural Resources Code §91.402). See what you can sign, which extras you may refuse, what happens if you refuse, and five steps to take before you sign.

Read the full guide: https://royaltyclerk.com/texas-division-orders?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=division-orders-in-texas&utm_content=guide
Try the free decimal calculator: https://royaltyclerk.com/tools/decimal-interest-calculator?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=division-orders-in-texas&utm_content=tool
Look up any Texas lease: https://royaltyclerk.com/texas-lease-lookup?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=division-orders-in-texas&utm_content=lease-lookup

Chapters
0:00 Introduction
0:19 What a division order is
0:44 Seven things it may contain
1:26 Extras you may refuse
1:56 What happens if you refuse
2:23 It cannot change your lease
2:56 Rebuild the decimal first
3:24 Signed already?
3:41 Five steps before you sign
4:12 Ask how they got the number
4:29 What to do next

Sources shown in the video
- Texas Natural Resources Code §91.401 (definitions) and §91.402(c), (e), (g), (h)
- Royalty Clerk guide: Texas division orders
- Sample order: a fictional company, lease and owner. Worked example: made-up numbers

Royalty Clerk works only for mineral and royalty owners. We take nothing from operators.

metadata.title: Don't Sign Your Division Order Until You Check This Number
metadata.author: Mineral View
metadata.shortDescription:
A division order just landed in your mailbox, and your operator wants you to sign. But there's one decimal on that document that controls the size of every royalty check you'll ever receive — and if it's wrong, you could be paid far less than you're owed for the life of the well.
In this video, we walk Texas mineral owners through how to verify your decimal interest in under 10 minutes, using a simple formula you can check yourself. Then we break down three lease provisions — transportation, marketing fees, and compression/processing — that can quietly shrink your royalty check, and what to look for before you sign anything.
Whether you recently inherited land in Texas or you've owned mineral rights for years, this is the paperwork walkthrough most owners never get.
— — — — —
FREE TOOL Create your free Mineral View account: [INSERT MINERAL VIEW LINK] Explore the oil and gas activity connected to your Texas minerals and understand what your paperwork actually means.
— — — — —

00:25 What a division order decimal means
01:05 The decimal formula
01:45 Example: 0.015625 vs 0.0078125
02:35 $781 vs $1,562 example
03:20 What else to check before signing
04:10 Lease provisions and deductions
05:00 What to do if something looks off
05:40 Final reminder for mineral owners
— — — — —
If this helped, subscribe to Mineral View for more practical, no-hype mineral owner education. And tell us in the comments: have you ever spotted a discrepancy on a division order or royalty statement?

Division order obligations, lease terms, deduction rights, and royalty payment rules can vary by state, lease language, operator practices, and individual facts. Consult a qualified Texas oil and gas attorney before signing any division order, lease, amendment, or related document.

If your decimal is right and your deduction language is documented, but your original lease had unfavorable clauses from the beginning, you may still be receiving less than you expected every month. The three provisions I just showed you are usually controlled by what was signed on day one. That is what the next video covers. I'm going to walk you through the lease clauses that cost mineral owners the most and what to look for before you ever sign. If this video helped you understand your division order, subscribe to Mineral View for more practical mineral owner education. And if you want to better understand the activity connected to your own Texas minerals, create a free Mineral View account using the link in the description. I will see you in the next video.

metadata.title: Division Orders (Oil & Gas 17.2)
metadata.author: Energy Law Professor
metadata.shortDescription:
Oil companies often want an agreed division order to determine how oil from a well will be divided among the various parties entitled to a share. 

Why is this so important for oil companies? And what happens if the terms of the division order differ from the terms of the lease or non-participating royalty interest that a party has agreed?

Class 17; Video 2

John S. Lowe, Owen L. Anderson, Christopher S. Kulander, Monika U. Ehrman, Burke W. Griggs, James W. Coleman, Cases & Materials on Oil & Gas Law (8th Edition) https://faculty.westacademic.com/Book/Detail/338274
pp. 405-412

Background Reading:
James W. Coleman, The Third Age of Oil and Gas Law, 95 Ind. L.J. 389 (2020), https://scholar.smu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1705&context=law_faculty
