metadata.title: What the Decline Curve Means for Mineral Investments with Troy W. Eckard - Mineral Royalties 101
metadata.author: Eckard Enterprises | Oil & Gas Investing
metadata.shortDescription:
Troy W. Eckard, CEO and Manager of Eckard Enterprises, explains decline curves for producing wells, what impacts that decline curve, what's changed, and how it impacts your investment.

0:00 Introduction to decline curves
0:54 Explaining the initial rate of flow rate
3:45 Artificial Fracking 
4:04 Components to the initial flow rate raising.
7:48 Why it is important to understand the decline curve
- - -

Unlock the power of direct energy investing. Whether you're an accredited investor seeking portfolio diversification, long-term passive income, or smarter tax-advantaged strategies, this channel provides the education and insights you need to invest confidently in U.S. oil and gas assets. 

What You’ll Learn on This Channel 

Our videos are designed to help investors understand and evaluate opportunities in the energy sector, including: 

- Clear explanations of mineral rights, royalties, and working interest 
- Education on oil and gas investing and the U.S. energy industry 
- Market insights, trends, and economic outlooks 
- Tax-advantaged investment strategies 
- Expert discussions from industry veterans, including Troy W. Eckard 

 Contact Us: https://lp.eckardenterprises.com/contact-our-team?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=youtube_videos_2026&utm_content=youtube_2026_mineral_rights


- Book a Call with a Wealth Manager 
https://eckardenterprises.com/contact/ 
- Download the Mineral Rights Investing E-Book 
https://eckardenterprises.com/contact/ 
- Learn About Working Interest and Tax Benefits 
https://eckardenterprises.com/investing-in-oil-and-gas-wells/ 
- How Real Estate Investors Use a 1031 Exchange for Mineral Rights 
https://eckardenterprises.com/1031-exchange-mineral-rigfhts/ 
 

Download the Eckard Insight App 

Apple: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/eckard-insight/id1554729689 
Google: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.eckardenterprises.investments&hl=en_US&pli=1 
 

About Eckard Enterprises 

Eckard Enterprises is a family-owned oil and gas company built on 40 years of experience in the U.S. energy industry. Founded by Troy W. Eckard, the firm focuses exclusively on identifying, acquiring, and developing tangible energy assets for accredited investors seeking long-term, strategic wealth building. 

 

Connect With Us

LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/eckard-enterprises 

Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/eckardenterprises/

metadata.title: Why More Mineral Assets May Never Get Sold
metadata.author: Minerals & Royalties Authority LLC
metadata.shortDescription:
Karl Brensike explains how the Minerals & Royalties market has evolved as more public companies, insurance capital, continuation vehicles, and other large institutional buyers have entered the space.

As more capital competes for scaled mineral portfolios, Karl believes the most attractive place to be may be at the grassroots level—acquiring minerals early and feeding those assets into an increasingly deep pool of long-term buyers with lower costs of capital. That dynamic is a major part of the opportunity he sees for Harvest Mineral & Royalty Partners.

Watch the full episode of Minerals Fund of Funds for Ground Game Aggregators w/ Karl Brensike - Managing Partner of Harvest Mineral & Royalty Partners:

https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/minerals-fund-of-funds-for-ground-game-aggregators-w/id1502759760?i=1000776405919

Tim shares a theory on how the exit playbook for large Minerals & Royalties portfolios may be changing.

Instead of building a portfolio solely to sell or take public, scaled mineral platforms may increasingly use continuation vehicles and recapitalizations to bring in long-duration yield investors and keep owning the assets for another 10–15 years. Tim points to the growing number of institutional mineral platforms as evidence that long-term ownership could become a much bigger part of the private equity playbook.

metadata.author: Steven Hatcher | Minerals Guy
metadata.shortDescription:
Own mineral rights? Get a private, no-obligation offer on your minerals: https://deal.mineralsguy.com/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=organic&utm_campaign=mineral-rights-management-101-ep-3&utm_content=description_top

In this video, I explain how to review your oil and gas lease as part of building a minerals management file. I walk through four questions every mineral owner should answer: who are the parties, what property is covered, when does the lease expire, and how much royalty does it provide.

What you'll learn:
- Identify the lessor and lessee, including whether the lease has been assigned.
- Find the property description in the lease or Exhibit A.
- Understand the execution date, primary and secondary terms, and lease savings clauses.
- Locate the royalty provision and learn how royalties and deductions are addressed.

Minerals Guy provides tailored content and resources to oil and gas mineral and royalty owners across the country with the goal of educating and empowering owners to better understand mineral rights as an asset class and the potential value of their minerals and royalties.

Steven Hatcher is the creator of Minerals Guy. He is a professional mineral buyer, an oil and gas attorney and has spent the last decade buying and selling oil and gas properties across the country. metadata.title: Introduction to Royalties (Oil & Gas 14.1)
metadata.author: Energy Law Professor
metadata.shortDescription:
A royalty is a cost-free share of oil and gas production. This video looks at the typical language for the oil royalty and the gas royalty in a lease. It also considers how oil and gas companies should pay royalties when natural gas prices turn negative as they have sometimes done in recent years and likely will more in the future. It examines what royalty oil and gas companies pay when they sell oil and gas under a long-term contract that may differ from the current market price. And it looks at how to treat separate payments to natural gas companies that may or may not be related to the sale of gas.

Class 16; Video 1

Citations: 
John S. Lowe, Owen L. Anderson, Christopher S. Kulander, Monika U. Ehrman, Burke W. Griggs, James W. Coleman, Cases & Materials on Oil & Gas Law, https://faculty.westacademic.com/Book/Detail/338274
pp. 303-323

Background Reading:
James W. Coleman, The Third Age of Oil and Gas Law, 95 Ind. L.J. 389 (2020), https://scholar.smu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1705&context=law_faculty

metadata.title: What is the Railroad Commission?
metadata.author: Commission Shift
metadata.shortDescription:
The Railroad Commission of Texas (RRC), with its misleading name, has long been a source of mystery to everyday Texans. It’s an important state agency with the power to oversee oil and gas development. The RRC’s decisions affect every Texan in some way.

It’s time to #ChangeTheName of the commission so that it better reflects what the agency actually does. This will help Texans understand what they’re voting for in a railroad commissioner and who to contact when they have concerns. 

Watch our video and comment if you want to see the RRC change their name!

SUBSCRIBE: If you enjoy this video, please consider subscribing to Commission Shift's youtube channel and newsletter. We'd be thrilled to stay in touch:  https://commissionshift.org/contact/  

SUPPORT: You can support Commission Shift's work of reforming oil and gas oversight in Texas by making a donation: https://commissionshift.org/donate/

SOCIAL MEDIA: join us on Instagram, Facebook and Twitter @CommissionShift

RAILROAD COMMISSION OPEN MEETING: Every month the state oil and gas agency hosts a virtual open meeting. The open meeting is a good opportunity to learn more about oil and gas rules and operations, and give public input if you are impacted by abandoned or orphaned wells, or any industry-related pollution. RSVP to learn more and tune in: https://bit.ly/RRCOpenMeeting

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

La Comisión de Ferrocarriles de Texas (RRC), con su nombre confuso, ha sido durante mucho tiempo una fuente de misterio para los tejanos. Es una importante agencia estatal con competencia para supervisar la explotación de petróleo y gas. Las decisiones de la RRC afectan a todos los tejanos de una manera u otra.

Es hora de #CambiarElNombre de la comisión para que refleje mejor lo que la agencia realmente hace. Esto ayudará a los tejanos a entender lo que están votando en un comisionado de ferrocarriles y a quién contactar cuando tengan preocupaciones.

¡Mira nuestro video y comenta si quieres que el RRC cambie su nombre!

SUSCRIBIR: Si disfrutas este video, por favor suscribete al canal de YouTube de Commission Shift y al newsletter. Nos encataría estar en contacto:: https://commissionshift.org/es/contact/

APOYO: Puedes apoyar el trabajo de Commission Shift para reformar la supervisión de petroleo y gas en Texas haciendo una donación : https://bit.ly/CSDonar

MEDIOS DE COMUNICACIÓN SOCIAL: Únete a nosotros en Instagram, Facebook y Twitter @CommissionShift 

REUNIÓN ABIERTA DE LA COMISIÓN DE FERROCARRILES: Todos los meses la agencia estatal de petroleo y gas organiza una reunión abierta virtual. Esta reunión es una buena oportunidad para conocer más sobre las normas y operaciones de petroleo y gas, y dar tu opinión públicamente si te viste afectado por un suministro abandonado, o por la contaminación relacionada con el sector. Responde a la invitación para saber más y sintoniza: https://bit.ly/RSVPespRRC

Um so let's talk about yeah the monitoring enforcement that was item 548. Yeah. Um, there's probably some other stuff. Do you have any other specific questions about this, SJ? Um, no. I'm just looking forward to, you know, digging in and seeing how many and what kinds of recommendations the railroad commission takes this year. And um I did double check the numbers. Um of those thousand or,00 comments that were submitted, 412 were from commission supporters using our form. A lot of them personalized that form, made edits, and sent it in. metadata.title: Permian Resources (PR): How They Beat Negative Gas Prices
metadata.author: The Byte-Size Brief
metadata.shortDescription:
Permian Resources (PR) generated a record $751 million in adjusted free cash flow for the quarter ended June 30, 2026, despite local Waha Hub natural gas prices plummeting to negative $9.52 per thousand cubic feet. This deep dive examines the operational agility and financial strategies that allowed the company to navigate extreme pricing volatility while maintaining a 0.5x net debt to EBITDAX leverage ratio.

We analyze the company's ground game acquisition strategy, which involved 190 microtransactions year-to-date, and explain how these land deals enable longer horizontal laterals to reduce costs. The discussion also covers the $100 million increase in 2026 capital expenditure guidance, clarifying why this reflects a strategic increase in working interest rather than systemic service inflation.

Key topics include:
- 00:00 The Waha Hub pricing collapse and associated gas challenges.
- 03:22 Q2 2026 consolidated financial performance and cash flow.
- 04:21 Breakdown of the $100 million CapEx guidance hike.
- 07:40 Operational pivots: Curtailing gas and utilizing firm transportation.
- 10:08 Using workover rigs to offset lost crude revenue.
- 11:34 The Tetris-style ground game acquisition strategy.
- 13:11 Water recycling and slim hole casing engineering.
- 15:10 Regulatory risks in New Mexico and commodity dependence.
- 19:41 Four key checkpoints for H2 2026: Volume, capital discipline, gas normalization, and leverage.

Does a fragmented acquisition strategy built on hundreds of small deals scale long-term without creating insurmountable administrative failure points?

This video is for informational purposes only. Investment decisions are your own responsibility.

#PermianResources #PR #OilAndGas #EnergyInvesting #PermianBasin #FinancialAnalysis

Traditionally operators run a 9 and 5/8 inch outer steel casing to secure the wellbore. >> Okay. >> Permian Resources shifted to running an 8 and 5/8 inch outer casing and placed a 5.5 inch production casing inside it. >> But wait, shrinking the diameter by a single inch, I mean that sounds like a rounding error. >> It does until you multiply that 1-in reduction across an 11,000-ft lateral wellbore. >> Oh, right. >> The volume of raw steel required drops significantly. And even more importantly, the volume of specialized cement required to pump down the well to secure that steel against the rock formation drops drastically. >> That makes a ton of sense. >> Saving that much cement and steel across dozens of wells heavily insulates them from the macroeconomic inflation of raw materials. >> It is really brilliant engineering. So, we have this aggressive Tetris style acquisition strategy and operational maneuvering that can pivot from gas to oil on a dime. But, you know, as an impartial observer looking at the data, I see some glaring vulnerabilities here. >> Oh, there are definitely risks. >> Right. By putting all their chips exclusively on the Delaware Basin and specifically funneling about 65% of their 2026 activity into New Mexico, aren't they building this highly efficient fortress right on top of a regulatory fault line? >> It is a critical vulnerability. >> Yeah, to be fair, the company explicitly acknowledges this in their Q2 form 10-Q risk disclosures, specifically regarding geographic concentration and government regulations. Operating in New Mexico presents vastly different hurdles than operating in Texas. The Texas side of their portfolio, places like Ward County, that kind of acts as a stabilizing regulatory hedge, right? >> Exactly. >> Cuz Texas generally offers a highly predictable permitting environment, mostly on private lands. But if New Mexico is their designated growth engine, what are the specific mechanical risks over there? >> Well, in New Mexico, they face strict evolving state-level produced water regulations. >> Which ties back to the recycling. >> Right. We just talked about how vital water recycling is to their $5.55 LOE. If the state tightens rules on how that water can be handled or stored, those costs will inevitably rise. Furthermore, much of the land in New Mexico involves federal leases. >> Which brings in Washington. >> Exactly. That exposes them directly to federal permitting rules, environmental reviews, and potential leasing pauses. >> And the objective reality is that federal land policy and state environmental regulations can swing wildly with a single election cycle. >> Oh, absolutely. >> If you have 65% of your capital tied up in a state with complex federal oversight, literally a stroke of a pen in Washington could delay your entire drilling schedule. The regulatory risk is highly concentrated. >> It is incredibly concentrated, and it feeds right into an equally pressing vulnerability, which is commodity dependence. I mean, we just spent 20 minutes discussing how beautifully they managed the Waha gas crisis, but the reality is their revenue is overwhelmingly driven by crude oil. >> So, are they protected if the bottom just falls out of the global crude market? >> Only partially. They maintain what you'd call a moderate rolling hedging strategy. Currently, they have WTI crude swaps protecting 50 to 70,000 barrels a day at a price range of $63 to $66 per barrel. >> Well, wait, they are producing almost 200,000 barrels a day. >> Exactly. Which means roughly 2/3 of their oil production remains completely unhedged, exposed to the open market. Management has stated their corporate free cash flow break-even point sits in the low 40s per barrel. >> That's a huge gap. >> It is. If global crude drops toward that break-even point, the entire narrative we've been unpacking, the record $751 million in cash, the dividend sustainability, the rapid debt redemption, it all evaporates very quickly. >> It is a really high-leverage bet on the underlying commodity remaining stable. And I want to push back on the execution risk of the ground game itself, too. >> Go for it. >> We love the Tetris analogy because it sounds clean and logical. But practically speaking, executing 190 small deals seems infinitely more complicated logistically than just securing one massive corporate merger and absorbing their staff and systems. >> Oh, it is incredibly labor-intensive. Think about what a microtransaction actually is. You aren't buying a skyscraper, you are buying mineral rights from dozens of individual families or small private operators. >> It's extremely fragmented. >> Very. Replacing 100% of your developed reserves through 190 microtransactions requires flawless execution on a granular administrative level. >> You were dealing with complex title work, land integration, and weird legacy contracts. >> Exactly. If the land department misses a title defect on just a tiny parcel, or if the geology on a new bolt-on doesn't perfectly match the surrounding acreage, the projected production they are promising to the market simply won't materialize. >> So, there's no room for error. >> Right. When you rely on hundreds of small acquisitions, you introduce thousands of potential points of failure. The administrative burden is immense. >> Okay, so we have dissected the core contradictions here. We understand the financial mechanisms of working interest, the physical realities of associated gas and workover rigs, and obviously the concentrated regulatory risks. Let's bring this all together for everyone listening. >> Let's do it. >> If you are reviewing this company's upcoming earnings report, what are the specific verifiable metrics to watch for base strictly on management's own guidance? Let's establish the checkpoints. >> So, there are four conditional checkpoints for the second half of 2026. And, to be clear, this isn't a verdict on whether to buy or sell the equity, but rather a scorecard to measure management's operational execution. >> Right, just tracking the data. >> Yes. >> What's number one? >> First is the volume check. Management guided that second half 2026 oil production will cross the 200,000 barrels per day threshold. The data needs to verify if all those 190 newly acquired ground game assets are fully integrating and actually delivering those promised barrels to the surface. >> Okay, got it. The second metric I'd be watching closely is the capital discipline check. They raised the full year CapEx midpoint to $1.95 billion, which we discussed was largely driven by working interest increases. >> Yes. >> Can they hold their second half cash capital expenditures strictly under the $1 billion mark? Cuz if they keep it under a billion, it proves that the CapEx hike was indeed a calculated one-time adjustment. But if they blow past that, it might signal that systemic service inflation is finally creeping into their operations. >> That's a great point. And while you watch the spending, the third metric to watch is the gas normalization check. Management stated that the gas wells they curtailed in Q2 were brought back online in late June. >> Right. >> Will the Q3 revenue actually reflect normalized natural gas volumes? Because that outcome entirely assumes that new regional pipeline capacity successfully comes online to relieve that Waha pricing bottleneck we discussed earlier. >> And finally, the leverage check. They sit at that pristine 0.5x net debt to EBITDAX ratio right now. With all this fragmented acquisition activity and the commitment to the base dividend payout, will that 0.5x ratio hold steady by year end? >> That's the million-dollar question. >> Because if that leverage ratio ticks up significantly without a corresponding crash in global commodity prices, you really have to question the cash generation durability of the newly acquired land. >> Exactly. Those four metrics, volume, capital discipline, gas normalization, and leverage, they will provide a clear mathematical picture of how well this operational machine is actually running. >> It really leaves you with a fascinating dynamic to mull over. Think back to that Tetris board analogy. The ground game strategy is incredibly brilliant right now because there are still open disjointed spaces on the Delaware Basin map to exploit. >> Right, there's still room to play. >> But at what point does Permian Resources simply run out of accretive adjacent acres to quietly buy? When that board is completely full and they are forced to look outside their core stronghold to replace the reserves, what happens to that peer-leading cost structure? It is the ultimate ceiling on their strategy and definitely something to think about.

metadata.title: Quantifying Shale Performance Drivers Across 100,000 Wells | Ryan Hassen, whitson | whitCon 2026
metadata.author: Whitson Academy
metadata.shortDescription:
Is a shale just a shale? Ryan Hassen shares what whitson learned training neural networks on more than 100,000 wells across 10 North American shale basins. He compares how lateral length, frac fluid intensity, wellbore azimuth, water cut, fluid window, spacing and depletion drive performance. Some behave about the same in every basin, while others need tuning basin by basin. He discusses building a library of analogs for plays with few wells, and the selection bias that comes with it.

📅 Recorded: October 20, 2026
🎤 Presenter: Ryan Hassen, whitson
📍 Location: whitCon 2026, Norris Conference Centre, Houston, TX
🗂️ Slides: https://whitson.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/19-Ryan-whitson_1.pdf

metadata.title: Permian Resources: Record Cash Flow vs. Waha Gas Crisis
metadata.author: The Byte-Size Brief
metadata.shortDescription:
Permian Resources (PR) delivered a record $751 million in adjusted free cash flow for the second quarter of 2026, despite navigating negative Waha natural gas prices. This analysis examines how the company utilized operational agility and a unique ground game acquisition strategy to maintain a 0.5x net debt-to-EBITDA ratio while increasing full-year capital expenditure guidance to $1.9–$2.0 billion.

Outline:
00:00 The Q2 Earnings Contradiction
01:46 Financial and Cash Flow Deconstruction
03:30 Operational Mechanics and Strategy
05:36 Acquisitions and the Ground Game
07:43 Specific Risks and Triggers
09:24 Conditional Checkpoints for Q3

The company’s performance was bolstered by a $97.81 per barrel oil realization, which acted as a subsidy against localized gas pricing that hit negative $9.52 per thousand cubic feet. By curtailing high gas-to-oil ratio wells and accelerating workover rig deployment, management successfully optimized output. However, the strategy of executing 190 micro-bolt-on acquisitions introduces risks regarding operational complexity, supply chain inflation, and reliance on high oil prices. Investors should monitor Q3 metrics, specifically whether oil production exceeds 200,000 barrels per day and if capital expenditures remain under $1.0 billion for the second half of the year.

Will this high working interest bolt-on strategy continue to yield record cash flow if oil prices normalize below $75?

This video is for informational purposes only. Investment decisions are your own responsibility.

and a profound contradiction that
emerged from their official earnings
release for the fiscal quarter ending
June 30th, 2026.
Here's the situation.
The company generated a record $751
million in adjusted free cash flow. That
is a massive number. But they did this
while simultaneously absorbing deeply
negative Waha natural gas prices out in
West Texas
and hiking their full-year capital
expenditure guidance.
In this explainer, we are going to
unpack three crucial conclusions.
First, we'll dissect this central
earnings contradiction. How record cash
flow coexists with a localized pricing
collapse.
Second, we'll reveal what the market
might be missing regarding Permian's
unique operational agility in the field.
And third, we will establish the exact
integration risk checkpoints you must
monitor in the upcoming third quarter
release.
The paradox right at the center of this
analysis is stark and honestly
fascinating. On one hand, Permian
delivered that massive record-breaking
adjusted free cash flow of $751 million.
On the other hand, they achieved this
while fighting a severe regional
commodity price dislocation. We are
talking about Waha gas prices, the local
pricing hub for West Texas natural gas,
plunging as low as negative $9.52
per thousand cubic feet during the
second quarter.
Think about what negative pricing
actually means in the field. Producers
literally have to pay midstream
operators to take their gas away. It
transforms a revenue stream into a
massive localized cost liability
overnight. So, the central question we
are answering today is how exactly does
a Delaware Basin operator manage to
expand its footprint, increase its
capital spending, and navigate highly
toxic local gas prices without
completely rupturing its balance sheet?
Let's move directly into section one,
financial and cash flow deconstruction.
Looking at the consolidated financial
data from their August 2026 earnings
report, the sheer scale of the cash
conversion happening here is remarkable.
For the three months ending June 30,
Permian Resources deployed cash capital
expenditures of $521 million. dollars.
On that spend, they delivered a
staggering $1.506 billion in operating
cash flow. That is nearly a three-to-one
conversion ratio of capital spent to
cash generated. It demonstrates an
immense level of capital efficiency at
the operational level.
All of that trickles down to the bottom
line, resulting in that record $751
million in adjusted free cash flow,
which represents a nearly 50% sequential
increase from the prior quarter.
And during this exact same period, they
maintained a highly disciplined
production profile, averaging 198.1
thousand barrels of oil per day,
representing a solid 3% sequential
volume growth.
But to really understand the margin
here, we have to look closely at the
pricing environment they successfully
captured.
The key to unlocking this performance
lies in Permian Resources' reported Q2
realization price of $97.81
per barrel of oil.
This massive cash conversion was
heavily, heavily supported by this
robust realized oil price. It completely
demonstrates the critical importance of
having a strong liquid weight in an
operator's overall production mix.
While natural gas was absolutely
bleeding cash at the local Waha hub,
Permian's unhedged oil barrels were
commanding exceptional premiums in the
market. When you are capturing nearly a
hundred dollars a barrel on roughly
200,000 barrels a day, that revenue acts
as a massive subsidy for the entire
operation. It essentially overrides the
localized headwinds and floods the
balance sheet with cash. It's the
ultimate operational buffer.
Operational mechanics and strategy.
Now, high oil prices alone do not fully
explain this record cash generation.
Let's be honest, any operator can catch
a lucky break with a macro commodity
tailwind.
The real answer to Permian's
outperformance and the market blind spot
we mentioned earlier lies in the
company's tactical, field-level response
to distressed natural gas markets.
Instead of just blindly pumping
production and paying midstream
companies to offload their gas at
negative $9.52 per MCF,
management made a very specific tactical
decision. They proactively choked back
high GOR wells. These are wells with a
high gas to oil ratio that are heavily
exposed to the Waha Hub.
Dynamically adjusting midstream flow
rates without damaging wellbore pressure
or causing subsurface sand issues
requires highly precise reservoir
engineering. It is certainly not
something every operator can execute
smoothly on the fly.
By reducing natural gas production by
approximately 20% quarter over quarter
and leaning on their firm transportation
and hedging contracts, they successfully
turned a severe liability into a
positive 38 cents per MCF realization.
That single tactical move resulted in an
estimated $75 million revenue uplift on
their natural gas sales compared to
simply letting the wells run at negative
spot prices.
And then once Waha pricing improved in
late June, they seamlessly returned all
previously curtailed wells right back to
production.
Conversely, while they were shutting
down unprofitable gas, they rapidly
accelerated profitable oil. As co-CEO
Will Hickey noted on the August earnings
call, when oil pricing remained robust,
field teams aggressively deployed a 50%
increase in workover rigs.
If you're unfamiliar, a workover rig is
deployed to perform maintenance, repair,
or enhancement on an existing well to
optimize its output.
By surging these rigs into the field,
they directly improved run times and
quickly accelerated incremental barrels,
which directly drove that 3% sequential
volume growth we saw in the financials.
They matched their operational tempo
exactly to the commodity price signals
in real time. They pulled back hard on
the gas and slammed the accelerator on
the oil.
Acquisitions and the ground game.
How does an operator continuously grow
its core inventory without executing a
highly dilutive multi-billion dollar
corporate mega deal?
Permian Resources is the largest pure
play Delaware Basin operator,
controlling roughly 535,000 net acres.
Instead of buying entire companies and
taking on all their bloated overhead and
legacy issues, Permian utilizes a
fragmented ground game acquisition
strategy. They aggressively target
off-market micro bolt-on properties that
are immediately adjacent to their core
footprint. They leverage a massive
proprietary data set and deep local
relationships to find deals others
simply don't see.
This localized intelligence allows them
to surgically expand their footprint
block by block right in their own
backyard.
Let's quantify that ground game to see
what it actually looks like in practice.
Year to date in 2026, they have spent
approximately 1.05 billion dollars. But
consider exactly how they spent it.
Across roughly 190 separate individual
micro transactions.
This is tedious, labor-intensive title
work. Executing 190 separate deals means
190 different title opinions, individual
lease negotiations, and deploying
landmen across multiple counties.
It is significantly harder to execute
than one large corporate buyout, but it
completely prevents the premium dilution
typically associated with major M&A.
Through these 190 deals, they
accumulated 54,000 net leasehold acres
and 20,000 net royalty acres.
They are prioritizing higher working
interests over immediate production.
The crown jewel of this recent run was a
standalone 520 million-dollar bolt-on in
Ward County. This specific deal added
acreage that perfectly offsets their
existing asset base and provides an
extended runway of high return
inventory.
Crucially, this aggressive expansion
tempo was funded without stressing the
balance sheet. As of June 30, their
leverage remained pinned at the floor of
their target range at exactly 0.5x net
debt to EBITDA.
Think about that for a second. They
spent over a billion dollars executing
nearly 200 complex land deals and still
maintained a pristine fortress balance
sheet. That exact combination of
aggressive capital deployment and strict
leverage discipline is what generated
the historic cash flow metrics we
reviewed earlier.
Specific risks and triggers.
While the historical results are
incredibly robust, proper analysis
requires us to interrogate the
forward-looking vulnerabilities
triggered directly by this specific
acquisition strategy.
A direct consequence of their ground
game success is the official increase in
full year 2026 capital expenditure
guidance, which now ranges between 1.9
and 2.0 billion dollars.
The mechanics here are straightforward.
When you buy a larger percentage of a
drilling unit through your ground game,
you become responsible for a
correspondingly larger percentage of the
drilling costs moving forward.
Furthermore, they allocated 25 million
dollars specifically for integrating and
developing that new Ward County asset.
Simply put, overall capital spending is
going up because their ownership share
across the basin is going up.
The strategic trade-off here is clear,
and these are the exact execution risks
we must track.
Increased inventory and scale come at
the direct cost of higher capital
intensity.
First, there is the immense operational
complexity and overhead of integrating
190 fragmented land titles seamlessly
into their drilling schedule without
causing rig delays.
Second, management explicitly noted
supply chain inflation pressing on
diesel and casing materials. This
directly connects back to their
operational agility. Remember that 50%
increase in workover rigs we discussed?
Pushing more rigs into the field
requires burning more diesel and
utilizing more steel casing, compounding
their exposure to this specific
inflation risk.
Third, the persistent vulnerability to
Waha midstream bottlenecks hasn't
vanished.
Negative gas pricing could easily return
and heavily strain their curtailment
strategy.
And finally, there is a heavy,
undeniable reliance on sustained high
oil realizations.
The entire machine, funding the ground
game, raising CapEx, and paying the
dividend, requires crude oil to stay
strong.
Next quarter conditional checkpoints.
Because our analysis is as of October
17th, 2026, we are sitting directly on
the precipice of their next earnings
release.
To assess whether this higher capital
strategy is actually generating
shareholder value, we must establish
strict operational thresholds.
In the upcoming third quarter release,
the market must verify specific promises
made by management. First, second half
oil production must breach the 200,000
barrel per day mark. This will prove the
newly acquired acreage is actually
yielding results. Concurrently, second
half capital expenditures must remain
strictly capped below 1.0 billion
dollars to prevent cash burn. We also

spending hasn't degraded the balance
sheet, meaning the leverage ratio must
be maintained right around that 0.5x
level.
Finally, the board previously declared a
Q3 base dividend of 16 cents per class A
share. Any deviation from these four

of those 190 ground game deals is not
proceeding as efficiently as modeled,
and capital destruction may be
occurring.
So, the crucial point to take away from
this analysis is this. Permian Resources

working interest bolt-on strategy

$100 premium and normalize below the $75

Austin Lee, now Tax Partner, explains how depletion is calculated and works in the oil and gas industry.

segments.text: So, Austin, you mentioned depletion earlier.
Tell me, how does the depletion allowance work in oil and gas properties and how it is calculated?
So, depletion is a pretty complex calculation.
There's two different types of depletion. There's both
cost depletion and statutory depletion or you'll hear percentage depletion is what its called.
Percentage depletion is probably the easiest to understand. Typically its going to be 15%
of your gross income. So pretty straightforward. You do have a few limitations on your net income
for percentage depletion. So, if you have a net loss, you're not allowed to take percent
depletion. If you have really 65% of the total net income of your company or the investments,
you're going to be capped at that, but that's getting a little bit in the weeds.
So, I think that the main benefit of statutory depletion that a lot of people don't know about
is that you can actually take depletion in excess of your basis. So that's a fun accounting term we
like to use - basis. Where we've got basically the total cost of whatever you invest into something,
so that would be how much that you put into the venture, that's going to the be the basis. And
typically, you know, if you were to buy a depreciable asset, or something like that,
you're going to be able to depreciate that asset down to zero. Well, percentage depletion works
that whatever you invest into the project, you get to take depletion on the revenue not only to zero,
but actually beyond. So, you that 15% as long as you have that investment.
Cost depletion is a little more complex of a calculation where you're going to be
basically calculating the least hold cost that you have and compare the reserves year over year
and kind of go through a little bit of a formulaic calculation in order to determine
kind of the total cost of the asset and then kind of the economic depletion that is being
removed from that asset - basically the reserves that are being depleted.
So that's the main difference between those two,
Another thing to keep in mind between those two if you are choosing to calculate both,
the IRS allows you to deduct the higher of the two of those. So you don't get to take both, you get
to take the higher of those two. So I would say, typically for people that have passive investment,
royalties, you're going to have more of a focus on percentage depletion, just because it's a little
bit easier to calculate. Really, other types of investors that are kind of in a passive role,
percentage depletion is kind of of the one that we see most typically.
Makes sense. Makes sense.

metadata.title: Percentage Depletion for Mineral Owners: The 15% Deduction You Should Know (+ Live Q&A!)
metadata.author: Tracy Lenz
metadata.shortDescription:
Sept 16th 2026
Oil & Gas Minerals
Live Q&A Office Hours #59

Percentage Depletion for Mineral Owners: The 15% Deduction Most Royalty Owners Have Never Heard Of

If you get a royalty check, you get a tax deduction that goes with it. It is called percentage depletion, it is 15% of the royalties you were paid, and it comes back every year for as long as the wells pay you. It does not matter whether you bought the minerals, inherited them, or were given them, and it does not stop when your basis is gone. Most owners have never heard of it, and it is the first thing I ask about when someone shows me a tax return with royalties on it.

Today is the basics, start to finish, for the owner and for the preparer they hand the 1099 to:

1. What depletion is. Your minerals are a bucket that empties a little every month, and the tax code lets you deduct for the part that is gone. Who qualifies (anyone with an economic interest, which a royalty is) and who does not.
2. The 15%. Where the number comes from, what "gross income from the property" means, why a lease bonus does not count, and a worked example: $10,000 in royalties becomes $8,500 of taxable royalty income before anything else.
3. Where it goes on the return. Schedule E, Part I: line 4 is the royalties, line 18 is the depletion. What to look at on last year's return tonight.
4. The fine print. The 65% of taxable income cap and what carries forward, the 1,000 barrel a day limit that almost no individual owner will ever touch, and why depletion is figured property by property when the 1099 lumps everything by operator.
5. The other number. Cost depletion in one slide: when it can beat the 15%, why a recent inheritance is the case to check, and why it needs an engineer. That one gets its own hour later this fall.
6. Why it is in the news. Two bills in the House, one that would end percentage depletion and one that would expand it for marginal wells. Both sit in committee. Nothing has changed for your 2026 return.

Live demo at the 30-minute mark: chat picks a county, we pull a report card on a real tract in Core, read what the wells should be paying against the decimal, take 15% of it out loud, and show the well-by-tract list a preparer needs to do this property by property.

Warm-up question for the chat: You inherited minerals and nobody in the family knows what was ever paid for them. Can you still take a depletion deduction? Answer at the end.

I am a petroleum engineer, not a CPA or an attorney. This session is education, not tax or legal advice. Your preparer makes the call on your return.

Welcome to our Office Hours Live Stream, where I'll be taking your questions, big or small, on anything oil & gas! Whether you're curious to hear our frequently asked questions (FAQs) or want to submit something new in the chat, this session is a great opportunity to get real-time insights and practical tips.

Our public tool for mineral insights and value:
www.PecanEstimate.com

Learn how to get started with an Essentials or Core portfolio at: https://pecantreeog.com/pricing

Request an appraisal, a date-of-death valuation, or a custom project here:
https://www.pecantreeog.com/intake-form

Send us an email with a question or comment one below:
kelly@pecantreeog.com

Earlier sessions this one builds on:
Percentage Depletion 101, the short version (July ROAR, at 52:51): https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uhBChnIIHd0
Gifting Minerals Before Year-End (the step-up in basis, which is what makes cost depletion worth a look): https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hjXMF1YQWb8
FAQs for CPAs Before You Put a Number on Minerals: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s6QbyYmibOA

metadata.author: Protect Wealth Academy
metadata.shortDescription:
Discover powerful, legal strategies to reduce your tax burden through investments in oil, gas, and mineral rights.

Learn practical insights on:

- Key tax deductions and credits available to investors
- Depreciation, depletion allowances, and intangible drilling costs
- How to structure investments for maximum tax efficiency
- Common pitfalls to avoid with the IRS

Whether you're already investing or are looking to diversify with tax-advantaged opportunities, this session will deliver actionable strategies you can use immediately.

metadata.shortDescription:
In this video, Rich Hofmann, CPA, JD, takes you through the most powerful tax deductions available for oil and gas investors. Whether you’re a seasoned industry participant or exploring your first energy investment, understanding these complex rules can help reduce your taxable income.

Throughout the video, Rich covers a range of critical topics—explaining how intangible drilling costs and key Internal Revenue Code sections (including §§ 263, 263(c), and 168) create upfront deduction opportunities, how depreciation and bonus depreciation accelerate write‑offs, the impact of active versus passive loss rules and material participation requirements on your ability to claim those losses, which expenses you can exclude from income, and how the depletion allowance lets you recover your investment over the life of a well.

Oil and gas investments come with unique tax benefits—but only if you know how to apply the rules correctly. From the election to deduct intangible drilling costs to navigating the passive activity limits and depletion rules, each strategy can materially impact your after‑tax return. 

Please like, comment, and subscribe if you found this video helpful. For tailored advice on your oil and gas ventures, visit our website:

Disclaimer:

This video is for educational purposes only and does not constitute legal, tax, or financial advice. Always consult a qualified professional regarding your specific situation.

metadata.title: The Economics of Owning an Oil Well Royalty Interest
metadata.author: Mr. Business
metadata.shortDescription:
Oil well royalty interests explained: how royalty checks are calculated, why payments rise and fall, how fast production declines, and what the taxes and risks look like, all with a hypothetical worked example.

If you've inherited mineral rights, own a royalty, or are just curious how oil and gas royalty income really works, this video breaks it down in plain English.

📌 WHAT YOU'LL LEARN
• What an oil and gas royalty interest actually is
• Royalty vs. working interest vs. NPRI vs. ORRI
• How net revenue interest (NRI) and decimal interest are calculated
• A 5-year hypothetical royalty example with real math
• The decline curve: why early checks aren't "normal"
• Oil price swings, differentials, and post-production deductions
• Taxes: ordinary income, depletion, and inherited minerals (general overview)
• How royalties are valued and sold
• Risks, scam red flags, and who this asset is suited for

⏱️ TIMESTAMPS
0:00 Hook
1:05 Disclaimer and roadmap
2:30 What is a royalty interest?
5:00 Royalty vs. working interest (the alphabet soup)
8:00 How a royalty check is calculated
10:30 Full worked example (hypothetical)
14:00 The decline curve
16:30 Price, differentials, and deductions
19:00 Taxes
21:30 How royalties are valued and sold
23:30 The risks
25:30 Scams and red flags
27:30 Who is this for? (checklist)
29:00 Conclusion

💬 QUESTION FOR YOU
Do you own or have you inherited a royalty or mineral interest? Tell me in the comments what you'd like explained next.

👍 If this video helped, a like and subscribe helps the channel and means a lot.

⚠️ DISCLAIMER
This video is for educational and informational purposes only. It is not financial, investment, tax, or legal advice. I am not a licensed financial advisor, CPA, or attorney. All numbers and examples are simplified and hypothetical, and are not predictions or guarantees. Oil and gas investments involve significant risk, including the loss of your entire investment. Tax rules, royalty rates, and state laws vary and change. Consult a qualified professional before making any decisions. Companies mentioned are examples only, not recommendations.

📚 SOURCES TO VERIFY
• IRS Publication 535 (business expenses, depletion)
• Your state's oil and gas regulator / comptroller website
• SEC and your state securities regulator (investor alerts)

Look for language about whether the royalty is free of cost or at the well and whether post-production costs may be charged. You'll typically see the volume sold, the price per unit, the gross value, the taxes, any deductions, and the net amount. Learn to read it. metadata.author: Sovereign Energy Partners

Working interest and royalty interest are two of the most important concepts in direct oil and gas investing. They both provide exposure to energy production, but they differ significantly when it comes to costs, risk, cash flow, and potential returns.
➡️ Many investors assume these structures are interchangeable. In reality, the choice between a working interest and a royalty interest can have a major impact on your investment experience. Understanding who pays the costs, who receives the revenue, and how each structure responds to operational and market conditions is essential before evaluating any opportunity.
This video explores the advantages, tradeoffs, and practical differences between working interests and royalty interests. You'll learn how each structure generates income, why one may offer greater upside potential, why the other may provide a more passive approach, and how experienced investors often combine both within a broader energy investment strategy.

From drilling costs and operating expenses to revenue participation and risk exposure, this discussion provides a practical framework for understanding how ownership structures influence outcomes in the U.S. oil and gas sector.

equipment, covering operating expenses,

structure appeals to a different type of
investor. Let's start with working
interest. A working interest investor
owns a direct participation in the well
itself. That means they are financially
responsible for their proportional share
of drilling costs, completion costs, and

trade-off. Higher cost exposure, but

complete. A working interest investor
taking a 10% position would contribute
$100,000 towards those costs. In return,

revenue after operating costs generated
by that well. Now, if that well performs

several years, that 10% share can
translate into meaningful monthly cash
flow, and ultimately strong overall
returns. But, it's important to be
balanced here. Working interest also
means exposure to cost overruns,
operational inefficiencies, and
fluctuations in commodity prices. So,
while the upside is greater, the
variability is also higher. For
investors who are comfortable with a
higher degree of involvement, and are
seeking stronger upside potential,
working interest can be very compelling.
Now, let's look at royalty interest. A

the revenue generated by the well. But,
and this is the key distinction, they do
not pay for drilling or operating costs.

upfront capital tied to drilling, no
exposure to cost overruns, no ongoing
operating expenses. Instead, royalty
interest holders receive a percentage of
the top-line revenue. We refer to it as

share is typically smaller than that of

contribute to the drilling or operating

this example, the percentage is smaller.

significantly reduced risk. There are no
surprise capital calls, no operational
responsibilities, no exposure to rising
costs. It's a much more passive form of
participation. For many investors, this
makes royalty interest particularly
attractive, especially those who
prioritized a degree of predictability,
simplicity, and lower exposure to
operational risk. You can think of it as
a way to participate in the output of
the asset without being involved in the
mechanics of running it. When you put
the two side by side, the distinction
becomes very clear. Working interest,
higher involvement, higher risk
exposure, higher potential return.
Royalty interest, lower for
lower risk, lower potential return.
And importantly, neither structure is
inherently better. They simply serve
different purposes within a portfolio.
In fact, many experienced investors
choose to combine both. They might
allocate capital to working interest to
capture upside while also holding
royalty interest to create a lower risk
income base. That combination can help
balance volatility while still
maintaining meaningful return potential.
So, which structure do investors
typically prefer? The honest answer is
it depends on the investor. Some
investors are naturally drawn to working
interest because it offers greater
upside potential. It provides direct
participation in the asset and it can
generate stronger cash flow over time.
These investors are typically more
comfortable with variability and
understand the operational side of the
business. On the other hand, many
investors prefer royalty interest
because it provides exposure to
production. It avoids operational and
cost-related risks and it requires
significantly less involvement. In
practice, both structures play an
important role in the broader energy
investment landscape. More experienced
investors often think in terms of
portfolio construction, aligning
different types of exposure with their
overall financial objectives. For
example, a more conservative investor
might lean heavily towards royalty
interest, focusing on stability and
predictability. Whereas an investor
seeking higher returns and willing to
accept more variability might allocate
more capital towards working interest.
The key is alignment, not just with
return expectations, but with risk
tolerance and investment mindset. The
key takeaway is this: both working
interest and royalty interest provide
exposure to oil and gas production, but

return profiles. Understanding that
distinction is essential before
evaluating any specific opportunity
because ultimately, the structure you

metadata.title: Your Life as Every Level of a Landman
metadata.author: Untold Shifts
metadata.shortDescription:
Your life as every level of a landman, the oil-field job that starts in a courthouse basement reading deeds from 1911. You run title through a century of inheritances, knock on a farmhouse door, sit at a kitchen table with three feuding brothers, chase leases through a boom town, get certified, move in-house, lose it all in the bust and come back for the May 2026 federal lease sale, where one square mile sold for more than $357,000 an acre.

Sources: BLS (May 2025), the American Association of Professional Landmen, Pennsylvania's Guaranteed Minimum Royalty Act, the University of Houston, the Bureau of Land Management and Western Energy Alliance. The ~$100K salary is a pay-site estimate. Every character, county and company in the story is fictional.

#landman #oilandgas #povstory

segments.text: Somewhere under a cow pasture in Texas,
there's oil. And before a single drill
touches the ground, somebody has to
figure out who actually owns it. That
somebody is you. You're a landman. Not a
lawyer, not an engineer, not a rough
neck. You're the person who digs through
hundred-year-old courthouse books,
knocks on farmhouse doors, and sits at
kitchen tables [music]
asking families to sign away the right
to drill under their land.
This year, the federal government
auctioned off drilling rights in the
Peran Basin, and one square mile sold
for more than $350,000
an acre. Every one of those acres
started [music] with a landman reading a
dusty deed. You're about to start at the
bottom of that business in a courthouse
basement with a flashlight and a legal
[music] pad. Level one,
the courthouse.
You're 23. You're sitting in a county
courthouse basement at 8 in the morning
and your entire job is reading
handwriting from 1911.
Every oil deal begins here in the deed
records. Your boss hands you a list of
trackcts and says, "Find out who owns
them." So, you pull the giant leather
[music] books off the shelves one by one
and trace every sale, every inheritance,
every divorce. The government doesn't
track landmen as a job of their own. The
closest category, title, examiners, and
abstractors, [music]
has a median of about $28 an hour.
That's about right for you. The clerk
behind the counter is a woman named
Darlene, who has worked here 31 years
[music] and knows every family in the
county. She tells you which ones are
going to fight. She's never [music]
wrong. By noon, you've got a cramp in
your hand, dust in your nose, and a
family tree drawn [music] on a legal pad
that looks like a spiderweb.
By 5, you realize one of the owners died
in [music] 1962 and never left a will.
Level two, running title. The family
living on this land doesn't own what's
underneath it, and they have no idea.
This is the part nobody outside the
[music] business understands. In a lot
of oil country, the land on top and the
minerals underneath can be owned by
completely [music] different people.
Somebody's great-grandfather sold the
farm in 1948, but kept the mineral
rights, and those rights [music] got
split between his eight kids, who split
them between their kids. You run title
all the way back, deed by deed, until
you can [music] prove who owns every
sliver. Today you find out a single
quarter section has 26 [music] owners
spread across nine states and two of
them are in prison. You call your boss.
He says, "Great. Find all of them." You
buy a [music] second legal pad. Darlene
brings you a cup of coffee without
asking. You take it as [music] a sign
that you're going to be here a while.
Level three, the door. You're standing
on a farmhouse porch holding a contract
and the man inside is watching you
through the curtain with a shotgun
leaning by the door. You're a field
landman. [music] Now, most field landmen
are independent contractors hired
through brokers to represent [music] the
oil company to the landowner. Your job
is to get leases signed. A lease [music]
pays the owner two ways. a bonus upfront
for every acre and a royalty, a share of
whatever the well produces.
In Pennsylvania, [music] state law won't
even recognize a lease unless it
guarantees the owner at least 1/8. The
man on the porch finally opens [music]
the door. His name is Walt. He's 74.
He's been offered leases before, and he
thinks every [music] oil company is a
thief. You don't argue. You ask him
about the old barn. 40 minutes later,
[music] you're sitting at his kitchen
table looking at photos of his wife, and
the contract is still in your bag, which
is exactly where it should be. Level
four, the kitchen [music] table.
Three brothers who haven't spoken in 9
years are sitting at the same kitchen
table, and your contract is the only
thing they agree is a bad idea. Walt's
minerals didn't pass [music] to Walt
alone. When his father died, they were
split between him and his brothers.
[music] One wants the money. One wants a
higher royalty. One just wants to make
the other two miserable. You learn that
the hardest part of this job isn't
geology or law. It's families. You
explain the bonus. You explain the
[music] royalty. You explain it again
slower to the brother who [music] keeps
saying you're a crook. Walt's daughter
takes you aside on the porch and asks if
this is a fair deal for her dad. You
tell her to have a lawyer read it. She
looks surprised that you said that. By
sunset, two brothers have signed. The
third tells you to get off his land. You
drive home in the dark, already planning
[music] which pie to bring next week.
Level five.
The boom. The motel is full. [music] The
courthouse opens at 8:00. And there are
already 20 landmen sitting on its front
steps [music] at 6:00 in the morning.
Oil prices are high and every company
wants acorage at the same time.
Suddenly, you're one of hundreds of
landmen pouring into a small town that
has one diner and [music] one stoplight.
The courthouse record room gets so
crowded the clerk starts handing out
numbers like a deli counter. Day rates
climb. You're making more money than you
ever have, and you're spending half of
it on a motel [music] room that smells
like diesel. Everybody is racing. If a
rival landman signs a family before you
do, that acorage is gone. You eat lunch
in your truck so you don't lose [music]
your seat at the record table. Darlene,
back in your old county, sends you a
text. It just says, "Slow [music]
down." You don't. Nobody slows down in a
boom. That's how you know it's a boom.
Level six, getting certified.
You've done this for 5 years, and now a
professional association wants you to
prove it on a test. The American
Association of Professional Landmen
certifies landmen in levels, registered
[music]
landman, registered professional
landman, and at the top, certified
professional [music] landman. Without a
college degree, the professional level
takes five years [music] of real land
work. The top certification takes at
least seven, plus sponsors who already
hold it, plus an exam you get 8 hours to
finish. You study at night in that same
motel room surrounded by old title
[music] opinions. You learn the words
you've been using for years and finally
what they actually mean on paper.
pooling, curative, depth severance. The
certificate comes in the mail in a
cardboard tube. You don't hang it up.
You leave it in the truck under the
[music] seat next to the second legal
pad that started all of this. Level
seven in-house. You traded your truck
and your motel room for a downtown
office with a view. [music] And the
first week, you missed the dirt roads.
An oil company hires you as an in-house
landman. Now you're the one managing the
field land men, trading acreage with
other companies, [music]
and negotiating the agreements that
decide who drills what. Pay sites put
the typical landman salary at around
$100,000 a year. [music] There's no
official government number for this job,
so treat that as an estimate, [music]
but your paycheck agrees with it. You
wear a tie for the first time since your
cousin's wedding. Your days are
spreadsheets, [music]
maps on giant screens, and meetings
where engineers ask whether you've
cleared title on a well they want to
drill next month. You have. You always
have. That's the job [music] now. Saying
yes and making sure it's true. Level
eight, the bust. Oil just fell off a
cliff and the meeting on your calendar
this afternoon has no title, [music]
just an HR representative's name. Booms
end. When prices collapse, [music]
companies stop drilling. And when they
stop drilling, they stop paying people
to find more land. Researchers at the
University of Houston [music] counted
the damage from the last big crash. From
late 2014 through mid 2020, [music]
Houston's upstream oil industry lost
about 80,000 jobs, [music] roughly a
third of the entire sector. Landmen were
part of that. Your meeting lasts [music]
11 minutes. You box up your desk. Your
old field landman [music] stop calling.
Not because they're angry, but because
they're unemployed, too. You go home and
pull out that cardboard tube from under
the seat. You call Darlene. She tells
you the courthouse is quiet now. She
tells you it always comes back. She's
never wrong. Level nine, the lease sale.
You're watching an online auction where
a [music] company just bid more for one
square mile of desert than most people
will earn in 10 lifetimes.
It comes back.
In May of 2026, the Bureau of Land
Management held the largest onshore oil
and gas lease sale in US history. About

videos.full_text: Somewhere under a cow pasture in Texas, there's oil. And before a single drill touches the ground, somebody has to figure out who actually owns it. That somebody is you. You're a landman. Not a lawyer, not an engineer, not a rough neck. You're the person who digs through hundred-year-old courthouse books, knocks on farmhouse doors, and sits at kitchen tables [music] asking families to sign away the right to drill under their land. This year, the federal government auctioned off drilling rights in the Peran Basin, and one square mile sold for more than $350,000 an acre. Every one of those acres started [music] with a landman reading a dusty deed. You're about to start at the bottom of that business in a courthouse basement with a flashlight and a legal [music] pad. Level one, the courthouse. You're 23. You're sitting in a county courthouse basement at 8 in the morning and your entire job is reading handwriting from 1911. Every oil deal begins here in the deed records. Your boss hands you a list of trackcts and says, "Find out who owns them." So, you pull the giant leather [music] books off the shelves one by one and trace every sale, every inheritance, every divorce. The government doesn't track landmen as a job of their own. The closest category, title, examiners, and abstractors, [music] has a median of about $28 an hour. That's about right for you. The clerk behind the counter is a woman named Darlene, who has worked here 31 years [music] and knows every family in the county. She tells you which ones are going to fight. She's never [music] wrong. By noon, you've got a cramp in your hand, dust in your nose, and a family tree drawn [music] on a legal pad that looks like a spiderweb. By 5, you realize one of the owners died in [music] 1962 and never left a will. Level two, running title. The family living on this land doesn't own what's underneath it, and they have no idea. This is the part nobody outside the [music] business understands. In a lot of oil country, the land on top and the minerals underneath can be owned by completely [music] different people. Somebody's great-grandfather sold the farm in 1948, but kept the mineral rights, and those rights [music] got split between his eight kids, who split them between their kids. You run title all the way back, deed by deed, until you can [music] prove who owns every sliver. Today you find out a single quarter section has 26 [music] owners spread across nine states and two of them are in prison. You call your boss. He says, "Great. Find all of them." You buy a [music] second legal pad. Darlene brings you a cup of coffee without asking. You take it as [music] a sign that you're going to be here a while. Level three, the door. You're standing on a farmhouse porch holding a contract and the man inside is watching you through the curtain with a shotgun leaning by the door. You're a field landman. [music] Now, most field landmen are independent contractors hired through brokers to represent [music] the oil company to the landowner. Your job is to get leases signed. A lease [music] pays the owner two ways. a bonus upfront for every acre and a royalty, a share of whatever the well produces. In Pennsylvania, [music] state law won't even recognize a lease unless it guarantees the owner at least 1/8. The man on the porch finally opens [music] the door. His name is Walt. He's 74. He's been offered leases before, and he thinks every [music] oil company is a thief. You don't argue. You ask him about the old barn. 40 minutes later, [music] you're sitting at his kitchen table looking at photos of his wife, and the contract is still in your bag, which is exactly where it should be. Level four, the kitchen [music] table. Three brothers who haven't spoken in 9 years are sitting at the same kitchen table, and your contract is the only thing they agree is a bad idea. Walt's minerals didn't pass [music] to Walt alone. When his father died, they were split between him and his brothers. [music] One wants the money. One wants a higher royalty. One just wants to make the other two miserable. You learn that the hardest part of this job isn't geology or law. It's families. You explain the bonus. You explain the [music] royalty. You explain it again slower to the brother who [music] keeps saying you're a crook. Walt's daughter takes you aside on the porch and asks if this is a fair deal for her dad. You tell her to have a lawyer read it. She looks surprised that you said that. By sunset, two brothers have signed. The third tells you to get off his land. You drive home in the dark, already planning [music] which pie to bring next week. Level five. The boom. The motel is full. [music] The courthouse opens at 8:00. And there are already 20 landmen sitting on its front steps [music] at 6:00 in the morning. Oil prices are high and every company wants acorage at the same time. Suddenly, you're one of hundreds of landmen pouring into a small town that has one diner and [music] one stoplight. The courthouse record room gets so crowded the clerk starts handing out numbers like a deli counter. Day rates climb. You're making more money than you ever have, and you're spending half of it on a motel [music] room that smells like diesel. Everybody is racing. If a rival landman signs a family before you do, that acorage is gone. You eat lunch in your truck so you don't lose [music] your seat at the record table. Darlene, back in your old county, sends you a text. It just says, "Slow [music] down." You don't. Nobody slows down in a boom. That's how you know it's a boom. Level six, getting certified. You've done this for 5 years, and now a professional association wants you to prove it on a test. The American Association of Professional Landmen certifies landmen in levels, registered [music] landman, registered professional landman, and at the top, certified professional [music] landman. Without a college degree, the professional level takes five years [music] of real land work. The top certification takes at least seven, plus sponsors who already hold it, plus an exam you get 8 hours to finish. You study at night in that same motel room surrounded by old title [music] opinions. You learn the words you've been using for years and finally what they actually mean on paper. pooling, curative, depth severance. The certificate comes in the mail in a cardboard tube. You don't hang it up. You leave it in the truck under the [music] seat next to the second legal pad that started all of this. Level seven in-house. You traded your truck and your motel room for a downtown office with a view. [music] And the first week, you missed the dirt roads. An oil company hires you as an in-house landman. Now you're the one managing the field land men, trading acreage with other companies, [music] and negotiating the agreements that decide who drills what. Pay sites put the typical landman salary at around $100,000 a year. [music] There's no official government number for this job, so treat that as an estimate, [music] but your paycheck agrees with it. You wear a tie for the first time since your cousin's wedding. Your days are spreadsheets, [music] maps on giant screens, and meetings where engineers ask whether you've cleared title on a well they want to drill next month. You have. You always have. That's the job [music] now. Saying yes and making sure it's true. Level eight, the bust. Oil just fell off a cliff and the meeting on your calendar this afternoon has no title, [music] just an HR representative's name. Booms end. When prices collapse, [music] companies stop drilling. And when they stop drilling, they stop paying people to find more land. Researchers at the University of Houston [music] counted the damage from the last big crash. From late 2014 through mid 2020, [music] Houston's upstream oil industry lost about 80,000 jobs, [music] roughly a third of the entire sector. Landmen were part of that. Your meeting lasts [music] 11 minutes. You box up your desk. Your old field landman [music] stop calling. Not because they're angry, but because they're unemployed, too. You go home and pull out that cardboard tube from under the seat. You call Darlene. She tells you the courthouse is quiet now. She tells you it always comes back. She's never wrong. metadata.shortDescription:
Want to get into mineral rights? Start with Your First Mineral Prospect, my 30-minute, $27 workshop: https://learnminerals.com/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=organic&utm_campaign=what-does-a-landman-actually-do&utm_content=description_top

The term “landman” is getting thrown around a lot lately thanks to that new Taylor Sheridan show. But what does a landman actually do in real life?

Most days, I’m behind a desk—researching, sourcing, and negotiating deals.
 
But every now and then, you step out and meet the folks on the other side of those contracts. And that’s where the real stories live.

________________________________________________________________________

Own mineral rights? Get a private, no-obligation offer: https://deal.mineralsguy.com/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=organic&utm_campaign=what-does-a-landman-actually-do&utm_content=description_footer
Learn the mineral rights business ($27 workshop): https://learnminerals.com/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=organic&utm_campaign=what-does-a-landman-actually-do&utm_content=description_footer
Email Steven directly: steven@mineralsguy.com

________________________________________________________________________

About Minerals Guy:

Minerals Guy provides tailored content and resources to oil and gas mineral and royalty owners across the country with the goal of educating and empowering owners to better understand mineral rights as an asset class and the potential value of their minerals and royalties.

Steven Hatcher is the creator of Minerals Guy. He is a professional mineral buyer, an oil and gas attorney and has spent the last decade buying and selling oil and gas properties across the country. He is an expert in oil and gas mineral rights, having worked in the private practice of law, for oil and gas operators, and for mineral and royalty acquisition companies.

metadata.shortDescription:
Want to get into mineral rights? Start with Your First Mineral Prospect, my 30-minute, $27 workshop: https://learnminerals.com/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=organic&utm_campaign=what-landman-gets-completely-wrong&utm_content=description_top

If you’ve watched Landman, you’ve seen the Hollywood version of the oil and gas industry: drilling rigs, explosions, cartels, and crisis management. Great television. Terrible career advice.

In this video, I break down what a real Landman actually does and show you how people are using the same skill set to buy, broker, and invest in mineral rights.

The truth is that most Landmen aren’t running around oil fields putting out fires. They’re researching ownership records, tracing chain of title, analyzing mineral assets, talking to mineral owners, and putting deals together.

More importantly, those same skills can be used to build a business of your own.

In this video, you’ll learn:
✔ What the TV show Landman gets wrong
✔ What a real Landman actually does
✔ The difference between a contract Landman and a mineral buyer
✔ The 4-step mineral acquisition process
✔ The 5 core skills every successful Landman needs
✔ How one Learn Minerals member landed a $58,000 deal with no prior industry experience
✔ Why mineral rights are one of the largest overlooked asset classes in America

Whether you’re curious about becoming a Landman, learning mineral rights investing, or building a career in oil and gas, this video will give you the real roadmap, not the Hollywood version.

metadata.title: How to locate your mineral rights on a map (and research oil and gas wells)
metadata.author: Blue Mesa Minerals
metadata.shortDescription:
If you are like most people who inherit mineral rights, you have no idea where to start looking for information.

You might have inherited it from a relative that kept poor records, or perhaps you didn’t even know you owned mineral interest until a landman contacted you, offering to lease your minerals.

Even if you inherited your mineral from a well-organized relative, it’s still new to you, and everyone has to start somewhere.

Let’s start by locating the legal description, which will help you find the property on a public GIS viewer.  Once you’ve found your property, you can explore the wells in which you own interest as well as the oil and gas activity in the surrounding area.  Finally, all of the information should be added to a mineral management spreadsheet.

You can read more about locating your mineral interest, find your state's GIS, and download the Free Mineral Management Spreadsheet at:

https://bluemesaminerals.com/locating-your-minerals/

Here is the Texas Railroad Commission's Public GIS Viewer that I used in this video:

https://gis.rrc.texas.gov/GISViewer/

For those who want to sell their mineral rights, request a quote at:
https://learn.bluemesaminerals.com/
keywords: find mineral interest on a map

metadata.title: The Path of the Landman — Powering the World
metadata.author: AAPL America's Landman
metadata.shortDescription:
The Path of the Landman tells the story of the land professional's journey of converting ideas into energy. Bringing a fresh awareness of the landman's crucial role in the energy industry, it dispels myths and misconceptions while highlighting the importance of the land profession and energy business to our local communities, states, country and world by providing the basic necessities for a modern life, as well as national security and a strong economy.

Learn more about the video https://bit.ly/3RriAQt.

Learn more about AAPL https://bit.ly/3B2ywmw. 

Learn more about the AAPL Educational Foundation https://bit.ly/3O5jvTS.

metadata.title: How are Mineral Rights Valued? | How Oil and Gas Activity Impacts the Value of Your Mineral Rights
metadata.author: Steven Hatcher | Minerals Guy
metadata.shortDescription:
Own mineral rights? Get a private, no-obligation offer on your minerals: https://deal.mineralsguy.com/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=organic&utm_campaign=how-are-mineral-rights-valued-how&utm_content=description_top

In this video, I explain how oil and gas activity can affect the value of mineral rights, from leasing and permitting through drilling, completion, and production. I discuss how proximity to activity and development risk factor into value, and why mineral rights may be most valuable in the months after a new well begins producing.

What you'll learn:
- How pooling and drilling spacing units can include mineral owners in production
- The activity spectrum, from leasing and permitting to drilling, completion, and production
- Why proximity to activity and line of sight to development matter
- Why mineral rights may be most valuable in the months after first production

________________________________________________________________________

Want to get into the mineral rights business? Start with my 30-minute, $27 workshop: https://learnminerals.com/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=organic&utm_campaign=how-are-mineral-rights-valued-how&utm_content=description_footer
Get a private, no-obligation offer on your minerals: https://deal.mineralsguy.com/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=organic&utm_campaign=how-are-mineral-rights-valued-how&utm_content=description_footer
Email Steven directly: steven@mineralsguy.com

________________________________________________________________________

About Minerals Guy:

Minerals Guy provides tailored content and resources to oil and gas mineral and royalty owners across the country with the goal of educating and empowering owners to better understand mineral rights as an asset class and the potential value of their minerals and royalties.

Steven Hatcher is the creator of Minerals Guy. He is a professional mineral buyer, an oil and gas attorney and has spent the last decade buying and selling oil and gas properties across the country. He is an expert in oil and gas mineral rights, having worked in the private practice of law, for oil and gas operators, and for mineral and royalty acquisition companies.

Only two things in life are guaranteed: death and taxes. Mineral rights don't get an exception. A listener wrote in about a tiny, recurring property tax bill on non-producing minerals in Kansas and asked the question: what actually happens if I just don't pay it? We answered their question in MRP 340: Listener Questions July 2026 (https://mineralrightspodcast.com/mrp-340-listener-questions-july-2026/)  and that question prompted this episode, because the honest answer is that property tax on minerals is complicated — and getting it wrong can, in the wrong state, actually cost you the minerals themselves.
 

Be sure to check out the show notes at mineralrightspodcast.com (https://mineralrightspodcast.com/mrp-342-property-taxes-on-mineral-rights-and-what-happens-if-you-dont-pay/)  for links to the resources mentioned in this episode.

metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode, we explore the complex world of mineral rights with expert Matt Sands. Learn how mineral rights work, how to value and acquire them, and the opportunities they present for land investors.

If you are looking for resources on how to get started, please check out this special offer from Matt Sands. https://mineralrights.teachable.com/p/mineral-rights-basics-investing?affcode=1232686_dv2-zs_p

Chapters
00:00 Introduction to Mineral Rights
02:20 Understanding Mineral Rights and Their Value
04:33 Types of Mineral Rights
07:34 Getting Started in Mineral Rights Investing
11:28 Due Diligence and Title in Mineral Rights
19:02 Monetizing Mineral Rights
22:29 Leasing vs. Purchasing Mineral Rights
26:01 Geographical Focus in Mineral Rights Acquisition
32:03 Economics of Underwriting Mineral Rights Deals
32:32 Valuing Mineral Rights: The Basics
39:09 Mineral Rights vs. Surface Rights: What to Know
40:36 Building a Career in Mineral Investments
43:30 Navigating Land and Mineral Ownership
45:20 Tax Strategies and Conservation Easements
51:21 Educational Resources for Mineral Investors
56:07 Building a Team for Mineral Investments
Resources
https://mineralrightspodcast.com
https://mineralrights.teachable.com/p/mineral-rights-basics
