My guest in this episode is Matt Sands. Matt is an engineer with over 24 years of oil & gas industry experience. He was previously employed with Shell Exploration & Production Company and served in various engineering, planning, and leadership roles.  Matt owns Silverheels Investments LLC, a mineral rights and royalty interest consulting and investment company. He is currently the President of the National Association of Royalty Owners (NARO), Immediate Past President of the Rocky Mountain Chapter of NARO, and is a Certified Mineral Manager (CMM).

Matt graduated from the Colorado School of Mines with a BS in Engineering with a Mechanical Specialty and a Minor in Public Affairs.

When not helping other mineral owners, he enjoys spending time with his family in the Colorado outdoors cycling, camping, fishing, skiing, and golfing.

metadata.title: MRP 310:  Strategic Portfolio Management: How to Sell Mineral Rights at Peak Value
metadata.author: Matt Sands
metadata.shortDescription:
Many mineral owners face a common challenge: they have substantial wealth tied up in mineral rights, but their monthly royalty income has declined significantly as wells age and production drops.
 

In this episode, we explore when it makes strategic sense to sell portions of your mineral portfolio to create more stable cash flow, reduce concentration risk, and diversify into other asset classes like a rental property. We discuss how to identify which properties are at peak value and therefore ideal candidates for sale, the mechanics of 1031 exchanges that allow you to defer capital gains taxes, and practical strategies for finding reputable buyers. And while we generally recommend that you should hold on to your mineral rights, we challenge the conventional wisdom that you should "never sell" mineral rights. Instead, sophisticated asset management requires understanding your overall portfolio while acting proactively to maximize value to meet your changing financial needs.
 

As always, be sure to check out the show notes at mineralrightspodcast.com (https://mineralrightspodcast.com/mrp-310-strategic-portfolio-management-how-to-sell-mineral-rights-at-peak-value/)  for links to the resources mentioned!
 

Disclaimer: This episode and accompanying show notes are provided for general information purposes and should not be construed as financial, legal, or investment advice. For guidance specific to your situation, please consult with qualified legal and financial professionals.

metadata.title: MRP 293:  Why Your Royalty Checks Keep Dropping (And How to Predict What's Next)
metadata.author: Matt Sands
metadata.shortDescription:
In this technical but accessible episode, we demystify Decline Curve Analysis (DCA), the proven scientific method that oil companies have used for 80 years to predict how much oil and gas a well will produce over its lifetime. This episode is essential listening for mineral owners who want to understand how their future royalty payments are calculated and why their checks start high and then decline over time. Be sure to listen as I tell you how you can learn to forecast your future royalty payments yourself (and when you have your minerals valued you will understand the process that is used).+
 

As always, links to the resources mentioned can be found in the show notes at mineralrightspodcast.com (https://mineralrightspodcast.com/mrp-293-why-your-royalty-checks-keep-dropping-and-how-to-predict-whats-next/) .

metadata.title: Mineral Rights Explained: What You Own and Where to Start
metadata.author: National Association of Royalty Owners
metadata.shortDescription:
New to mineral rights? Whether you inherited minerals, received them as a gift, or are helping your family get organized, start with one question: what do these records actually tell you?

This practical introduction from the National Association of Royalty Owners (NARO) explains deeds, oil and gas leases, division orders, and royalty statements. Learn the difference between gross acres and net mineral acres, why an ownership fraction is different from a payment decimal, and where to look when records or royalty payments are missing.

Start with one property. Understand the documents. Ask your next question with more confidence.

Explore NARO membership by visiting https://www.naro-us.org/join.
Connect with other mineral and royalty owners, keep learning, and build the confidence to make informed decisions about what you own.

CHAPTERS
00:00 Where to start with mineral rights
00:18 Deeds, leases, division orders, and royalty statements
01:41 Mineral ownership and legal descriptions
02:50 Gross acres vs. net mineral acres
03:24 Undivided ownership vs. lease royalty
03:53 Finding your family's ownership records
04:42 Ownership records vs. company payment records
05:24 Payment decimals and missing royalties
06:05 Questions to ask, taxes, and protecting information
07:43 Your next step and NARO membership

What mineral-ownership question would you like us to explain next? Share your question in the comments, but keep personal and financial details private.

Subscribe for more practical mineral-owner education from NARO.

For general education, not individual legal or tax advice. Illustrations are fictional examples, not surveys or determinations of ownership. Laws, documents, and individual circumstances vary.

#MineralRights #RoyaltyOwners #NARO

segments.text: You may have inherited minerals, received a gift, or just starting to help your family get
organized. You don't have to sort everything out at once. Start with one property and one
question. What do these records actually tell you? Put the papers side by side.
Deeds and other title documents provide a written record of ownership transfers.
They're typically recorded with the county clerk and recorder's office or the equivalent office in
the county where the property is located. Look for what was granted, who received it, what was kept,
and the legal description of the property. Before signing anything, understand which rights the
document affects and who the person contacting you represents. If you have unfamiliar terms
before you, consult with a qualified professional before you commit. An oil and gas lease sets terms
for exploration, production, and royalties. Leasing development rights is different from
selling your mineral interest outright. If your property is already leased, try to find a copy of
the lease that impacts your interest. Its royalty provisions answer a different question from the
ownership fraction in a title document. A division order identifies the share of production revenue
the company plans to pay you for the property, the well, or the unit it covers. Your interest
on a division order is usually shown as a decimal. A unit can combine multiple tracks for development
and sharing production. A royalty statement explains a payment from sales of oil and gas
or other products. A purchase offer, a tax form, a property evaluation. Each serve a different
purpose. In the United States, surface rights and mineral rights can be held together or separately,
and either can have several owners. When mineral rights are severed from surface ownership,
they're called severed mineral rights. Mineral rights are interest in real property,
like a home or tract of land. You're dealing with ownership in real estate, not just a
royalty check. Think of property ownership as layers of a cake. Surface, mineral, water, and
air rights don't always belong to the same person. Even the right to lease minerals, and the right
to receive royalties can be separated. Rights may be transferred, leased, or sold separately,
depending on state law and what the documents say. Land is identified by a legal description,
not just a street address like many people are used to. The section township range and
county locate land in many states and other survey systems were also used across the United States.
In our example, the northeast quarter written as NE14 is 160 acres. Actual surveyed acreage of a
section can vary. Let's zoom in on that northeast quarter. 160 gross acres. That's the track's size,
not automatically the mineral acreage you may own. For the sake of this example, assume title records
establish that you own an undivided 1/8 mineral interest throughout the entire tract. 160 * 1/8 is
20 net mineral acres. The math is straightforward. Finding the title documents that support your
ownership fraction is the important part and also can be the more difficult part. Take a moment.
Do you think those 20 net mineral acres describe a separate corner or fractional mineral interest
across the whole tract? Many are surprised to find out it's a fractional interest across the whole
tract, not a fenced off corner. 1/8 mineral ownership is also different from a 1/8 lease
royalty rate. In minerals, when two numbers look alike, ask a share of what under which document?
A royalty statement is a starting point, not a complete ownership record. You may own
non-producing minerals that generate no current royalty payments. Search county records for your
family member or ancestor as the granter, the person who transferred an interest or the grantee,
the person who received an interest. Start with the county clerk and recording office
in the county where the property is located. Follow references to early
recorded documents and attached exhibits. Online availability of title records varies by county,
and some records go back further than others. If a record isn't online, ask the recording office
how to obtain it. It's possible you or a landman who researches property records may need to search
in person. Documenting ownership and updating the paying company's records are two different jobs.
The paying company may be the operator or another company. A check in your name doesn't
resolve a gap in the recorded chain of ownership. Requirements depend on the state, the situation,
and the company or operator. Check the company's owner relations guidance, or ask which records
they need. For unclear deed language, ownership disputes, transfers, or other legal questions,
contact an oil and gas attorney in the state where the property is located. Discuss operating cost
bills or joint interest billings with that attorney. Depending on the interest type,
different ownership obligations may be involved. Your payment decimal is the fraction used to
calculate your share of revenue for the interest or payment line it applies to. It isn't a list
of everything your family owns or automatically the fraction on a mineral deed. A nearby well
alone doesn't prove you're owed royalties. If you receive a division order, ask the paying
company which records and calculations support its decimal. For missing payments, ask whether funds
are being held in what's often called suspense, or maybe they're being accumulated towards a payment
minimum. You can also ask the operator or the company what records are needed to put you in pay
status. Official state unclaimed property programs are another place to check for unpaid funds.
When contacting an operator or paying company, include your owner number. If you don't have one,
share what you do have. The well name, legal description, county and state, and the family
member's name, who they may have in their records. Ask specific questions such as how a division
order decimal was calculated or which sales month a payment covers. Look for owner relations or a
designated owner contact on the company's official website before calling a general number. Follow
the company's submission guidance and keep the response with that property's records. Keep your
mailing address current with each paying company and ask the county recording and tax offices what
updates they need, too. Ask a tax professional knowledgeable about oil and gas or minerals,
about income taxes, and any separate local property taxes. Taxes shown on a royalty statement
may not cover everything you owe. Some mineral interests held for investment or business can
qualify for a 1031 exchange, which may defer tax when exchanged for other qualifying real estate.
A personal residence generally doesn't qualify. Strict rules and deadlines apply to 1031, so get
tax and exchange guidance before selling. Protect tax identifiers such as your social security
number and sensitive family or trust information. Before recording documents that may feel private,
ask an attorney what must be recorded and what can remain private. If an answer from an operator,
attorney, or other professional leaves a gap in what you feel like you need to know, make that
gap your next question. Your next step will depend on your unique situation. Keep asking questions,
keep learning, and take it one step at a time. The National Association of Royalty Owners was
founded by Owners for Owners. Since 1980, we've brought together mineral and royalty owners,
industry professionals, and dedicated advocates across the country to educate,
empower, and support people like you. Become an NRO member. Learn from others,
share your experience, and build the confidence to make informed decisions about what you own.
Wherever you are in your mineral ownership journey, you don't have to navigate it alone.

metadata.author: Royalty Clerk
metadata.shortDescription:
Your royalty check is one formula: volume times price times your decimal interest, minus severance tax and any deductions your lease allows. We work a sample oil line and a sample gas line end to end, show where your decimal comes from, explain Texas payment deadlines, and show how to check your own stub line by line.

Free tools from Royalty Clerk:
- Royalty calculator: https://royaltyclerk.com/tools/royalty-calculator?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=v3
- Texas lease lookup: https://royaltyclerk.com/texas-lease-lookup?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=v3

0:00 Intro
0:36 The formula
1:04 Your decimal
1:50 Volume
2:29 Price
3:01 Gross value
3:21 Tax and deductions
3:59 A gas line
5:15 When it's due
5:53 Check your own stub
6:33 Free tools

General information, not legal, tax or investment advice. Sample numbers, families and documents are illustrations, not real owners. For your own situation, talk to a Texas oil and gas or probate attorney.

metadata.title: Cessation, Dry Hole, & Continuous Operations Clauses (Oil & Gas 12.2)
metadata.author: Energy Law Professor
metadata.shortDescription:
Another common kind of constructive production clauses is the dry hole, cessation of production, or continuous operations clause. These related clauses are typically designed to let the oil and gas company keep a lease if the oil and gas company is consistently working to obtain oil and gas production from the property even if the primary term runs out during its labors, or even if production stops, or even if the first well it drills is dry. metadata.title: Vertical vs Horizontal Drilling | Directional & Multilateral Wells Explained | Lesson 7
metadata.author: Carbon Strata Solutions
metadata.shortDescription:
🎯 **Should you drill vertically, directionally, or horizontally?**

Choosing the right well configuration can influence reservoir access, drilling complexity, cost, and production performance.

Welcome to Lesson 7, the final lesson in our Drilling Engineering Learning Series.

**In this lesson, you will explore:**
- Vertical drilling and its applications.
- Directional drilling and well trajectory concepts.
- Horizontal wells and reservoir contact.
- Multilateral well configurations.
- Engineering considerations when selecting a well configuration.

Using **Explain → Demonstrate → Practise**, you will compare different drilling approaches and apply your understanding to an illustrative well-selection scenario.

🎓 Suitable for petroleum engineering students, drilling professionals, reservoir engineers, and beginners.

📚 Explore more engineering learning: https://carbonstrata.org

🏭 Need customised drilling engineering materials, university teaching resources, or professional training?

📩 Contact: support@carbonstrata.org

🔔 **SUBSCRIBE** for more practical engineering lessons, worked examples, and technical learning series from CarbonStrata.

#DirectionalDrilling #HorizontalDrilling #WellDesign #DrillingEngineering #PetroleumEngineering

segments.text: If drilling a vertical well were always
best, directional drilling would have
little purpose.
In practice, a reservoir may lie away
from the surface pad, be thin and
laterally extensive, or contain several
separate targets.
A well trajectory is therefore a
business and technical choice, not a
preference for a fashionable shape.
This final introductory lesson compares
four common configurations and asks you
to choose an initial concept for stated
cases.
The outcome is to distinguish vertical,
directional, horizontal, and
multilateral well configurations.
The practical competency is to recommend
a starting trajectory with a clear
rationale and one stated tradeoff.
You are screening concepts, not
producing a final trajectory design.
Real decisions need geological
uncertainty, casing and completion
design, torque and drag, geomechanics,
well integrity, access, cost, and
regulatory constraints.
The diagram compares four shapes.
A vertical well aims essentially beneath
its surface location.
A directional well follows a controlled
non-vertical path to reach an offset
target.
A horizontal well includes a lateral
section to increase contact along a
reservoir interval.
A multilateral well has multiple
branches from a shared main bore.
These descriptions explain geometry.
They do not tell us which option is
economic or safe in a specific field.
That requires screening against a real
objective.
Screening begins with the target and
constraints.
Is the reservoir directly below the
allowed pad?
Is steering required to avoid a surface
obstacle?
Would an extended reservoir contact
improve performance?
Would several branches create value
exceeding additional complexity?
Even if a horizontal well improves
potential contact, it may be harder to
drill, clean, case, or complete.
Good engineering compares the benefit
with the
cost and risk.
Our demonstration starts with a target
1.2 kilometers laterally away from the
permitted surface pad.
A vertical well from this pad would not
reach the target.
A directional trajectory is therefore
the logical starting concept.
We would still need to test steering
feasibility, downhole constraints,
geomechanics, equipment, collision risk,
costs, and completion requirements.
The demonstration teaches how a specific
constraint drives a preliminary
selection, not how to finalize a
directional well plan.
For your final practice, consider three
cases.
First, a reservoir target is directly
below the pad.
Second, the reservoir is long and thin
and may benefit from extended contact.
Third, a target is offset beneath a
restricted surface area.
Choose an initial well configuration for
each.
Give one technical advantage and one
tradeoff.
Pause the video for 5 minutes.
Make a three-row table and resume after
completing it.
The first screening choice is vertical
for the target beneath the pad.
The second could be horizontal if
reservoir continuity, completion
feasibility, and economics support the
choice.
The third is directional to reach the
offset target.
Multilateral wells may make sense for
multiple compartments, but they add
junction and completion complexity.
Full credit requires both the proposed
choice and the qualification.
A trajectory recommendation without a
stated assumption is not a complete
engineering argument.
We have now completed seven introductory
lessons.
You have traced the rig systems,
calculated fluid pressure, interpreted
drilling indicators, balanced pump
pressure and power, assessed the
pressure window, identified well control
warnings, and selected well path
concepts.
For the final competency portfolio,
submit your seven practice outputs and a
one-page summary explaining how these
decisions connect.
This series gives a structured
foundation, but it does not replace the
depth of the original 14 week university
course or field certification.

metadata.title: Oil and Gas Accounting 102: Practical Case Study | Income Statement & Balance Sheet
metadata.author: Duahbed Consult
metadata.shortDescription:
Ready to see Oil and Gas accounting in action? In this second session, we apply the theory introduced in our previous session to a real-world scenario. Watch as we solve a comprehensive practical question for Duahbed Oil Company, calculating the financial impact of exploration, dry holes, and development costs under both the Successful Efforts (SE) and Full Cost (FC) methods.

What You’ll Master in This Video:
Real-World Case Study: Step-by-step financial reporting for a Texas-based lease acquisition.
Income Statement Preparation: How to calculate Net Profit vs. Net Loss based on your chosen accounting method.
Balance Sheet Construction: Learn which costs—like G&G and exploratory dry holes—get capitalized as assets and which get written off.
DD&A Calculations: Understanding the difference in Depreciation, Depletion, and Amortization expenses between SE and FC.
The "Dry Hole" Impact: See exactly how an unsuccessful $1.4M exploratory well hits your bottom line differently under each method.


Video Chapters:
0:00 - Introduction & Case Study Overview 1:30 - Breaking Down the Costs: Acquisition, Exploration & Development 2:50 - Income Statement: Revenue & Expense Recognition 4:00 - Handling G&G and Exploratory Dry Holes 6:40 - Comparing Net Loss (SE) vs. Net Profit (FC) 8:50 - Balance Sheet: Statement of Financial Position 10:15 - Capitalizing Acquisition and Development Costs 13:30 - Calculating Total Assets and Net Book Value 15:45 - Final Comparison: Net Assets under SE vs. FC 16:15 - Preview: Joint Ventures, Underlift & Overlift 





Key Takeaways from the Duahbed Case:
Net Results: Under the Successful Efforts method, the company recorded a $1.3M Net Loss, while the Full Cost method showed a $110,000 Profit for the same period.
Asset Valuation: Full Cost accounting resulted in significantly higher Net Assets ($2.77M) compared to Successful Efforts ($1.36M) due to the capitalization of unsuccessful exploration.
Make sure to LIKE, COMMENT, and SUBSCRIBE to master your accounting finals! 🚀

metadata.title: CITRINE - WORKFLOW- Decline Curve Analysis
metadata.author: KAPPA Engineering
metadata.shortDescription: In this video the list of available DCA models is presented together with the multi-well scaling of decline curve analysis.

segments.text: decline curve analysis
PCA
one of the primary uses of citrine is to
perform decline curve analysis
for the purpose of estimating recoveries
for oil and gas Wells
the citrine project for this
demonstration contains several Wells
drawn from four different reservoirs
this video showcases a quick method to
perform decline curve analysis on all
the wells in a working set field H Wells
go to the analysis tab
in this mode only one well is displayed
in the dashboard at a time however
multiple decline curve models can be
displayed and compared
the analysis dashboard contains six
plots by default including decline
parameter and decline Factor versus time
plots in addition to standard decline
curve analysis plots
the plots can be changed if needed and
the layout can be saved as a template
Field age Wells is the well group of
interest and Field age well 25 is the
representative well for the group
and it is selected for decline curve
analysis
to initiate decline curve analysis click
on the create DCA button to bring up the
dialog several DCA models are available
in citrine including hyperbolic power
law exponential
stretched exponential Duong
logistic growth and SRV bounded
first create a hyperbolic model
in the time interval selection window
move the start time marker to exclude
the early Flowback data
click ok
the model has been matched to the Wells
data and added to the plots
the model can be manipulated on the
plots to get a better match or an
automatic regression can be used instead
to use the automatic regression click on
the parameters button to access the
model's parameters dialog
parameters can be adjusted manually
or using their slider and the check
boxes toggled off to exclude some
parameters from regression
set up the regression weight between
rate and cumulative production
both of which make up the objective
function
run the regression
close a window and observe the match has
now improved to add a second DCA model
click again on the create DCA button
this time select the Duong model
exclude the early time portion of the
data set the regression weight between
rate and cumulative production and click
ok
the second DCA model has been created
add a third DCA model this time a power
law exponential model
maximize the cumulative time plot
to see the forecast on the plots click
on the auto scale data and model to
reveal the entire span of data and model
this way DCA models can be compared and
used for making decisions on possible
range of eurs
minimize the plot
a tabulated comparison of the models can
be viewed by clicking on the compare
results button
this brings up the analysis results
window
all the analyzes for a given well can be
compared here
close the window
DCA analysis can be performed for each
well individually also citrine has the
end well functionality that allows the
applying of an existing analysis from
one well to all the other Wells
automatically
to accomplish this click on the end well
icon and in the resulting multi-well
analysis dialog ensure the model
selected is the desired DCA model
notice that the other Wells are selected
as the target
set the regression weight and then click
ok
notice that the model has been applied
to the other wells in the group
and it was adjusted to match each Wells
data
you can toggle between Wells to see the
match for each well
and individual Wells match can be
improved individually if needed
to see the DCA model for all wells in
one view switch mode to data and
activate a dashboard
select all Wells by clicking on the
select all button
set the plots to Auto scale data and
model
all the wells are displayed together
with their reference models
go back to analysis mode
to see a summary of the analysis results
for all the wells click on the results
summary icon
the results can be exported to economic
packages including Aries Mosaic or 2XL
let us export the results in an Aries
compatible format
this concludes this video on decline
curve analysis in citrine to learn more
please visit our website
for more information contact support at
kappaeng.com
or your local Kappa office

metadata.title: MRP 226:  How to Use the Texas Railroad Commission Website
metadata.author: Matt Sands
metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode we walk you step-by-step how to use the Texas Railroad Commission Website to find your minerals or royalties on a map to determine if you should be getting paid on a well. We also show you how to download important documents related to your wells, how to see how much oil & gas was produced and sold in a given month, and more.
 

Be sure to check out the accompanying YouTube video (https://youtu.be/gFgW6n9nb-c)  to see this in action.
 

As always, show notes with the links to the resources mentioned in this episode can be found at mineralrightspodcast.com (https://mineralrightspodcast.com/mrp-226-how-to-use-the-texas-railroad-commission-website) .

metadata.shortDescription:
The Railroad Commission of Texas' Case Administration Service Electronic System (RRC CASES) allows you to search and view the agency's case information online, including processed case documents. The case information is updated throughout the day.
https://www.rrc.texas.gov/hearings/rrc-cases/

metadata.shortDescription:
In Episode 11 of ComboCast, the team takes a deep dive into the Haynesville Shale, exploring the surge in drilling activity, major acquisitions, and renewed investment in one of North America's most active natural gas plays. From international investors and LNG demand to rising development costs and evolving well economics, the team breaks down what's driving interest in the basin and why operators continue to invest despite fluctuating natural gas prices.

The team also breaks down ComboCurve's latest Haynesville Top Wells Report, analyzing more than 2,000 wells to uncover production trends, well performance, and key economic metrics across the basin's major subplays. They explore the impact of modern completion techniques, redevelopment opportunities, and the factors influencing IRR and well profitability. Plus, the team answers a question from a Texas A&M engineering student about what a career in petroleum engineering looks like and the opportunities available in the industry.

Chapters:
00:00 - Introduction
01:25 - Why the Haynesville Is Gaining Attention
02:38 - Haynesville Deal Activity vs. the Permian
03:33 - LNG Demand and International Investment
05:43 - Natural Gas Prices and Well Economics
06:39 - Western Haynesville and New Development
10:55 - Haynesville History and Redevelopment Opportunities
14:20 - Haynesville Subplays and IRR Performance
16:59 - Breaking Down the Haynesville Top Wells Report
18:40 - Well Performance, Production Data, and Economics
21:57 - Comstock, Jerry Jones, and New Investments
26:06 - A Day in the Life of a Petroleum Engineer

Learn more about ComboCurve

metadata.title: [whitson webinar] Advancing Gas EOR in Shale: Lessons from a Chevron-led Permian Pilot
metadata.author: Whitson Academy
metadata.shortDescription:
In this webinar, Devesh Kumar shares lessons from a Chevron-led gas EOR pilot in the Permian Basin, exploring what was learned from taking gas injection EOR into the field in a shale reservoir and what those results can teach us about future unconventional EOR development.

🎙️ Presenter: Devesh Kumar, Chevron
📅 Recorded:September 16, 2026
🕘 Original Live Session: 9:00–10:00 AM CST | 8:00–9:00 AM MST | 16:00–17:00 CEST


Originally presented at URTeC 2026, **“Advancing Gas EOR in Shale: Lessons from a Chevron-Led Permian Basin Pilot”** brings real field experience into a topic that is often dominated by modeling and theory.

The work was completed by D. Kumar, J. Alvarez, P. Takulhoon, K. Krezinski, A. Rey, M. Srivastava, and T. Malik of Chevron.

metadata.title: Utica Shale Explained: The $114B Oil Play Under Ohio (And Your Power Bill)
metadata.author: FutureWise Energy
metadata.shortDescription:
Utica Shale Explained: The $114B Oil Play Under Ohio (And Your Power Bill)

The Utica Shale under eastern Ohio, western Pennsylvania, and West Virginia just quietly became one of America’s most important oil and gas stories. Oil output from the Utica/Point Pleasant hit a record 48 million barrels in 2025, up nearly 40% in a single year, while the basin still supplies a meaningful slice of U.S. gas. In this FutureWise Energy deep‑dive, we cover how the Utica went from “gas below the Marcellus” to a record‑setting oil play, EOG’s $5.6B Encino acquisition and “foundational play” strategy, the rise of Ascent, Gulfport, Infinity, EQT and others, the impact of AI data centers and LNG exports, and what thousands of remaining locations and ~$4/Mcf breakevens mean for prices and jobs over the next 10–20 years.

That's where operators now chase light oil with a lot of associated gas and natural gas liquids. Slide east and deeper, and you hit a a rich gas and condensate belt. metadata.title: Range Resources Marcellus Shale Field Tour
metadata.author: Range Resources Corporation
metadata.shortDescription: Take a complete look at how Range develops Marcellus shale wells.  We take a look at planning, drilling, completions and ultimately  production from the shale formation.

metadata.title: Working Interests in Oil & Gas: Cash Flow and Tax Breaks for Physicians | PIMD Podcast
metadata.author: Passive Income MD
metadata.shortDescription:
Could oil & gas “working interest” be the most underutilized tax and cash flow strategy for high-income professionals?

In this episode of the Passive Income MD Podcast, Peter Kim interviews Troy Eckard, CEO of Eckard Enterprises, to break down the opportunities—and risks—of investing directly in U.S. energy development.

💡 Key Takeaways:
✅ Working interest vs. mineral rights explained through a real estate analogy.
✅ Massive tax advantages: potential 100% year-one deductions under current legislation.
✅ How modern drilling technology reduces risk and boosts recovery.
✅ Expected payout timelines: first checks often within months, with the majority of capital returned in 1–2 years.
✅ Why due diligence and operator experience are essential before investing.

🌐 Explore educational resources: Eckard Insights App & videos
📲 Learn more about Troy Eckard’s work: Eckard Enterprises

📲 Follow us on Instagram: @passiveincomemd
💬 Join our Facebook community: Passive Income Docs
🎧 Listen on Apple & Spotify: The Passive Income MD Podcast

metadata.title: MRP 203:  How to Navigate Inheritance Issues with Minerals and Royalties
metadata.author: Matt Sands
metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode, we talk about how to navigate inheritance issues with mineral rights and royalties. Whether you're an heir that finds yourself in possession of these valuable interests, or someone who wants to ensure a smooth transition for future generations, inheriting mineral rights and royalties can be a complex and challenging process. 
 

We provide valuable insights into these challenges and the considerations involved in inheriting mineral rights and royalties. In addition to discussing the importance of understanding what you own and how to manage it we cover strategies for transferring ownership and avoiding inheritance disputes.
 

Download my free Inheritance Resource Guide for the complete list of my favorite resources to help you on your journey! (https://unique-motivator-6128.ck.page/a9a5938274)

Kyle D. Venema, owner and founder of Venergy Momentum Oil & Gas, answers your most common questions about mineral and royalty ownership. For more information, visit our extensive FAQ page at www.venergymomentum.com/faq.

metadata.title: Vertical, Deviated & Horizontal Wells Explained | Drilling Manual
metadata.author: Energy Vision Global
metadata.shortDescription:
In this video, I explain the difference between vertical, deviated, and horizontal wells in a simple and practical way.

You will learn:

what a vertical well is

what a deviated well is

what a horizontal well is

why these well types are used in oil and gas operations

how well trajectory depends on target location, reservoir geometry, and drilling objectives

This video is useful for:
oil and gas students, fresh drilling engineers, petroleum engineers, geologists, wellsite professionals, and anyone who wants to understand well planning basics.

If you are learning drilling engineering or directional drilling, this video will help you build a strong basic concept.

Topics covered:
vertical well explained
deviated well explained
horizontal well explained
difference between vertical deviated and horizontal wells
directional drilling basics
well trajectory in oil and gas
petroleum engineering basics

Subscribe to Energy Vision Global for more videos on oil & gas, environment, and engineering concepts.

#oilandgas 
#drillingrig 
#OilAndGas 
#DrillingEngineering 
#directionaldrilling  
#petroleumengineering  
#VerticalWell 
#DeviatedWell 
#HorizontalWell 
#energyvisionglobal 
#Fun with Drilling Engineering
#offshore oil rig 
#Erigworld-Ajay Verma
keywords: difference between vertical deviated and horizontal wells

segments.text: Hello and welcome to Energy Vision
Global. In today's session, we will
understand the difference between
vertical,
deviated
and horizontal whales in a simple and
practical way. This is one of the most
important basic concept in drilling and
directional well planning especially for
students, fresh engineers and
professionals working in oil and gas
operations.
So let's begin with a simple idea.
A well is drilled hole in the earth
created to reach a subsurface target.
The target may be an oil reservoir, a
gasbearing formation or a zone plant for
injection,
evolution or monitoring.
Now, one important point to understand
is that not all whales are drilled in
the same direction. The whale path
depends on several factors such as the
location of the target, the reservoir
geometry,
surface restrictions
and the overall production objective.
Based on that, whales are commonly
classified into three main types.
vertical whales, deviated whales and
horizontal whales.
Let's look at them one by one.
A vertical whale is the simplest type of
whale. It is drilled almost straight
downward from the surface towards the
target. In this case, the bottom of the
whale is nearly directly below the rig
location.
A common point many people ask is when
do we choose a vertical whale?
A vertical whale is usually selected
when the reservoir target lies directly
below the rig and there is no strong
need to change the direction of the
whale path.
In practical terms, this type of whale
is simpler to plan, easier to control
and generally less complex from a
directional drilling perspective.
So the main advantage of a vertical W is
its simplicity.
At the same time there is an important
limitation
because the veil intersects the
reservoir over a short interval.
Reservoir contact is often smaller
compared with the horizontal well.
Now let's move to the deviated well.
A deviated whale is intentionally
drilled away from the vertical
direction. Instead of going straight
down, the whale is guided at an angle to
reach a target that is not directly
below the rig. This is where the
difference start to become more
interesting.
One thing many viewers wonder is whether
a deviated whale is the result of an
unwanted change in direction. In fact,
it is not. A deviated whale is planned
intentionally as part of directional
drilling.
So why is this done? There are several
practical reasons. Sometimes the target
lies away from the drilling location.
In other cases, surface access may be
restricted by infrastructure,
current offshore platform positions or
environmental limitations.
In many developments, multiple wells are
drilled from a single pad of platform
and deviated wells make that possible.
This means the main advantage of a
deviated well is flexibility. It allows
engineers to reach subsurface targets
that cannot be accessed efficiently with
a simple vertical wheel. However,
compared with a vertical well, it
requires more careful planning, better
directional control, and accurate survey
monitoring.
Now, let's discuss the horizontal whale.
A horizontal whale usually starts as a
vertical well. Then at a plant depth,
the well begins to build angle, passes
through a curved section and finally
continues almost horizontally the
reservoir.
This naturally leads to an important
point. Why are horizontal wells so
important in modern drilling? The answer
is reservoir contact.
Instead of crossing the formation over a
short interval, the veil remains inside
the reservoir for a much longer
distance. The larger contact area can
significantly improve production
potential.
So the main advantage of a horizontal
whale is that it maximize exposure of
the producing formation. This is
especially valuable in thin reservoirs
and in developments where production
efficiency is critical.
Of course, the benefits comes with added
complexity. Horizontal whales are more
demanding to design, drill and complete.
They often require advanced directional
drilling tools, accurate realtime
measurements and in many cases gering
support.
Now let's simplify the difference
between all three. A vertical well goes
straight down and is the simplest
option. A deviated well is drilled at an
angle to reach a target away from the
rig location. A horizontal well starts
vertically, changes direction and then
continues through the reservoir
horizontally to maximize reservoir
contact. So in practical terms, vertical
wells means simplicity and direct
access.
Deviated whale means directional
flexibility
and horizontal veil means greater
reservoir exposure.
Now why does this matter in real
operations?
Because understanding these well types
is essential for drilling engineers,
directional drillers, MWD and LWD
personnel, geologist and anyone involved
in well planning or field development.
Once this concept is clear, it becomes
much easier to understand why different
wells are planned in different ways and
why trajectory designed is so important
in oil and gas operations.
So to summarize today's session,
a vertical whale is drilled almost
straight downward and is the simplest
whale type. A deviated whale is
intentionally drilled at an angle to
reach a target away from the rig
location.
A horizontal well starts vertically then
runs and continues through the reservoir
horizontally to maximize formation
contact.
Each of these field types has its own
purpose, advantages and operational
importance in the oil and gas industry.
Thank you for watching Energy Vision
Global. If you found this session
useful, don't forget to like, share, and
subscribe to the channel. And let me
know in the comments which oil and gas
topic you would like to see next on
Energy Vision Global.

metadata.title: How to Use the Oklahoma Corporation Commission Website to Find Your Mineral Rights
metadata.author: Matt Sands
metadata.shortDescription:
Justin and I show you how to use the Oklahoma Corporation Commission website map to find your mineral rights and royalties to determine if you should have an interest in an oil and gas well.  We also show you how to search for your wells to download official production data from the Oklahoma Tax Commission website to help you audit your royalty checks.

My Mineral Management Basics Online Course - Understand what you own. Gain the power to manage your minerals and royalties: https://mineralrights.teachable.com/p/mineral-rights-basics

Podcast Episode where I show you how to audit your royalties: 
https://mineralrightspodcast.com/mrp-97-a-quick-end-of-year/

Spotify: https://bit.ly/3d3Ey7l

Google Podcasts: https://bit.ly/36KZmOP

...while you are there, please leave a rating and review

metadata.title: The Largest Single Natural Gas Deposit Ever Discovered in America
metadata.author: GeoScope
metadata.shortDescription:
The Largest Single Natural Gas Deposit Ever Discovered in America.

In 2004, a geologist talked his company into re-entering a well they had already written off. The rock he wanted to test had been drilled through, logged, and ignored for a hundred and twenty years.

Two years earlier, the USGS had assessed that formation at under two trillion cubic feet of gas — a rounding error. Today it's the largest single natural gas deposit ever found in America, and the reason the United States became the world's largest LNG exporter.

This is the story of the Marcellus Shale: why it was invisible in plain sight, what had to go right 390 million years ago for it to exist, and why the thing that finally unlocked it wasn't a technology at all.

in southwestern Pennsylvania, where
nothing about the surface suggests
energy of any kind. And yet, beneath

Hayfields, tree lines, a gravel road, 20

Road wouldn't know to slow down.

20-story building is tall.
It doesn't announce itself.
No seeps, no domes, nothing at surface
that hints at scale. And unlike almost
every other great deposit on Earth, it
didn't need to hide.
It was never hidden at all.
Drillers punched straight through it for
120 years and logged it as a nuisance.

17 years later, the same agency would

The formation is the Marcellus Shale.
And what makes the Marcellus exceptional

sitting in plain sight the entire time.
And the reason nobody could see it
wasn't a failure of exploration.

>> It was a failure of definition.
This is Geoscope. And this is the story
of how the largest natural gas deposit
in America spent 120 years being thrown
away.
The Appalachian Basin is the oldest
producing oil and gas region on Earth.
The modern industry starts here in 1859.

else.
And drillers noticed it.
Black shale gives gas shows. It kicks.
It flares.

It was so reliably unproductive, it
became a landmark. You knew where you
were the moment you hit it.
It also had a category, and the category
was the problem.
The Marcellus was a source rock, the
kitchen where hydrocarbons are cooked,
not the pantry where they're stored.
Source rocks make gas. Reservoirs hold
gas.

In 2003, Range Resources drilled a well

where somebody compared that Alabama

ft.

[music] free.

metadata.title: How to Find Oil & Gas Info for North Dakota (For Free!)
metadata.author: Matt Sands
metadata.shortDescription:
In this video, we show you how to find oil & gas data using the North Dakota Department of Mineral Resources – Oil & Gas Division website.  Unlike most states, North Dakota requires a paid subscription to download important documents or to see how much oil & gas was produced by your wells in a given month.

Be sure to watch until the end for an easy way to view production data for your wells for free.

We go over some advanced topics in this video.  If you are just getting started and want to learn more about the basics of how to manage your minerals & royalties (or the basic due diligence steps when researching a potential property to buy), check out my online course, Mineral Management Basics:

https://mineralrights.teachable.com/p/mineral-rights-basics

What you'll learn in Mineral Management Basics

Across seven separate course modules, you'll learn everything you need to know about the basics of mineral management:

- Introduction to Oil and Gas Interests
- Important Documents for Mineral and Royalty Owners
- How to Perform a Title Search
- How to Locate Your Property
- Discover the Oil and Gas Potential of your Property
- (BONUS) Find out if you have missing royalties!

Links Mentioned in this Video:

The Show Notes with links to other helpful resources:
https://mineralrightspodcast.com/mrp-238-how-to-find-oil-and-gas-info-for-north-dakota/

Free Royalty Audit Worksheet. Keep track of your wells, perform a quick end of year royalty audit against your 1099’s, or do a full audit, all using this helpful tool:
https://unique-motivator-6128.ck.page/b0cb60b55c

North Dakota DMR Oil & Gas Website:
https://www.dmr.nd.gov/oilgas/

MRP 134: Overview of the Williston Basin and Bakken Shale:
https://mineralrightspodcast.com/mrp-134-overview-of-the-williston-basin-and-bakken-shale/

PECAN TREE OIL & GAS: Pecan Tree was founded by Tracy Lenz as Limited Liability Company in January 2020 (registered Texas Engineering Firm F-21124) to bridge the gap between mineral owners and the confusing, high-dollar world that is oil and gas. After being on the operator side for over a decade, Tracy witnessed firsthand how mineral owners rarely can afford the same data, experts, or software to be on a level playing field with the operators and buyers, yet have MORE at stake when deciding what to do with their minerals. Pecan Tree’s focus and efficiency make these resources available without a hidden agenda. We don’t buy minerals, we don’t work with billion dollar companies, and we run our shop 100% debt free. This flexibility lets us be innovative with technology, maintain the highest of standards (work quality, customer service, and ethics), and tailor pricing and scope to each client’s specific needs. 

~~~~~~~~~~~~~ 
ABOUT TRACY: 
- Over 16 years in the industry with over 14 years of experience analyzing and evaluating oil & gas properties 
- Licensed Professional Engineer in the State of Texas, PE# 132654 
- Certified Mineral Appraiser by the International Institute of Mineral Appraisers (IIMA), #2020-06 
- Master of Science in Petroleum Engineering from the University of Southern California 
- Bachelor of Science in Petroleum Engineering from the University of Texas at Austin 
- Experience with oil & gas minerals in Texas, Oklahoma, New Mexico, Louisiana, Gulf of Mexico, North Dakota, Utah, Colorado, and Kansas.

metadata.title: THE COST OF DRILLING AN OIL WELL | 8 Million and NO GUARANTEES
metadata.author: The Crude Files
metadata.shortDescription:
Right now, somewhere in West Texas, a crew is drilling two miles down and then two miles sideways. By the time they finish, about $8 million is gone. For one hole. And nobody can promise it will pay back.

In this video we follow every dollar of a modern shale well, from a handshake on a farm road to the first barrel in a tank. We look at why fracking costs more than the drilling itself, why wells are cheaper per foot than ten years ago but still need expensive oil to make sense, and the bill almost nobody mentions: plugging the well when the oil stops.

What you'll learn:
• Three very different wells: old vertical, modern shale and deepwater offshore, and what each one costs
• Leases, bonuses and royalties (12.5%–25%), seismic surveys, permits and the well pad
• The rig day rate and why "speed is money" in modern drilling
• How the well is built: surface casing, blowout preventer, the curve and a two-mile lateral
• Why completion (fracking) is often the biggest bill, and the "$700 per lateral foot" number
• Why small operators pay more for the same rock
• The full receipt: roughly $7–10 million for a Permian shale well
• The Dallas Fed breakeven: about $65 a barrel for a new well
• Offshore: about half a million dollars a day for a deepwater rig
• Marginal wells, orphan wells and the cost of plugging
• Why a shale well loses more than 70% of its output in the first year

CHAPTERS
0:00 One hole, $8 million
0:38 Three wells, three price tags
1:48 Before the bit: leases, seismic and permits
3:32 The rig: the meter starts running
6:26 Fracking: breaking the rock
9:03 After the hole: oil, water and gas
10:09 Adding it all up
11:04 The $65 question
11:58 Offshore: half a million a day
12:51 The small guy's gamble
13:37 The bill at the end: plugging the well
14:17 The hole that starts dying on day one

⚠️ Costs are approximate and vary by location, operator and year. Figures marked "reported" or "illustrative" on screen are estimates. Educational only, not investment advice.

SOURCES
• U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA): Permian share of U.S. crude production
• Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas, Dallas Fed Energy Survey, Q1 2025 (breakeven prices)
• Permian Resources, Q4 2025 results (drilling and completion cost per lateral foot), via Energy Central
• Enverus data via Oil & Gas Leads (well cost by operator type)
• Rystad Energy data via American Petroleum Institute (shale well decline)
• TGS (Permian average breakeven estimate)
• Railroad Commission of Texas (drilling permits)
• Landgate, OilPrice.com, Caddo Minerals (royalty rates)

Footage: Pexels. Archive images: U.S. Coast Guard, NASA, NOAA/CIRA, USGS, USFWS, BLM and Library of Congress (public domain). Music: original.

In this video, we're going to follow every dollar, from a handshake on a

We'll see why a well that costs less than it did 10 years ago still needs
expensive oil to make sense.
And at the end, we'll look at the cost almost nobody mentions, the one that
arrives after the oil stops.
Let's start with the first question.
Which well are we even talking about?
Because there isn't just one answer.
When people ask, how much does it cost to drill an oil well, they're picturing
one thing. In reality, there are three very different worlds.
World one, the old school vertical well, a straight hole, maybe a few thousand
feet deep in places like Kansas, Oklahoma, or parts of Pennsylvania.
This is the classic picture most of us have, a pump rocking up and down
on a lease road. Cost? It depends hugely on depth and location, but think
from a few hundred thousand dollars to a few million.
World two, the modern shale well.
This is what powers American oil today, a long horizontal well, drilled
and then fractured with high pressure water and sand.
In the Permian Basin, you're typically looking at somewhere around seven
to ten million dollars per well.
World three, offshore, rigs that float in thousands of feet of water, drilling
into the seabed. The numbers here leave the others far behind, and we'll
get to them near the end. The middle category matters most because that's
where America's oil actually comes from.
Today, the Permian Basin alone produces roughly half of all the crude oil
in the United States. So for most of this video, we're going to build one
of those wells, step by step.
But before anything is drilled, a lot of money gets spent on paper.
Every well begins with a person most Americans have never heard of, the
landman. A landman's job is to find out who owns what, and in the United
States, that is a stranger question than it sounds.
Because here, the land on top and the minerals underneath can be owned by
two different people. The company, called the Operator, has to sign a lease
with every mineral owner in the drilling area.
A lease usually pays two things.
First, a bonus, a one -time payment, usually quoted per acre, just for signing.
Second, a royalty, a share of everything the well produces.
Royalties today commonly run from about 1 eighth, 12 .5 percent, up to a
quarter, 25 percent, depending on how hot the area is and how badly the
operator wants the acreage.
That sounds small compared to the cost of the well.
But in a hot area, a company may be leasing thousands of acres.
Leasing alone can cost tens of millions before a single rig shows up.
Next comes the science. Geologists and engineers study seismic surveys,
old well logs, and rock samples.
They are trying to answer a single question.
Where, exactly, and how deep?
Then the paperwork. In Texas, you file for a drilling permit with the Railroad
Commission. Other states have their own agencies.
There are rules on spacing, on protecting water, on where the well can sit.
Finally, the physical preparation.
Bulldozers clear a pad, often five acres or more.
Crews build roads strong enough for trucks that weigh tens of tons.
They dig a lined pit or set up tanks for drilling fluid.
They bring in water. All of that, the pad, the road, the permitting, can
easily cost hundreds of thousands of dollars.
And the rig hasn't arrived yet.
Now it does. The day the bit first touches the ground has a name in the
industry. Spud. The well has been spudded in.
And from that moment, a meter is running.
A modern land rig is not owned by the oil company.
It's rented from a drilling contractor.
The rig, the crew, the fuel, the mud, the cement, and a long list of specialists
all built by the day. Daily costs for the whole spread can reach tens of
thousands of dollars. And that's before the expensive extras.
So here is the secret of modern drilling.
Speed is money. Every hour you save is cash you keep.
Companies have become obsessed with this.
In the last decade, drilling a Permian well went from a slow, careful job,
to something like a race. Operators now regularly brag about records.
The fastest well, the most feet drilled in a day.
Those records are why the cost of a well can fall even while steel, fuel,
and labor go up. So how does the well get built?
Step one, the surface hole.
The first section is drilled just a few hundred to a couple thousand feet
down. Why so shallow? Because the first thing the crew must protect is groundwater.
Once this hole is drilled, they lower a steel pipe called casing and pump
cement around it. That steel and cement sleeve is what separates the oil
well from the freshwater aquifers above.
It's one of the most important and most regulated steps in the entire process.
Step two, the blowout preventer.
On top of the wellhead goes a massive stack of valves, the BOP.
Its entire job is to slam shut if the well tries to flow when it shouldn't.
If you remember one piece of safety equipment from this video, it's this
one. We'll see later what happens when it fails.
Step three, going deeper. The crew drills thousands of feet more, running
more casing and cementing at each time.
The hole gets narrower as it goes, like a telescope folding in on itself.
Step four, the turn. Near the target layer, the drilling assembly begins
to curve. Over a few hundred feet, the bit goes from vertical to horizontal.
This is called the build section or the curve.
Step five, the lateral. Now the bit runs sideways through the oil bearing
rock for one mile, two miles, sometimes more.
In today's Permian wells, laterals of 10,000 feet or longer are common.
A driller sitting at the surface steers this bit with real -time data, keeping
it inside a layer of rock that may be only a few dozen feet thick from miles
away. Think about that. They are hitting a target, the thickness of a house,
at a depth of two miles while moving sideways.
And they do it in roughly a couple of weeks.
When the lateral is done, the last string of casing goes in and is cemented
in place. The drilling cost, the rig, the bits, the fluids, the steel, the
crews, often land somewhere in the range of two to four million dollars
for a modern shale well. The well exists now, but it isn't producing a drop.
To make it produce, you must break the rock.
Here's a fact that surprises most people.
In a modern shale well, drilling is often not the biggest expense.
The biggest expense is completion.
Completion is everything required to turn a hole into a producer, and the
heart of completion is hydraulic fracturing, fracking.
The rock that holds this oil is tight.
Shale and tight sandstone are like stone sponges with the holes sealed.
Oil is trapped in microscopic pores that don't connect.
A simple hole won't free it, so the crew creates the connection.
They lower perforating guns, which fire small shaped charges through the
casing and cement, punching holes into the rock.
Then trucks pump fluid down the well at enormous pressure, enough to crack
the rock itself. The fluid is mostly water, mixed with sand and a small
amount of chemicals. The sand's job is to prop the cracks open after the
pressure is released, and they don't do this once.
A two mile lateral is divided into dozens of stages, each fractured in turn.
Perforate, pump, plug. Perforate, pump, plug.
Dozens of times. How much goes in?
Millions of gallons of water per well, and millions of pounds of sand.
A big frack job looks less like a drilling site and more like a military
operation. Dozens of pumping trucks, sand storage towers, water lines laid
across the landscape. This is expensive.
Pump crews, sand, water handling, fuel, equipment.
And the longer the lateral, the more stages, the more everything.
If you remember only one number from this chapter, it's this one.
Oil companies measure their cost, not just per well, but per lateral foot.
In late 2025, one of the biggest Permian operators reported drilling and
completion costs of roughly $700 per lateral foot.
Do the math on an 11,000 foot lateral, and you get about $7 .7 million.
Another report put the same figure at around $775 per foot in 2024.
Industry data tracking drilling and completion across the lower 48 shows
averages ranging from the mid $6 million range to the low $9 million range,
depending on the company. The smallest operators typically pay the most,
around $9 million per well, because they don't have the buying power or
the efficiency of the giants.
Small and private equity backed operators with tightly run programs have
averaged around $6 to $7 million.
Same rock, same oil. A gap of roughly $2 million per well, just from how
well the company has run. Now the well is fractured.
Next comes a stage called flowback, when the well is opened and the pressure
pushes water, sand, and finally, oil and gas back up.
And now, finally, you get something to sell.
But you still can't sell it.
Oil doesn't come out of a well as a clean liquid.
It comes out as a messy stream of oil, water, and natural gas, often all
mixed. So the operator needs facilities, separators to split oil from water

to handle the produced water, and a way to deal with the gas.
That gas is a quiet problem.
Shale oil wells produce lots of gas alongside the oil.
If there's no pipeline to carry it, the gas has to be burned off, flared.
That's why you sometimes see flames at night on oil fields from space.
In the Permian, the ratio of gas to oil has been climbing for a decade,
which makes gas handling a growing part of the budget.
Then there's artificial lift.
A fresh shale well can flow on its own for a while, driven by pressure.
But as pressure drops, you need pumps.
Classic pump jacks, or electric submersible pumps, or gas lift systems.
Facilities and equipment can add hundreds of thousands of dollars to well
costs, and in some cases, more than a million.
Let's add it up. In illustrative modern Permian shale well, round numbers
roughly looks like this. Site, roads, permits, a few hundred thousand dollars.
Drilling, roughly two to four million.
Completion, the fracking, roughly three to five million.

Total, somewhere around seven to ten million dollars, depending on the lateral
length, the depth, the geology, and the company.
figures are approximate and vary by operator and basin.
Now, a number that might feel off.
Is that expensive or cheap?

Exxon, Chevron, Shell, BP.

metadata.title: This Hidden Oil Field Beneath Texas's Permian Basin Could Change Everything
metadata.author: GeoFins
metadata.shortDescription:
This Hidden Oil Field Beneath Texas's Permian Basin Could Change Everything

West Texas oil isn't a secret. People already know the Permian Basin, the pump jacks stretching to the horizon, the drilling that started in the 1920s, the fracking boom of the last fifteen years. What almost nobody knows is that two miles beneath nearly every one of those wells sits a separate oil reserve nobody properly measured until 2016, rock that operators had been drilling straight through for decades without ever assessing it on its own terms.

It put technically recoverable resources at 20 billion barrels of oil and 16 trillion cubic feet of associated gas, nearly three times larger than the entire Bakken and Three Forks system in North Dakota. That the same agency had assessed just three years earlier, and at the time, the single largest continuous oil resource the USGS had ever measured anywhere in the country in the agency's entire history of conducting these assessments. That record didn't even last two years. In December of 2018, the agency assessed the Wolfcamp Shale again, this time in the Permian's other major sub-basin, the Delaware Basin in Far West Texas and Southeastern New Mexico. This time including an overlying formation called the Bone Spring alongside it in the same combined estimate. The new number came back at 46 and 1/2 billion barrels of oil, more than double the 2016 figure, alongside 281 trillion cubic feet of gas, and 20 billion barrels of natural gas liquids on top of that. The Interior Secretary at the time called it an early Christmas present for the country. Geologically, it was something plainer and considerably stranger to sit with. The exact same layer of rock, already assessed once as the largest deposit of its kind in American history only two years earlier, turning out to be less than half the size of what sat quietly under the other half of the very same basin the whole time. You may already know the Bakken. It's one of the most talked about oil stories of the last 20 years. An entire formation across North Dakota and Montana that sat mostly untouched for decades until its 2006 discovery well finally proved it could be produced at real commercial scale, kicking off a boom that reshaped small towns across the Northern Plains almost overnight. The Wolfcamp never had that single dramatic moment, no discovery well anyone remembers by name, no lone geologist credited with a breakthrough in interviews decades later. And yet the 2016 assessment of it just the Midland Basin portion alone already outsized the entire combined Bakken and Three Forks estimate from 2013 by a wide margin before the Delaware Basin's own numbers had even been calculated. Whatever attention the Basin earned for its dramatic reveal and its overnight boom towns, the Wolfcamp earned by simply outlasting a century of people driving straight past it, one stack completion at a time without anyone bothering to formally ask how big the ignored layer sitting beneath their feet actually was until the drilling data left them no other choice. None of that size is an accident of measurement and none of it happened quickly. It goes back roughly 300 million years to the early Permian period when a broad platform of uplifted crust called the Central Basin Platform split what's now West Texas into two separate deepwater troughs running side by side, the Midland Basin to the East and the Delaware Basin to the West, each one filling independently over millions of years. Along the rims of both troughs, reef complexes built up in shallow sunlit water, the way modern coral reefs grow off the coast of Australia today, layer upon layer of carbonate skeleton accumulating over millions of years and eventually hardening into the massive limestone formations. The earliest Permian oil men, men like the crew at Santa Rita, would target directly with their vertical wells at decades later, following the same shallow reef trend across county after county. But the centers of both basins, cut off from that shallow oxygen-rich shelf environment by the platform and the reefs ringing it, kept quietly filling with fine mud and organic material settling out of deep, poorly oxygenated water for millions of years at a stretch, exactly the kind of still starve setting that produces an outstanding source rock rather than an obvious one anybody would notice from the surface. That mud became the Wolfcamp and unlike the reservoirs sitting above it that Santa Rita and its successors had targeted for decades, it was never meant to be a container in the conventional sense at all. It's both the source of the oil and the reservoir holding it at the same time, generated in place over tens of millions of years and never required to migrate anywhere or get trapped by a dome or an arch or any of the structures conventional geologists spent a century learning to map. That's exactly why nobody could see it coming with older exploration methods, no matter how carefully they studied the rock above it. A rock that makes its own oil and keeps it exactly where it formed gives away nothing at the surface and nothing obvious in a well log, unless you already know to look for oil sitting directly inside the source rock itself rather than migrating out of it into something else nearby. The same tightness that made it functionally useless to a driller working in 1960, a rock that would barely flow at all under the technology available, then is the same fundamental property that kept every drop of oil it ever generated from escaping anywhere else over the following quarter billion years, sealed inside its own source by nothing more than its own stubborn lack of permeability. Getting that oil out required almost exactly what unlocked the Marcellus a thousand miles to the northeast around the same general era. Horizontal wells drilled sideways through the layer instead of straight down through it, the way every earlier Permian well had been drilled, followed by hydraulic fracturing designed to crack open a rock too tight to flow through under its own pressure by any other means available. The Wolfcamp cooperated with that approach for reasons baked [music] directly into its own mineral makeup, a mix of fine carbonate and silica-rich mud brittle enough to fracture into a genuine branching network instead of simply absorbing the pumped pressure and closing back up the moment it eased off, the way a softer more clay-heavy shale elsewhere in the country tends to behave under the same treatment. Layer that brittleness on top of a source rock already generating oil across an area covering both basins at once, and the ingredients that made the Wolfcamp nearly worthless to a 1960s driller working with cable tools turn out to be precisely the same ingredients that made it enormous to a driller working the same exact ground 50 years later with horizontal rigs and slickwater fracturing crews. None of this shows up if you're just watching another well pad go up along a farm road outside Midland or Odessa, indistinguishable from a thousand others scattered across the same flat country. But across its full 100 years of production from 1920 through 2020, the Permian Basin as a whole has produced something on the order of 63 billion barrels of oil equivalent. And unconventional plays like the Wolfcamp and now account for more than half of all domestic drilling investment in the entire country, roughly a third of total American oil production on their own, and enough combined output that the basin functions today as one of the primary factors setting the world price of oil. A single stretch of West Texas and New Mexico scrubland effectively pulling on a lever that reaches every gas pump on the planet. A rock that spent decades getting drilled through on the way to somewhere supposedly more valuable is now the single largest reason the country produces as much oil as it currently does year after year without most of the people driving past those pump jacks ever knowing the layers name. The men who drilled Santa Rita in 1923 weren't wrong about where the oil was, not by any measure. They found an entire province stretching across two states and it's still producing a century later, still supporting towns that didn't exist before the discovery. The Wolfcamp sat directly beneath nearly every one of the wells that followed them for the next 100 years, generating and holding its own separate fortune in rock too tight for anyone to take seriously until the tools finally caught up with what had been sitting there the entire time patiently through a century of drill bits passing through it on the way to somewhere else. Sometimes the largest reserve in the country isn't hiding somewhere remote that nobody thought to look. It's sitting directly under 100 years of drilling records in the interval between the zones everyone already knew to chase, waiting for someone to finally ask what the rock in between the real targets had actually been doing all along. If that's the kind of story you're here for, there's more where this came from.

metadata.shortDescription:
In preparation for tax season, this episode provides an update on the taxation of minerals and royalties for the 2023 tax year. It covers key considerations that mineral and royalty owners should be aware of when it comes to their tax obligations and key tax credits and deductions that all mineral and royalty owners should know about.
 

Download my free tax guide (https://unique-motivator-6128.ck.page/irs-valuation-resource-guide)  for links to my top resources around mineral rights and royalty interest taxation and be sure to check out the show notes: (https://mineralrightspodcast.com/mrp-234-mineral-rights-and-royalties-tax-strategies) for links to the other resources mentioned in this episode.

metadata.title: Inherited Mineral Rights in Texas: The Affidavit of Heirship, Step by Step
metadata.author: Royalty Clerk
metadata.shortDescription:
When a Texas mineral owner dies without a will, the royalties often stop until the heirs prove who they are. Using a fictional sample family, we walk through what happens at death, the four-year will clock, who inherits, how to fill out an affidavit of heirship, who can sign it, recording it in every county, and when you need a court instead.

Free tools from Royalty Clerk:
- Affidavit of heirship guide: https://royaltyclerk.com/affidavit-of-heirship-oil-gas-texas?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=v5
- Inherited mineral rights in Texas: https://royaltyclerk.com/inherited-mineral-rights-texas?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=v5
- Estate mineral report: https://royaltyclerk.com/estate?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=v5

Chapters:
0:00 Intro
0:36 What happens at death
1:12 If there's a will
1:42 Meet the Whitfields
2:24 The affidavit
3:12 Who signs
3:45 Record it, then send it
4:25 When it's not enough
4:54 Two things heirs miss
5:54 Free tools

General information, not legal, tax or investment advice. Sample numbers, families and documents are illustrations, not real owners. For your own situation, talk to a Texas oil and gas or probate attorney.

segments.text: Grandpa Walt died 3 years ago. No will.
Just a ranch house, a pickup, and a
drawer full of royalty stubs. Then the
checks stopped. The oil company didn't
lose the money. It's holding it and
waiting for one thing, proof of who owns
Walt's minerals now. In Texas, for
families without a will, that proof is
very often a short document called an
affidavit of heirship. Here's how it
works, step by step with a sample
family. This is general information, not
legal advice. For your own family, talk
to a Texas probate attorney.
When a mineral owner dies, the minerals
pass like any other property.
If there's a will, to the people named
in it, once the will is probated. If
there's no will, to the heirs Texas law
sets out in the estates code.
Who those heirs are depends on the
family, and on whether the minerals were
separate or community property. Either
way, the oil company keeps the old name
on the account or stops paying until it
sees proof. And while there's reasonable
doubt about who owns the interest, Texas
law lets it hold the royalties without
interest.
First, a word about wills, because
there's a clock.
In Texas, a will generally can't be
admitted to probate after the fourth
anniversary of the death. Many families
with minerals probate a will as a
muniment of title,
a simpler route that transfers the
property without a full administration.
So, if Walt had left a will in that
drawer, the first call would be to a
probate lawyer before the 4 years run
out. But Walt didn't leave a will, so
let's meet his family.
Here's our sample family. They're
fictional, but the shape is common.
Walt married twice. His first wife,
June, died in 1990.
They had two children, Carol and Dean.
Dean died in 2018 and left a son, Sam.
Walt then married Rosa. They had one
daughter, Lilly. Rosa is still living.
Who inherits what depends on Texas law,
on which marriage the minerals came
from, and on whether they were separate
or community property.
That's a lawyer's calculation and we
won't do it here. But notice what
matters for the affidavit. Every
marriage and every child, including Dean
who died and his son, Sam.
So, what is an affidavit of heirship?
It's a sworn statement signed before a
notary by someone who knew the family
saying when the owner died, who they
married, and who their children are.
Texas even provides a form for it in the
estates code, section 203.002,
titled affidavit of facts concerning the
identity of heirs. It's not a court
order. It's a statement of facts sworn
by a witness. It lists the date of
death, every marriage and how it ended,
every child living or not, and whether
the owner left a will. Recorded in the
county's deed records, it becomes part
of the chain of title. And once it has
been on record for 5 years, Texas law
treats it as prima facie evidence of the
facts in it.
Who should sign it? Someone with
personal knowledge of the family.
Ideally, someone who doesn't inherit
anything.
A long-time neighbor, a family friend, a
pastor. Operators and title companies
often ask for two such witnesses. If you
can't find anyone like that, ask the
company or a lawyer what they'll accept.
And the most common reason an affidavit
fails, a missing child. A child from an
earlier marriage or a child who died and
left children of their own, like Dean's
son, Sam.
Once it's signed and notarized, record
it.
Take the original to to county clerk in
the county where the minerals are and
record it in the real property records.
If the family owns minerals in several
counties, record it in each one. Then
send each oil company a packet, a copy
of the recorded affidavit, a certified
death certificate, and each heir's
address and W-9. And ask two questions
in writing. What else do you need to pay
the heirs? And how much have you held
since the death? The money held in
suspense belongs to the owners of the
interest. Once the papers are accepted,
ask for all of it.
An affidavit doesn't work for every
family.
Each company decides what it accepts.
Many take a recorded affidavit for a
small interest. For a large interest or
when the family list is in doubt, some
will ask for a court judgment declaring
heirship under chapter 202 of the
estates code. There's no deadline for
that proceeding. It can be brought
anytime after the death. That's when a
probate attorney earns their fee.
Two more things heirs often miss.
First, find every interest. Walt might
own minerals in counties you've never
heard of. Check his stubs, his 1099s,
the county mineral rolls, and unclaimed
property under his name. Second, the
value at the date of death.
For federal tax, inherited property
generally takes its fair market value at
the date of death as its basis. So that
number matters if the heirs ever sell.
The state's production records and the
prices in the months before the death
give a defensible starting figure.
Let's recap the Whitfield's to-do list.
Look for a will and mind the 4-year
clock. Map every marriage and every
child. Have a disinterested witness sign
the affidavit before a notary. Record it
in every county where there are
minerals. Send each company the packet
and ask for everything held since the
death. And for anything complicated,
call a Texas probate attorney.
Royalty Clerk's Heirship Guide lists the
papers each situation needs. And our
estate report finds the Texas interests
under a name and values them at the date
of death. If your family is going
through this right now, I hope this made
the next step clearer. Thanks for
watching.
