metadata.title: Watch This Before Selling Mineral Rights! | Types of Mineral Buyers and Who to Avoid!
metadata.author: Steven Hatcher | Minerals Guy
metadata.shortDescription:
Own mineral rights? Get a private, no-obligation offer on your minerals: https://deal.mineralsguy.com/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=organic&utm_campaign=watch-this-before-selling-mineral-rights&utm_content=description_top

In this video, I explain how to evaluate mineral buyers and distinguish professional buyers from fly-by-night groups. I also discuss red flags to watch for when considering a sale of your mineral rights.

What you'll learn:
- How to check an individual buyer’s identity and use your gut when assessing them
- What to look for on a mineral buyer’s website and in online search results
- Red flags including evasiveness, missing company information, and high-pressure sales tactics
- Why not to sign unsolicited mail that looks like a check, legal agreement, or mineral deed

________________________________________________________________________

Want to get into the mineral rights business? Start with my 30-minute, $27 workshop: https://learnminerals.com/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=organic&utm_campaign=watch-this-before-selling-mineral-rights&utm_content=description_footer
Get a private, no-obligation offer on your minerals: https://deal.mineralsguy.com/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=organic&utm_campaign=watch-this-before-selling-mineral-rights&utm_content=description_footer
Email Steven directly: steven@mineralsguy.com

________________________________________________________________________

About Minerals Guy:

Minerals Guy provides tailored content and resources to oil and gas mineral and royalty owners across the country with the goal of educating and empowering owners to better understand mineral rights as an asset class and the potential value of their minerals and royalties.

Steven Hatcher is the creator of Minerals Guy. He is a professional mineral buyer, an oil and gas attorney and has spent the last decade buying and selling oil and gas properties across the country. He is an expert in oil and gas mineral rights, having worked in the private practice of law, for oil and gas operators, and for mineral and royalty acquisition companies.

metadata.title: How Mineral Owners Get Paid (The Truth About Royalties)
metadata.author: PetroPeak Investments LLC
metadata.shortDescription:
What is an oil and gas mineral investment, and how does a mineral owner actually get paid?

In this PetroPeak Investments educational video, John Jordan explains how mineral ownership works, how operators lease and develop mineral rights, how royalty revenue is generated, and some of the key differences between mineral ownership and working-interest ownership.

Topics covered include mineral rights, royalty interests, producing minerals, future development, operator activity, commodity-price exposure, and the role mineral ownership can play in direct energy investing.

CHAPTERS
0:00 - Demystifying Oil and Gas Mineral Investments
0:47 - Separating Surface and Mineral Rights
1:24 - Buying Minerals Versus Drilling Companies
2:11 - Royalty Interests vs Working Interests
2:55 - Producing Assets vs Future Drilling Potential
3:34 - Why Investors Choose Mineral Interests
3:59 - The Critical Role of Location and Geology

PetroPeak Investments focuses on producing U.S. oil and gas mineral and royalty interests.

Educational content only. This video is not an offer to sell securities or a recommendation to make any particular investment.

segments.text: What is an oil and gas mineral
investment?
If you've ever looked at investing in
oil and gas, you've probably come across
terms like mineral rights, royalty
interest, working interest,
and overriding royalties.
They can make the investment sound much
more complicated than it really is. So,
let's start with the most basic
question.
What exactly is an oil and gas mineral
investment? Well, I'm John Jordan,
managing partner at Petro Peak
Investments, and I've spent most of my
career evaluating and developing oil and
gas assets.
At Petro Peak,
we invest primarily in producing mineral
and royalty interests.
So, I want to use these videos to
explain how this part of the energy
business actually works.
So, let's start with the mineral
ownership. In the United States,
ownership of minerals below the surface
can be separated from ownership
of the surface land itself.
That mineral owner has the right to
develop those minerals,
or more commonly, lease those rights to
an oil and gas operator.
The operator
might be a company like Exxon Mobil,
Conoco Phillips, Occidental, or one of
hundreds of other producers.
In exchange for allowing the operator to
drill and produce the minerals, the
mineral owner typically receives a
royalty.
And that is where the investment comes
in.
Instead of buying the company drilling
the wells, you're buying an ownership
interest in the minerals themselves, and
participating in the royalty revenue
generated by those minerals. So, how
does the money flow?
Let's use a very simple example. Assume
an operator drills a well on acreage
where the mineral owner has negotiated a
20% royalty.
When the well produces and sells a
million dollars worth of oil and gas,
approximately 200,000 of that revenue is
allocated to the royalty owner
or owners
based on how much each owner possesses
of the underlying minerals. The
remaining revenue belongs to the
operator and its working interest
partners
who are responsible for the drilling,
completing, and operating of the well.
That's one of the major distinctions
between royalty ownership and working
interest ownership.
The mineral or royalty owner
participates in production revenue but
does not pay the drilling and operating
cost of the well.
That doesn't mean mineral investing is
risk-free.
Production declines, commodity prices
change, development schedules change,
operators make different capital
allocation decisions,
and the value of the mineral acreage can
vary enormously depending on location,
geology,
existing production, future drilling
inventory, royalty rate, and operator
activity.
Those are all things we'll explore in
future videos. Another important
distinction is whether you're buying
minerals under wells that are already
producing or where you're primarily
expecting future drilling.
At Petro Peak, we tend to focus on
assets that already have some producing
wells.
That means there is existing production
history and existing cash flow that can
be evaluated when making the investment.
Future development can then provide
additional upside if new wells are
drilled.
That's very different from buying
acreage where essentially all of the
investment return depends on wells
that that haven't been drilled yet.
So, why are investors interested in oil
and gas minerals? There are several
reasons.
They can provide direct exposure to oil
and natural gas production. They can
generate ongoing cash distributions.
They don't generally require the mineral
owner to fund drilling or operating
costs.
And a good mineral position can
participate in additional wells drilled
on the acreage over time.
But just like real estate, location
matters enormously.
Two mineral interests only a few miles
apart can have completely different
values because of geology, well
performance, operator activity,
development timing, and the terms of the
underlying leases. That's why evaluating
the asset is much more important than
simply saying, "I own minerals in the
Permian Basin." or "I own minerals in
the DJ Basin."
So, what's the key takeaway? The
simplest way to think about mineral
investing is this.
You're purchasing an ownership interest
in the resource and participating in the
revenue generated when the operator
develops and produces it
without taking on the same capital
obligations
as the company drilling the wells.
So, in the next videos, we'll start
breaking down some of the concepts that
determine whether a mineral investment
is attractive or not.
If you're interested in learning more
about oil and gas and mineral investing,
subscribe to Petro Piq channel and
follow along.

metadata.title: MRP 352:  Mineral Rights News October 2026
metadata.author: Matt Sands
metadata.shortDescription:
What do carbon dioxide, a Texas ranch entrance, and a summit in Washington have in common? Each one could affect your royalty checks. In this month's news episode, we cover a start-up selling captured CO2 to oil producers, which could keep older wells producing for years. We also look at a Texas family that turned down a $21,000 pipeline offer and won a $7 million jury verdict, and at why new pipelines could end the negative gas prices West Texas royalty owners have been seeing. Then we discuss President Xi's visit to Washington and why China may be better prepared for high oil prices than many people realize. We finish with the latest rig count, which is slowly climbing as the price of crude oil stays high
 

As always, links to the articles mentioned in this episode can be found in the show notes at mineralrightspodcast.com (https://mineralrightspodcast.com/mrp-352-mineral-rights-news-october-2026/) .

videos.full_text: [music] >> Are you ready to make the most of your oil and gas mineral rights? Welcome to the Mineral Rights Podcast. Get the knowledge and resources you need to manage your minerals and royalties. Here is your host, Matt Sands. >> [music] >> Hello and welcome to the Mineral Rights Podcast. I'm your host Matt Sands and I'm joined by my co-host Justin Williams and we're here to help you make the most of your minerals and royalties. In this episode we're going to cover the latest mineral rights and energy news for October of 2026 and uh this month we have some very interesting stories that range from CO2 to pipeline right-of-ways and easements to uh China and the visit that is currently going on as we're recording this with Xi Jinping is in Washington and you know what could potentially happen from that from an energy perspective and all of the political goings-on there. And then at the end we'll obviously talk about the latest rig count and talk about where trends are are showing uh things are headed. So, Justin, what did you think about this month's uh stories? >> Pretty varied. We're not we're not really on uh one defined topic here. So, it's interesting some months the news seems taken over with uh just one topic, but got some interesting stories. >> Yeah, very interesting stories. Let's Speaking of that, let's dive into this first one uh about the climate startup that is signing CO2 deals with three US oil producers. >> Yeah, so cuts to US uh federal incentives for carbon capture projects in an uncertain regulatory environment going forward prompted some startups to move from solely capturing and storing carbon dioxide to selling it to oil companies to help them boost oil recovery. So, Matt, interesting to see the free market taking over here, but certainly a a viable model. Uh carbon management uh engineering company Spurious, for example, has recently signed preliminary agreements with three US oil and gas producers to sell them captured CO2 for enhanced oil recovery or EOR operations. >> Yeah, this is a really interesting one, and I am not surprised at all that the CO2, you know, the carbon capture and sequestration projects have basically come to a halt because the tax incentives were dialed back under the Trump administration, just because there's really no organic market for CO2. It's a political and I guess that's the best way to put it, but just an artificial market that's created through tax credits at at the current moment. So, the the real utility of CO2, obviously there's industrial uses and things like that, but then enhanced oil recovery is in in the context of our show is certainly the largest and most important use for CO2, and one that oil companies are willing to pay for because there's an economic benefit to it. Because when they take CO2, inject it into oil reservoirs, they're able to extract more oil. This enhanced oil recovery or secondary or tertiary recovery is basically taking wells that have been producing, and they have declined to the point where additional energy needs to be put into the reservoir to extract that incremental barrel of oil. When you inject CO2, it revitalizes these mature fields by reducing the oil viscosity, allowing it to to flow more easily, and it increases the reservoir pressure again, which again pushes the oil to the well bore of these wells, and then it can be produced. You know, when you have uh you know, primary production, which is when you have a pump jack there, maybe then secondary recovery is a water flood. Once those sort of start to peter out, they can use CO2 to push even more oil out, and it's really interesting with most of the time this is done in conventional plays where you have vertical wells, and they can drill the injection well in strategic places to push the oil towards the producing wells and to increase production. And when you look at the production curve from an enhanced oil recovery field or a well, it's like flat. It's really interesting because you're you're adding pressure back into the reservoir, so it doesn't have that natural decline that you normally see with most naturally declining oil and gas wells. You actually sort of artificially keep it flat for an extended period of time. Um so this is a huge benefit to uh mineral owners that have royalties on these older uh more mature wells. And if you're in an area where, you know, particularly in Texas, you know, West Texas is a area that's ripe for this. And so, you know, potentially could be revitalizing the royalties from some of these more mature fields uh for some uh mineral royalty owners that are out there. So, I'm good to see these types of projects are moving moving forward and it's not not surprising because they stand on their own um, you know, economically just because there is an economic benefit again to um to companies investing in the CO2 infrastructure to get oil to these more mature fields because these incremental barrels of oil obviously are worth money and and companies will uh invest capital to extract that. >> Yeah, and there's no lack of uh speculation. There was a University of uh Houston report last month uh that found as many as 137 billion barrels of US oil are technically recoverable using EOR technology. And uh also mentions that most of those being in Texas and more than half of those being Texas considered favorable for using EOR. So, certainly an interesting market and uh you know, there's value there for the operators to pursue it. Hopefully be a competitive landscape as more companies get involved. >> Yeah, absolutely. Um let's talk about the second one now. >> Yeah, so the tensions with uh land owners rise as a raft of gas pipelines push through Texas properties. Matt, this is a really um it's a saga that's gone on for about 4 years. Um and it's a really interesting saga about the land owners against uh folks putting in the pipeline. And we were talking a bit before we hit record, but as we dive into this, do you want to talk a little bit about what is different with pipeline? Cuz you start to talk about utilities and easements and eminent domain and and things get a bit more complicated than if you're just talking a private piece of property. >> Yeah, this is really interesting. This really only pertains to the surface owner. And when pipeline company identifies pipeline route, they look at where that pipeline needs to go and they need to obtain the land in order to install the pipeline there and that's done through pipeline right of way. And so there is a length of pipeline that crosses your property. Typically, I think from my experience when I was doing pipeline work back at the beginning of my career, pipeline right of ways around 40 ft wide. metadata.title: MRP 4: How Mineral Rights are Valued
metadata.author: Matt Sands
metadata.shortDescription:
In this Episode, we feature a special guest, fellow mineral owner Justin Williams.

Many mineral rights owners are looking for the Mineral Rights MLS or Zillow/Trulia for minerals but unfortunately they don’t exist.  The reason for this is it is very difficult for a computer algorithm to accurately value minerals and also there is a lack of readily available data on actual prices paid in arms-length mineral transactions.

Don’t worry, because there is still hope! Mineral rights can be valued several different ways.  If there is a lot of activity in the area, you can use a combination of looking at comparable sales (the “Market Approach”) and having a qualified person perform a cash flow analysis (the “Income Approach”).  Listen to this episode where we also discuss an easy rule-of-thumb approach that you can use in some cases.

metadata.title: MRP 319:  Mineral Rights News February 2026
metadata.author: Matt Sands
metadata.shortDescription:
In this February 2026 news roundup, we analyze how Winter Storm Ferne disrupted nearly 2 million barrels per day of U.S. oil production and sent natural gas prices to all-time highs, with spot prices hitting over $30/mmBtu. We explore what these dramatic price spikes mean for your royalty checks and why this recovery looks different from the 2021 Texas grid crisis. We also examine the Trump administration's push to streamline oil and gas permitting on federal forest lands, Greenland's emerging role as a strategic mineral hub, and what flat rig counts signal about the industry's cautious approach to increasing production despite recent price volatility.
 

As always, links to the articles discussed can be found in the show notes at mineralrightspodcast.com (https://mineralrightspodcast.com/mrp-319-mineral-rights-news-february-2026/) .

metadata.title: MRP 299:  Mineral Rights News September 2025
metadata.author: Matt Sands
metadata.shortDescription: This episode covers several critical developments affecting mineral rights owners, from post-production deductions from royalty checks in North Dakotato Wyoming's controversial proposal for reclaiming abandoned mineral rights. We also discuss the recent Cactus Water Services Texas Supreme Court ruling on produced water ownership and how it provides clarity around hydrocarbons contained in produced water while leaving questions unanswered related to lithium and other valuable minerals. All this and more! As always, links to the articles discussed can be found in the show notes at mineralrightspodcast.com (https://mineralrightspodcast.com/mrp-299-mineral-rights-news-september-2025/) .

metadata.title: Mineral vs. Royalty: Stop Making This Investment Mistake
metadata.author: PetroPeak Investments LLC
metadata.shortDescription:
Mineral rights, royalty interests, and overriding royalty interests (ORRI) can all generate income from oil and gas production. But what exactly do you own, and why does it matter?

In this video, John Jordan, Founder and Managing Partner of PetroPeak Investments, explains the differences between these three types of oil and gas ownership and how each can affect income, future development opportunities, and long-term investment value.

We'll explore how mineral ownership works, what distinguishes traditional royalties from nonparticipating royalty interests (NPRI), and why overriding royalties are often tied to the life of an oil and gas lease.

You'll also see a practical example of how $100,000 in monthly well revenue is allocated among royalty owners, along with a discussion of why two interests generating identical monthly income can have very different investment values.

Topics covered:

Mineral rights and the value of future development

Royalty interests vs. working interests

Nonparticipating royalty interests (NPRI)

Overriding royalty interests (ORRI)

How oil and gas royalty payments are calculated

Why ownership structure matters when evaluating investments

At PetroPeak Investments, we focus on acquiring producing oil and gas mineral and royalty interests across major U.S. energy basins. Our approach emphasizes existing cash flow, disciplined underwriting, and evaluating opportunities for future development.

Learn more about PetroPeak Investments:
https://www.petropeak.com

Subscribe for more educational videos about mineral ownership, oil and gas royalties, energy investing, and the economics behind producing assets.

#MineralRights #OilAndGasRoyalties #EnergyInvesting #PetroPeakInvestments

This video is for educational purposes only and does not constitute investment, legal, or tax advice or an offer to sell securities.

segments.text: Two people can receive royalty checks
from the same oil well, but what they
actually own can be very different. One
might own the minerals beneath the
property, including the rights
associated with future leasing and
development. Another
might own only a royalty interest
that entitles them to a share of the
production revenue. And a third might
own an overriding royalty
tied to a particular oil and gas lease.
All three can generate income without
directly
paying to drill or operate the well.
But the differences
become especially important when you're
evaluating what those interests
are worth. I'm John Jordan with Petro
Peak Investments, and today we're going
to look at mineral ownership, royalty
interest, and overriding royalties.
How each works,
how they generate income,
and why understanding the differences
matter. Let's start with mineral
ownership. One of the unique
characteristics of property ownership in
the United States is that the minerals
beneath a property can be owned
separately from the surface.
Someone might own a piece of land,
including a house, buildings, and
everything on the surface, while another
person owns the oil and gas minerals
underneath that property.
A mineral owner generally has the right
to lease those minerals to an oil and
gas operator, subject to the specific
rights that they own.
When an operator wants to develop oil
and gas resources, they will negotiate a
mineral lease.
That lease can include an upfront
upfront bonus payment and a royalty
percentage
that determines how much of the
production revenue the mineral owner
receives.
Let's say you own 100 mineral acres, and
an operator offers a lease with a 20%
royalty.
If the operator drills a producing well
that includes your acreage, you could be
entitled to a proportionate share of the
revenue genera- generated by that well.
The actual payment depends on your
ownership, that acreage included in the
producing unit, and the terms of the
lease.
But, here's something important. Mineral
ownership isn't necessarily limited to
the revenue generated by existing wells.
Depending on the ownership structure and
the lease terms, it can also include
rights associated with future leasing
and future development. That means
mineral ownership may have value even
when there's very little production
occurring today. For example, a mineral
owner might receive revenue from a
handful of existing wells, but the
underlying minerals could eventually be
developed with additional horizontal
wells targeting different formations.
Now, that future development potential
is one of the reasons we look beyond
current production
when evaluating mineral acquisitions.
Now, let's talk about royalty interest.
A royalty interest generally entitles
its owner to a share of the oil and gas
produced from the property or the
revenue generated from that production
without requiring the owner to pay the
cost of drilling and operating the
wells. That's an important distinction
from a working interest. The working
interest owners are responsible for the
funding of drilling, completion, and
operation of the wells. The royalty
owner receives
an agreed share of production without
directly participating in those
development expenses.
There can still be deductions from
royalty payments including certain taxes
and post-production costs depending on
the lease and or the ownership
documents.
But, royalty owners generally are
responsible for paying their share of
the drilling and completion costs.
Now, here's where terminology can become
a little confusing.
When a mineral owner leases their
minerals to an operator, they typically
retain a royalty interest under that
lease.
But, someone can also own a royalty
interest without owning the underlying
mineral rights.
One example is what's called a
non-participating royalty interest or
NPRI.
An NPRI owner is entitled to a share of
production or production revenue, but
generally doesn't have the right to
negotiate leases or receive lease bonus
payments.
So, imagine two people receiving monthly
royalty payments from the same well.
One owns the underlying minerals and has
retained a royalty under an oil and gas
lease. The other owner owns a separately
conveyed non-participating royalty
interest. Both they receive royalty
revenue,
but the underlying rights they own are
different. And those interests can
become especially important when the
considering future leasing,
additional development, and long-term
value of the investment. The third type
of ownership I want to discuss is an
overriding royalty interest, commonly
called an ORRI. This is an important
category because it can look very
similar to a traditional royalty
interest from a cash flow perspective,
even though the underlying ownership is
different. An overriding royalty is
generally carved out of an existing oil
and gas leasehold working interest
rather than directly from the mineral
estate.
The overriding royalty interest owner
receives a specified
a share of production
or production revenue without paying the
drilling and operating costs associated
with that production. For example, an
operator or working interest owner might
convey a 2% overriding royalty interest
in a particular lease.
That overriding royalty interest owner
would generally be entitled to 2% of the
production revenue attributable to the
specified interest,
subject to the terms of the assignment
and the applicable adjustments.
But there's an important difference
between the overriding royalty interest
and traditional mineral ownership.
An overriding royalty is typically tied
to the underlying oil and gas lease.
In many cases, when that lease
terminates, the overriding royalty
interest terminates with it.
Unless specific provisions or other
circumstances preserve the interest.
Mineral ownership,
on the other hand, generally continues
even when an existing oil and gas lease
expires.
That distinction can have a significant
impact
on long-term value.
An overriding royalty interest might
generate attractive income from a group
of producing wells,
but the investor needs to understand the
underlying leases, the production
associated with those leases, and
whether there's potential for additional
drilling.
This doesn't make overriding royalties
inherently better or worse than other
royalty interests. It simply means there
are different factors to evaluate. And
when you're investing in oil and gas,
those underlying ownership details
matter. So, let's put some simple
numbers around these concepts. Suppose
an oil and gas well generates $100,000
of gross production revenue during the
month.
If the well is subject to a 20% land
owner royalty, that means $20,000 of the
production revenue is allocated to that
royalty burden before any applicable
adjustments.
Now, that doesn't mean one mineral owner
necessarily receives the entire $20,000.
If that owner holds only 10% of the
mineral interest represented by that
royalty burden, their share will be
$2,000 a month.
The remaining royalty revenue
would be distributed to the other
royalty owners according to their
respective ownership interests. Now,
let's consider an overriding royalty.
Suppose that same well is also burdened
by a 2% overriding royalty interest
calculated on the full gross production
revenue.
That overriding royalty interest would
generate $2,000 for the month before
applicable adjustments. So, in this
example, a mineral owner receiving a
portion of the landowner royalty and
overriding royalty interest owner would
each receive $2,000 in monthly revenue
from the same well.
But, remember, they don't necessarily
own the same underlying rights.
The mineral owner's interest may include
additional rights associated with the
mineral estate,
while the overriding royalty interest
owner's rights are generally derived
from and tied to the underlying
leasehold. The monthly royalty payments
might look nearly identical, the
long-term investment characteristics can
be very different. So, why do these
distinctions matter from an investment
perspective? Because two interests
generating exactly the same revenue
today can have different values.
Consider an overriding royalty that's
receiving income from a group of
producing wells.
Those wells may have been producing for
several years. Production is declining,
and there might be limited opportunity
for additional drilling under the
existing leases.
In that situation,
much of the investment's value may come
from the remaining production of those
existing wells.
Now, compare that with mineral ownership
in an area where operators are actively
developing new horizontal wells.
The existing production might be
relatively modest, but the mineral
ownership could provide exposure to
additional wells in the future.
That doesn't automatically make the
second investment more valuable. future
drilling isn't guaranteed. Operator
development plans can change,
commodity prices fluctuate, and a
mineral owner may wait years for
additional development that never
occurs. The important question is
whether the potential
future revenue justifies the purchase
price and the risks associated with the
investment.
When we evaluate mineral royalty
acquisitions at Petro Peak, we're not
simply looking at the revenue an asset
generates today.
We're examining the existing wells,
their production declines, remaining
reserves, the operators, the underlying
ownership rights, lease terms, and the
potential for future development. We
want to understand where the future
revenue is expected to come from and how
long those rights are likely to last
and how much confidence we can place in
those cash flows.
Sometimes an established producing
royalty with limited development
potential can be an attractive
investment
at the right price. Other times, a
mineral interest with relatively modest
existing production can provide
compelling value because of the
potential for future additional
drilling.
The overriding royalty interest can
offer attractive investment
opportunities when the producing assets,
lease terms, and acquisition economics
support the investment.
Ultimately, the objective is to
understand not just what an interest is
producing today, but what it may produce
over its remaining economic life
and whether the purchase price
appropriately reflects the opportunities
and the risks.
That analysis begins with understanding
exactly what you own.
So, the next time you hear someone
talking about mineral rights, royalty
interest, or overriding royalties,
remember that these terms aren't
necessarily interchangeable.
They can all provide exposure to oil and
gas production, but the ownership rights
behind that revenue can be quite
different.
Mineral ownership may include rights
associated with future leasing and
development. A separately owned royalty
interest may provide production revenue
without those additional rights.
And an overriding royalty generally
derives its value from the underlying
leasehold interest. Understanding these
differences is an important first step
towards understanding how oil and gas
royalty investments are evaluated.
I'm John Jordan with Petro Peak
Investments and thanks for watching and
I'll see you in the next video.

A royalty interest generally entitles its owner to a share of the oil and gas produced from the property or the revenue generated from that production without requiring the owner to pay the cost of drilling and operating the wells. That's an important distinction from a working interest. The working interest owners are responsible for the funding of drilling, completion, and operation of the wells. The royalty owner receives an agreed share of production without directly participating in those development expenses. There can still be deductions from royalty payments including certain taxes and post-production costs depending on the lease and or the ownership documents. But, royalty owners generally are responsible for paying their share of the drilling and completion costs. Now, here's where terminology can become a little confusing. When a mineral owner leases their minerals to an operator, they typically retain a royalty interest under that lease. But, someone can also own a royalty interest without owning the underlying mineral rights. One example is what's called a non-participating royalty interest or NPRI. An NPRI owner is entitled to a share of production or production revenue, but generally doesn't have the right to negotiate leases or receive lease bonus payments. So, imagine two people receiving monthly royalty payments from the same well. One owns the underlying minerals and has retained a royalty under an oil and gas lease. The other owner owns a separately conveyed non-participating royalty interest. Both they receive royalty revenue, but the underlying rights they own are different. And those interests can become especially important when the considering future leasing, additional development, and long-term value of the investment. The third type of ownership I want to discuss is an overriding royalty interest, commonly called an ORRI. This is an important category because it can look very similar to a traditional royalty interest from a cash flow perspective, even though the underlying ownership is different. An overriding royalty is generally carved out of an existing oil and gas leasehold working interest rather than directly from the mineral estate. The overriding royalty interest owner receives a specified a share of production or production revenue without paying the drilling and operating costs associated with that production. For example, an operator or working interest owner might convey a 2% overriding royalty interest in a particular lease. That overriding royalty interest owner would generally be entitled to 2% of the production revenue attributable to the specified interest, subject to the terms of the assignment and the applicable adjustments. But there's an important difference between the overriding royalty interest and traditional mineral ownership. An overriding royalty is typically tied to the underlying oil and gas lease. In many cases, when that lease terminates, the overriding royalty interest terminates with it. Unless specific provisions or other circumstances preserve the interest. Mineral ownership, on the other hand, generally continues even when an existing oil and gas lease expires. That distinction can have a significant impact on long-term value. An overriding royalty interest might generate attractive income from a group of producing wells, but the investor needs to understand the underlying leases, the production associated with those leases, and whether there's potential for additional drilling. This doesn't make overriding royalties inherently better or worse than other royalty interests. It simply means there are different factors to evaluate. And when you're investing in oil and gas, those underlying ownership details matter. So, let's put some simple numbers around these concepts. Suppose an oil and gas well generates $100,000 of gross production revenue during the month. If the well is subject to a 20% land owner royalty, that means $20,000 of the production revenue is allocated to that royalty burden before any applicable adjustments. Now, that doesn't mean one mineral owner necessarily receives the entire $20,000. If that owner holds only 10% of the mineral interest represented by that royalty burden, their share will be $2,000 a month. The remaining royalty revenue would be distributed to the other royalty owners according to their respective ownership interests. Now, let's consider an overriding royalty. Suppose that same well is also burdened by a 2% overriding royalty interest calculated on the full gross production revenue. That overriding royalty interest would generate $2,000 for the month before applicable adjustments. So, in this example, a mineral owner receiving a portion of the landowner royalty and overriding royalty interest owner would each receive $2,000 in monthly revenue from the same well. But, remember, they don't necessarily own the same underlying rights. The mineral owner's interest may include additional rights associated with the mineral estate, while the overriding royalty interest owner's rights are generally derived from and tied to the underlying leasehold. The monthly royalty payments might look nearly identical, the long-term investment characteristics can be very different. So, why do these distinctions matter from an investment perspective? Because two interests generating exactly the same revenue today can have different values. Consider an overriding royalty that's receiving income from a group of producing wells. Those wells may have been producing for several years. Production is declining, and there might be limited opportunity for additional drilling under the existing leases. In that situation, much of the investment's value may come from the remaining production of those existing wells. Now, compare that with mineral ownership in an area where operators are actively developing new horizontal wells. The existing production might be relatively modest, but the mineral ownership could provide exposure to additional wells in the future. That doesn't automatically make the second investment more valuable. future drilling isn't guaranteed. Operator development plans can change, commodity prices fluctuate, and a mineral owner may wait years for additional development that never occurs. The important question is whether the potential future revenue justifies the purchase price and the risks associated with the investment. When we evaluate mineral royalty acquisitions at Petro Peak, we're not simply looking at the revenue an asset generates today. We're examining the existing wells, their production declines, remaining reserves, the operators, the underlying ownership rights, lease terms, and the potential for future development. We want to understand where the future revenue is expected to come from and how long those rights are likely to last and how much confidence we can place in those cash flows. Sometimes an established producing royalty with limited development potential can be an attractive investment at the right price. Other times, a mineral interest with relatively modest existing production can provide compelling value because of the potential for future additional drilling. The overriding royalty interest can offer attractive investment opportunities when the producing assets, lease terms, and acquisition economics support the investment. Ultimately, the objective is to understand not just what an interest is producing today, but what it may produce over its remaining economic life and whether the purchase price appropriately reflects the opportunities and the risks. That analysis begins with understanding exactly what you own. So, the next time you hear someone talking about mineral rights, royalty interest, or overriding royalties, remember that these terms aren't necessarily interchangeable. They can all provide exposure to oil and gas production, but the ownership rights behind that revenue can be quite different. Mineral ownership may include rights associated with future leasing and development. A separately owned royalty interest may provide production revenue without those additional rights. And an overriding royalty generally derives its value from the underlying leasehold interest. Understanding these differences is an important first step towards understanding how oil and gas royalty investments are evaluated. I'm John Jordan with Petro Peak Investments and thanks for watching and I'll see you in the next video.

metadata.title: Exploring Directional Drilling: The Key to Modern Oil and Gas Drilling
metadata.author: Petro Learn
metadata.shortDescription:
Directional drilling is a complex process that has revolutionized the way we extract oil and gas from the earth. In this video, we'll be exploring the following: 

TIMESTAMPS 
00:00 Introduction to directional drilling
01:25 Well Profiles
04:20 Reasons for Directional Drilling

If you found this video helpful, don't forget to hit that subscribe button for more insights on the oil and gas field.

segments.text: Traditionally, drilling was done vertically straight down into the ground. While effective,
this method limits access to oil and gas reservoirs that aren't directly below the rig.
That s where Directional Drilling comes in.
Directional drilling allows engineers to guide the wellbore to deviate from the vertical path,
enabling us to reach oil and gas reserves that are even located kilometers away.
With directional drilling, the wellbore can be steered at different angles.
We use advanced technologies like downhole motors and steerable drill bits,
which are designed to change the direction of the wellbore in real-time while drilling.
These tools are equipped with sensors that send data back to the surface,
allowing drillers to make precise adjustments, guiding the well towards its target. Think of
it like driving a remote-controlled car underground, but way more complex. But
what is the path that will be followed to reach the target? Let s talk about well profiles!
First, what exactly is a well profile? In simple terms, it s the path a well takes
from the surface to the reservoir. Let s start with the vertical well,
the simplest and most traditional profile. It s drilled straight down with no deviation. Vertical
wells are still widely used when the target reservoir is directly below the drilling site.
Next, we have the build and hold profile, also known as the J-profile. In this design,
the well starts vertically, then gradually builds an angle until it reaches the desired inclination,
and it holds that angle until it penetrates the reservoir. This profile is used when the target
reservoir isn t directly below the drill site. It s common in offshore drilling,
where we need to reach reservoirs located miles away from the platform.
Up next is the S-profile. Like the J-profile, the well starts vertically and builds an angle,
but here s the twist. it drops back down to a more vertical angle near the bottom.
This profile is ideal for reaching deeper reservoirs that are horizontally offset
but at a different depth, making it a bit more versatile than the J-profile.
Now for the horizontal wells, which is one of the most powerful applications of directional
drilling. Once the drill bit reaches a certain depth, it curves and drills horizontally through
the reservoir. This method is especially useful for shale formations and tight oil reservoirs
where the oil and gas are trapped in narrow layers of rock. By drilling horizontally, we
expose much more of the wellbore to the oil-rich rock, significantly increasing production rates.
If you thought horizontal wells were long, wait till you see the extended reach wells.
These wells follow a similar horizontal trajectory but are drilled over much
longer distances. They re perfect for accessing distant reservoirs from a single surface location,
which is especially useful in offshore drilling. Next is the multilateral well. This advanced
profile has a main wellbore with multiple branches extending into different sections
of the reservoir. Multilateral wells are ideal for maximizing production from a
single well by tapping into various parts of the reservoir at once.
Lastly, let s talk about sidetracked wells. Sometimes, things don t go as planned,
maybe there s an issue like a stuck pipe, or we need to access a different part of the reservoir.
That s when we drill a secondary wellbore off the original known as sidetrack to
bypass the problem or hit a new target. So why use directional drilling? One key
benefit is increased access to oil and gas reservoirs that were previously unreachable with
traditional methods. It also reduces the number of drilling sites needed, which means less surface
disturbance and a smaller environmental footprint. In fact, with just one rig,
we can drill multiple wells radiating outwards, making it more efficient and cost-effective. This
makes directional drilling particularly useful in urban areas or environmentally sensitive
regions where surface drilling is limited. Of course, directional drilling isn't without
its challenges. Maintaining wellbore stability while drilling at different angles can be tricky,
and downhole equipment needs to be extremely durable to withstand high
pressures and temperatures. But with advancements in automation and AI-driven drilling technologies,
the future of directional drilling looks bright. So, that s a quick look at how directional
drilling is revolutionizing the oil and gas industry! It s efficient,
cost-effective, and helps us unlock oil and gas reserves that were once out of reach.
If you enjoyed this video, don t forget to like, subscribe, and hit that notification
bell so you don t miss out on our future content. Let us know in the comments what
other oil and gas topics you d like to explore next. Thanks for watching.

metadata.title: The Marcellus Shale Lecture Series: Greg Sovas on Permitting and Regulation (April 21)
metadata.author: UBCFA - University at Buffalo Center for the Arts
metadata.shortDescription:
The Marcellus Shale Lecture Series will provide an educational program organized around the theme of unconventional gas drilling in New York State.  Specific topics have been chosen to emphasize the facts of the gas industry, and its relationship to the economy and environment of New York State.  The series is designed to provide an objective presentation of the nature of unconventional gas drilling, regulation, and potential socioeconomic and environmental impact.
 
The goal of the series is to bring high-profile speakers to UB who are known experts in the different aspects of the oil and gas industry globally, and of the unconventional gas industry here in New York State. The speakers will share information to help provide the basis for rational discussion on environmentally responsible unconventional gas exploration and extraction in New York. The series is made up of two subseries: 1. General Overview and Global Context for Gas Drilling in New York; and 2. Specifics of Unconventional Gas Exploration and Extraction: Geology, Land Use, Legal Issues, and Environmental Impacts.
 
Lawmakers, property owners, industrialists, environmentalists, faculty, students and concerned citizens are all invited to attend all the lectures.  The series is offered free of charge.

metadata.title: Chesapeake Energy horizontal drilling method | Oil & Gas Industry
metadata.author: Oil & Gas Industry VDA

segments.text: After the well site has been carefully
prepared to meet environmental health
and safety standards, drilling can
begin.
This is an intricate operation requiring
a well-planned infrastructure, a variety
of processes, and expert well-trained
specialists are used to bring natural
gas to the surface. Chesapeake works
with these experts during every aspect
of the project while strictly adhering
to all individual state regulations.
During the drilling process, the rig is
in constant operation 24 hours a day, 7
days a week for approximately 21 to 28
days.
As an added precaution in some areas, a
protective mat covers 2/3 of the pad
site.
Utilizing heavy-duty industrial-strength
drill bits, a typical well is drilled in
several stages starting with a
large-diameter drill bit and then
successively smaller drill bits as the
drilling is advanced.
After drilling each portion of the well,
nested steel protective casing is
cemented into place.
This will protect ground water and
maintain the integrity of the well.
Initially, and prior to moving in the
drilling rig, a large-diameter hole is
drilled for the first 50 to 80 ft.
Conductor casing is then cemented into
place, stabilizing the ground around the
drilling rig and wellhead, and isolating
the well from most private water wells.
In the Marcellus area, the fresh water
zone extends to approximately 800 ft
below ground.
The fresh water zone consists of porous
sandstone and rock strata containing
water within the pore space of the rock.
Chesapeake utilizes air drilling until
the hole is advanced to an average of
100 to 200 ft below the base of the
fresh water zone.
This provides added protection to the
fresh water zone.
A series of compressors and boosters
generate the air that is used to lift
the rock cuttings and fresh water into
steel bins.
The rock cuttings are then disposed of
within state guidelines and permits.
The drilling equipment is retracted to
the surface and stored for the second
stage of drilling.
To protect the integrity of the hole and
to protect the surrounding deep
freshwater zone,
a second layer of steel casing, called
surface casing, is installed and
cemented inside the newly drilled hole
and conductor casing.
Cement is pumped down through the
surface casing and up along the sides of
the well to provide a proper seal. This
completely isolates the well from the
deepest of private or municipal water
wells.
A blowout preventer is installed after
the surface casing has been cemented.
The blowout preventer is a series of
high-pressure safety valves and seals
attached to the top of the casing to
control well pressure and prevent
surface releases.
Next, a small drilling assembly is
passed down through the surface casing.
At the bottom of the casing, the bit
drills through the float equipment and
cement, continuing its journey to the
natural gas target area, as deep as
8,000 ft below the surface.
The drilling method employed below the
surface casing uses drilling mud, which
is a non-hazardous mixture based on
bentonite clay or synthetic thickeners.
In addition to lifting the rock cuttings
out of the hole, drilling mud also helps
to stabilize the hole, cool the drill
bit, and control down hole pressure.
A few hundred feet above the target
shale, the drilling assembly comes to a
stop.
The entire string is retracted to the
surface to adjust the drilling assembly
and install a special drilling tool.
This tool allows Chesapeake to gradually
turn the drill bit until a horizontal
plane is reached.
The remainder of the well is drilled in
this horizontal plane while in contact
with the gas-producing shale.
Drilling continues horizontally through
the shale at lengths greater than 4,000
ft from the point where it entered the
formation.
Once drilling is completed, the
equipment is retracted to the surface.
Then, a smaller-diameter casing, called
production casing, is installed
throughout the total length of the well.
The production casing is cemented and
secured in place by pumping cement down
through the end of the casing. Depending
on regional geologic conditions, the
cement is pumped around the outside
casing wall to approximately 2,500 ft
above the producing shale formation or
to the surface.
The cement creates a seal to ensure that
formation fluids can only be produced
via the production casing. After each
layer of casing is installed, the well
is pressure tested to ensure its
integrity for continued drilling.
A cross-section of the well below
surface reveals several protective
layers:
cement, conductor casing, cement,
surface casing, drilling mud, production
casing, and then production tubing,
through which the produced gas and water
will flow.
Seven layers of protection.
Horizontal drilling offers many
advantages when compared to vertical
drilling.
Since horizontal wells contact more of
the gas-producing shale,
fewer wells are needed to optimally
develop a gas field.
Multiple wells can be drilled from the
same pad sites.
For example, development of a 1,280-acre
tract of land using conventional
vertical drilling techniques could
require as many as 32 vertical wells,
with each having its own pad site.
However, one multi-well pad site with
horizontal wells can effectively recover
the same natural gas reserves from the
1,280 acre tract of land
while reducing the overall surface
disturbance by 90%.

metadata.title: Oil and Gas Division Orders
metadata.author: Blue Mesa Minerals
metadata.shortDescription:
Division orders are a legal document, an agreement between the operator and the mineral owner about what you own to ensure accurate royalty revenue.  

There are a couple of pitfalls to watch out for, particularly:

1. Make sure the info is 100% accurate.
2. Ensure you understand and agree with the terms before signing.  

When in doubt, use the NADOA Model Form:
https://nadoa.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/11/div_ord.pdf

Free Mineral Management Spreadsheet:
https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1YFzqPEr97OJkF8Zh7MSBmun6Vc9WjlTddd4IjezBU58/copy

Learn more or request an offer at Blue Mesa Minerals: 
https://bluemesaminerals.com/

metadata.title: Don’t Sign that Division Order!
metadata.author: Richard Winblad
metadata.shortDescription:
Oil and gas mineral owners are often asked to sign a Division Order once there is production from an Oklahoma oil well.  This contains information about the owner and the well.  It also asks the mineral owner to verify information and imposes conditions not required by law.

Learn more here:
https://winbladlaw.com/division-order/

This video pertains to wells in Oklahoma and other states have different laws.

This is not legal advice and does not create an attorney client relationship.

The video discusses:
What is a Division Order?
Is the NADOA Model Division Order Okay?
What is the Decimal Interest Number?
Why Shouldn’t I Certify the Decimal Interest?
What should you send instead of a Division Order?
What if the Company Doesn’t Pay?
Can I refuse to return a Division Order?

metadata.title: What Your Decimal Interest Means (and How to Check It)
metadata.author: Royalty Clerk
metadata.shortDescription:
That long number on your royalty stub decides every dollar you are paid. Here is where it comes from, and how to check it.

Your decimal interest is your royalty fraction times your net mineral acres, divided by the acres in the unit. See how the number is built, why a small error adds up every month, and how to rebuild yours from your lease.

Read the full guide: https://royaltyclerk.com/learn/what-your-decimal-interest-means?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=what-does-your-decimal-interest-mean&utm_content=guide
Try the free decimal interest calculator: https://royaltyclerk.com/tools/decimal-interest-calculator?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=what-does-your-decimal-interest-mean&utm_content=tool
Look up any Texas lease: https://royaltyclerk.com/texas-lease-lookup?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=what-does-your-decimal-interest-mean&utm_content=lease-lookup

Chapters
0:00 One number, times everything
0:37 Three numbers build it
1:10 The royalty fraction moves it most
1:37 Royalty, override, working interest
2:07 A small error is not small
2:43 Why it changes
3:13 How to check yours
3:46 If it is off, ask in writing
4:08 What to do next

metadata.shortDescription:
💰 Converting royalty fractions to DOLLARS$

Understanding how to convert and apply the royalty decimal is one of the most important skills for a Division Order Analyst. Here's why:

- Oil and gas revenue is paid based on the ownership decimal, not the fraction. Being able to convert fractional interests (e.g., 1/8, 3/16, 1/5) into decimal form (e.g., 0.125, 0.1875, 0.20) is essential for accurate payment.
- Analysts use the royalty decimal to multiply by monthly production volumes and prices to determine the correct royalty payment amount.
- A small mistake in decimal placement can lead to underpayment or overpayment, both of which can result in financial disputes or legal issues.
- This tutorial will walk you through the process and give you a solid foundation for calculating royalty payments using correctly and confidently.

metadata.title: How Oil Well Royalties Work: Income, Decline Curves, Taxes & Risks
metadata.author: Mr. Business
metadata.shortDescription:
Ever wondered how people earn money from an oil well they don’t drill, operate, or pay to maintain? In this video, we break down the real economics of owning an oil and gas royalty interest, using simple language and hypothetical numbers.

You’ll learn:
✔ What a royalty interest is and how it differs from working interest and mineral rights
✔ How a royalty check is calculated step by step (net revenue interest, royalty rate, production, and price)
✔ Why oil wells decline over time and what that means for your income
✔ How oil prices, deductions, and operators affect royalty payments
✔ How royalty income is taxed, including the depletion allowance
✔ What to check before buying a royalty (title, lease, production history, operator)
✔ The real risks, including price swings, declining production, and scams

Chapters:
0:00 Intro: how royalty income works
2:00 What is a royalty interest?
5:00 Royalty vs. working interest vs. mineral rights
8:30 How a royalty check is calculated
13:00 The decline curve explained
17:00 Oil prices, deductions & operator risk
19:30 Taxes and depletion
21:30 Buying a royalty: pricing & due diligence
23:00 The real risks
24:15 Final thoughts

If this was helpful, like the video and subscribe for more plain-English breakdowns of real-world assets and income streams. Tell me in the comments what topic you want next.

Disclaimer: This video is for educational and informational purposes only. It is not financial, legal, or tax advice, and it is not an offer or recommendation to buy or sell any security or property interest. All examples are hypothetical and do not represent actual results. Oil and gas investments involve substantial risk, including the possible loss of all invested capital. Consult a qualified financial advisor, attorney, and tax professional before making any investment decisions.

segments.text: Imagine this, a company drills an oil

didn't pay for the drilling rig, you
didn't hire the crew, you didn't write a
check for the pipe, the pumps, or the

up in your mailbox or a deposit lands in
your bank account because oil is flowing
out of the ground beneath that land.
That is the basic idea behind an oil and
gas royalty interest. And for
generations of American families,
especially in places like Texas,
Oklahoma, North Dakota, and
Pennsylvania, it has been one of the
quietest and most misunderstood ways
that wealth is built and passed down.
But here's the thing. Royalties are also
surrounded by a lot of hype and a lot of
half-truths. Some people make them sound
like free money machines. Others dismiss
them as a gamble you should never touch.
The truth sits somewhere in the middle
and it comes down to economics, how the
money is calculated, how the income
changes over time, what gets deducted,

ownership, how a royalty check is

nothing here is personalized advice or a

including the possible loss of your
entire investment. Always do your own

professionals before making financial
decisions.
All right, let's get into it. Let's
start with the foundation. To understand
royalties, you first need to understand
how ownership of oil and gas works in
the United States. In most countries,
the government owns the minerals under
the ground. The United States is
different. Here, private individuals can
own the minerals beneath their land.
That ownership is often called the
mineral estate. And one of the unique
features of American law is that the
surface of the land and the minerals
underneath it can be owned by different
people. So, someone might own a ranch on
top while a completely different family
owns the oil and gas rights below. This
happens because over the last century or
so, landowners sold or kept the mineral
rights separately when they sold the
surface.
Now, if you own the minerals, you have
the right to lease them to an oil
company. A company that wants to drill
will sign what is called an oil and gas
lease.
In that lease, the mineral owner
typically receives two main things.
First, a bonus payment. That is an
upfront payment often calculated per
acre for signing the lease. Second, a
royalty. This is the share of production
the mineral owner keeps for the life of
the lease. A common royalty rate has
historically been 1/8, which is 12 and
1/2%. In more competitive areas in

20%, 25%, or even higher.
Here is the key point. The royalty owner

understand the different types of
interests because people mix these up
constantly, and the differences matter a
lot for the economics. There are a few
terms you will hear over and over. Let's
define them in plain English.
Mineral rights. This is the ownership of
the oil, gas, and other minerals under
the ground. Think of this as owning the
underlying asset. A mineral owner can
lease the rights to an operator, and
that lease is what creates the royalty.
Royalty interest. This is the right to
receive a percentage of production
revenue free of the costs of drilling
and operating the well. When people say
they own royalties, they usually mean
either they own minerals that are under
lease, or they have purchased a royalty
interest directly.
Working interest. This is very
different. A working interest owner pays
their share of the costs. That means
drilling, completing, and operating the
well. In return, they receive a larger
share of the revenue. If the well is a
big success, working interest owners can
earn very high returns. If the well is a
dry hole or costs more than expected,
they can lose a lot of money, and they
may be asked to pay additional costs.
Working interest is a much higher risk,
higher reward position, and it is
usually pursued by companies or
experienced high net worth investors.
Overriding royalty interest, often
called an ORRI. This is a royalty-like
interest that is carved out of the
working interest, usually created for a
geologist, a landman, or a company that
put a deal together. It is also free of
drilling and operating costs, but it
only lasts as long as the underlying
lease does.

royalty and working interest? Costs and
risk. Imagine a well costs $8 million to

owner who holds a
working interest would need to
contribute roughly $800,000
before they see a dime of revenue. A
